questions.title: Knapsack: an FPTAS with a full bit-complexity argument
questions.prompt: Construct the profit-scaling algorithm from scratch. Prove feasibility, the multiplicative guarantee and polynomial bit complexity. Explain why a DP polynomial in the numerical capacity is insufficient.
guide: For every feasible item, pᵢ≤Pmax≤OPT. Hence total scaled profit is at most n²/ε, so the basic DP has O(n³/ε) transitions.
For the optimum set O, K∑O p′ᵢ≥∑O pᵢ−|O|K≥OPT−εPmax. Optimality in the scaled DP and pᵢ≥Kp′ᵢ transfer this bound to the output.
Weights and profits are represented in binary; arithmetic on their sums uses polynomially many bits. If no feasible positive-profit item remains, return the empty solution.
questions.followup: Which implication would fail first if the main hypothesis were removed? Give an explicit obstruction.
questions.deliverable: A complete blackboard argument with definitions, every central implication, and explicit bounds or resource accounting.

questions.title: Scheduling schemes: large jobs, rounded types, configurations
questions.prompt: Design a dual-approximation feasibility test for a proposed T. Bound the number of large-job types and configurations, prove the rounding loss and small-job insertion bound, then state exactly which parameters are fixed for polynomial time.
guide: If pᵢ>εT, a T-load machine has fewer than 1/ε such jobs. Rounding to multiples of ε²T increases its large-job load by at most εT.
A machine configuration records counts of rounded types, not item identities. With ε fixed, the family of configurations is bounded independently of n.

If a small job of length at most εT is placed last, its start time is at most total load/m≤T whenever a T-schedule exists; its completion is at most (1+ε)T. Combine this with the rounding slack and rescale the internal ε.

questions.title: Bin packing: linear grouping and the additive term
questions.prompt: Reconstruct the linear-grouping injection that compares the rounded instance with OPT. Derive an asymptotic (1+O(ε))OPT+O(1) bound. Then prove why an absolute ratio below 3/2 would solve a two-bin partition decision problem.
guide: Rounding one block upward can be charged to the preceding block’s larger items; explicitly match items between adjacent blocks. The largest block is treated separately.
If a new bin is opened while placing an item smaller than ε, the earlier bins have load above 1−ε. Their count is controlled by total size/(1−ε).

For a partition instance of total size 2 with each item at most 1, OPT=2 exactly when a two-bin packing exists. An absolute ratio strictly below 3/2 must output an integer number of bins below 3 on YES instances.

questions.title: Random and biased assignments; derandomization
questions.prompt: Give a weighted MAX-SAT instance with both unit and long clauses. Compute the conditional-expectation update exactly, derive the length-dependent ratio, and explain the limitation of one common biased coin when negative literals are present.
guide: For independent marginals yᵢ, a clause fails with probability ∏positive(1−yᵢ)∏negative yᵢ. The conditional expression drops assigned false literals and becomes zero failure once a literal is true.
At a fair next bit, E[X|prefix] is the average of its two child expectations; choose a child at least as large. Recompute clause contributions in polynomial time.
A common bias improves positive unit clauses while harming negative ones. A guarantee must analyze the actual literal pattern; it cannot simply substitute p into 1−(1−p)^k for every clause.

questions.title: MAX-SAT rounding: recover 1−1/e and 3/4
questions.prompt: Derive the 1−1/e factor from the clause LP. Prove a 3/4 factor by comparing the better of fair and LP assignments, including the exceptional unit-clause case. Identify why averaging two global ratios loses the sharper bound.
guide: For k literals, AM–GM bounds failure by (1−z/k)^k, so success is at least [1−(1−1/k)^k]z for z∈[0,1]. This is at least (1−1/e)z.
The fair assignment gives at least (1−2^−k)z. Averaging with LP rounding gives 3/4 for k=1, at least 3/4 for k=2, and at least 3/4 for k≥3 using (1−2^−k)+(1−1/e)≥3/2.
The maximum of the two final objective values is at least their average for each joint outcome. For nonlinear rounding, verify the section’s condition on f separately instead of assuming f(y)=y.

questions.title: Prize-collecting Steiner tree: threshold rounding
questions.prompt: Rebuild the randomized-threshold analysis, including the integral that bounds E[1/α]. Show why selecting one arbitrary threshold need not satisfy both the connection-cost and penalty bounds.
guide: For a retained terminal, scaling the fractional connection vector by 1/α yields a feasible connection relaxation. Applying the available tree rounding bound gives a cost proportional to 1/α.
A terminal’s penalty contribution is its penalty multiplied by its exclusion probability. Compute this probability from its LP variable and the support of α.
The book’s optimized balance yields the factor (1−e^−1/2)^−1. The logarithm comes from integrating 1/α; replacing the distribution with its mean is invalid because E[1/α]≠1/E[α].

questions.title: Release-date scheduling: randomized α-points
questions.prompt: Specify the time-indexed LP and its completion-time expression. Prove that the rounded schedule respects release dates. Explain which random variable is integrated in the factor-2 analysis and how pseudo-polynomial time is addressed.
guide: A job contributes exactly pⱼ units of processing after rⱼ; machine capacity is at most one per slot. The average fractional processing time plus pⱼ/2 lower-bounds the integral completion time.
An α-point is the time by which α of the job’s fractional processing has accumulated. It is not a random independent machine choice.

The analysis bounds earlier ordered workload through the fractional prefix volumes, integrates over α, and sums with weights. A polynomial implementation needs time compression or a polynomially bounded horizon reduction, not merely a DP indexed by a binary-encoded horizon.

questions.title: Chernoff bounds and randomized unsplittable routing
questions.prompt: Derive the multiplicative Chernoff bound from the MGF, then use it to prove an O(log n/log log n) congestion bound when fractional congestion is constant. Explain the different regime W*=Ω(log n).
guide: For X=∑Xᵢ with independent Bernoulli variables, E[e^(tX)]≤exp(μ(e^t−1)); minimizing at e^t=a/μ gives Pr[X≥a]≤(eμ/a)^a for a≥μ.
With μ=O(1), choose a=C log n/log log n. The logarithm of the failure probability is −a log(a/(eμ)); a sufficiently large C absorbs a polynomial number of edges.
If μ≥c log n, a constant multiplicative increase already gives inverse-polynomial failure. Independence is across commodities; edge loads are not independent of one another and do not need to be.

questions.title: Gram matrices and the exact MAX-CUT ratio
questions.prompt: Derive the SDP and the angle probability without invoking the algorithm’s name. Characterize an interior minimizer of the ratio. Explain why negative edge weights invalidate this edgewise summation proof.
guide: For integral signs, Xᵢⱼ=sᵢsⱼ; dropping rank one leaves X≽0 and Xᵢᵢ=1. The relaxed objective is an upper bound for maximization.
Rotational symmetry reduces an edge to a plane; the separating normal directions occupy angular measure 2θ out of 2π, giving θ/π.
The stationary equation is 1−cos θ=θ sin θ. Compare both sides edgewise; multiplication by a negative weight reverses an inequality, so the standard nonnegative-weight hypothesis matters.

questions.title: IP ⊆ PSPACE: private information changes the recurrence
questions.prompt: Repair the naive max/average game-tree proof for a private-coin verifier. Give a one-bit example where E[max] differs from max[E]. Explain how conditional random-tape weights and exact acceptance numerators can be recomputed in polynomial space.
guide: Let a hidden fair bit be b and accept when the prover guesses b. A legal prover succeeds with probability 1/2, whereas maximizing separately after revealing b gives E[max]=1.

The strategy depends on the observed transcript, not on an unobserved private verifier configuration. Enumerate consistent random tapes to compute transition probabilities; do not give their identities to the maximization.

A useful integer recurrence is F(h)=the maximum number of accepting tapes consistent with public history h. At a prover move take max_y F(hy); at a visible verifier message sum F(hz) over the messages z, whose consistent-tape sets partition the current set. At a terminal history, enumerate and count accepting consistent tapes.

With a polynomial bound R on all private random bits, each F is at most 2^R and uses O(R) bits. The transcript, loop counters and recursive stack all have polynomial size. The root value divided by 2^R is the optimal legal acceptance probability.

questions.title: Kim–Vu: derivative expectations matter
questions.prompt: For triangle count in G(n,p), compute the mean and the first-, second-, and third-derivative expectation scales. Identify the dense and sparse regimes in the Kim–Vu parameters and explain why substituting only μ into a Chernoff formula is invalid.

questions.title: Shannon coding: random errors versus worst-case errors
questions.prompt: Prove a random-coding achievability bound at rate R<1−H₂(p). Separate the typical-error event from confusion with another codeword. Contrast this with the minimum-distance requirement for correcting every pattern of t adversarial errors.

questions.title: Tenure Game: the exact dyadic threshold
questions.prompt: Prove both directions of the threshold and the dyadic splitting lemma. Explain the induction that glues two equal-level chips into one higher chip, including the equality case W=1.
guide: Promotion from i to i−1 doubles the promoted chip’s weight; deletion removes the other side, so Wy+Wn=2W. Carole can maintain W<1, which excludes a level-zero chip.
If W≥1, there are two chips at some level unless the total is below one. Glue two level-i chips into one level-(i−1) chip and induct to obtain a split with both parts of weight at least 1/2.
Paul chooses that split, so either successor has weight at least one. The game ends in finitely many promotions, and it cannot end with no chips.

questions.prompt: Prove the O(√(n ln n)) upper bound against an adaptive Pusher. Explain the quantifier step from a random strategy with positive success probability against every fixed opponent strategy to a deterministic winning strategy. State what extra work yields the matching lower bound.

questions.title: Entropy: chain rule, conditioning and extremal families
questions.prompt: Prove |F|≤2^(∑H₂(pᵢ)) when pᵢ is the fraction of members containing coordinate i. Characterize equality, including the distinction between independent Bernoulli coordinates and a uniform distribution on an arbitrary family.
guide: For a uniform member X of F, H(X)=log₂|F|. Chain rule and conditioning give H(X)≤∑H(Xᵢ)=∑H₂(pᵢ).
Equality in subadditivity requires mutual independence of coordinates with nontrivial entropy. Uniformity on F then restricts F to a Cartesian product of its allowed coordinate values.
A small family may have unbiased individual coordinates and strong dependence; marginal entropies alone can substantially overcount its true logarithmic size.

questions.title: Dense-graph testing and the 3-coloring restriction tree
questions.prompt: Reconstruct the restriction-tree proof for testing 3-colorability. Explain why following only one guessed partial coloring is unsound. Derive how farness creates many restricting vertices and how depth bounds lead to a constant-size sample.
guide: A sampled graph is non-3-colorable only when every branch of possible partial colorings fails. A failed greedy coloring on one branch is not a certificate.
The potential is total remaining feasible-list size, initially at most 3n. A restricting vertex removes Ω(εn) list entries, giving depth O(1/ε).

Farness prevents all vertices from having harmless extensions: otherwise a global coloring with few monochromatic edges could be repaired cheaply. Chernoff bounds and a union bound over a bounded ternary tree finish the sample analysis.

questions.title: Triangle removal: a structural lemma becomes a tester
questions.prompt: Prove the sampling theorem assuming the triangle-removal lemma, with the correct ordered-versus-unordered normalization. Then outline the regularity/counting proof and explain why seeing no triangle is not evidence that only few edits are needed without the farness promise.
guide: If T≥δn³ unordered triangles, a uniform unordered triple is a triangle with probability T/C(n,3), asymptotically at least 6δ. The exact ratio is the quantity to use on finite n.
After q independent triple samples, miss probability is (1−T/C(n,3))^q≤exp(−qT/C(n,3)); q=O(1/δ) gives constant soundness.
Only rejection is a certificate. The lemma supplies δ(ε), whose dependence can be extremely poor; constant query complexity in n does not mean practical efficiency in ε.

questions.title: Dominance pruning without losing a continuation
questions.prompt: For 0–1 knapsack with positive integer weights and profits, maintain attainable pairs (weight,profit) after each prefix. Prove that deleting a pair dominated by another pair preserves an optimum after every possible suffix. Give an instance with exponentially many undominated pairs.
guide: If (w,p) is dominated by (w′,p′), where w′≤w and p′≥p, every suffix subset feasible after the first pair is feasible after the second and obtains at least the same profit. The two prefix witnesses use only already processed items, so appending the identical suffix causes no item reuse. This proves the invariant by induction.

Take w_i=p_i=2^i for i=0,…,n−1 and capacity 2^n−1. Every subset gives a different pair (s,s); lower weight always means lower profit. All 2^n pairs survive. Dominance alone gives an exact algorithm, but it does not establish polynomial running time in the binary input length.
questions.followup: How does the argument change if there is also a cardinality bound? State which states may safely dominate one another.
questions.deliverable: A continuation lemma, an induction, and an exponential frontier family.

questions.title: Scale using a computable half-optimum certificate
questions.prompt: For positive-profit knapsack, first discard overweight items. Solve its fractional relaxation by density order, and let G be the better of the whole-item greedy prefix and the highest-profit feasible item. Prove G≤OPT≤2G, then design profit scaling with K=εG/n and bound the DP range.
guide: The fractional optimum consists of a feasible whole prefix plus at most one fractional item. Its value is at most the prefix profit plus the full profit of that boundary item, both at most G. If all items fit, the prefix is optimal. Thus G is a feasible lower bound and the fractional solution certifies OPT≤2G.

Every surviving item has profit at most G, so each floor-scaled profit is at most n/ε and the usual state range is O(n²/ε). For an optimum O, rounding loses at most |O|K≤εG≤εOPT. Retain the minimum original weight per scaled total to obtain feasibility. The certificate uses a fractional upper bound and a feasible lower bound in different directions.
questions.followup: Can the certificate improve the approximation loss if the optimum uses at most k items?
questions.deliverable: A complete scaling algorithm with its certificate and state count.

questions.title: An FPTAS with an exact cardinality budget
questions.prompt: Given integer k≤n, maximize nonnegative profit subject to total weight≤B and at most k selected items. Construct an FPTAS with loss at most εOPT using a count dimension. State its running time and handle the case k=0.
guide: For k≥1 remove overweight items and let P be the largest remaining positive profit. A singleton is feasible, so P≤OPT. Set K=εP/k. A DP indexed by processed prefix, selected count c≤k, and scaled profit q stores the minimum original weight. Use only previous-prefix states for a 0–1 transition.

Each scaled item profit is at most k/ε; a feasible state has q≤k²/ε. A direct implementation therefore uses O(nk³/ε) transitions and O(k³/ε) memory. The optimum loses at most kK, and the DP maximizes the rounded objective within both exact constraints. For k=0 or no positive feasible item, return the empty set.

questions.title: Rounding weights buys capacity rather than profit
questions.prompt: Let B>0 and δ∈(0,1). Set h=δB/n, w′_i=floor(w_i/h), and B′=floor(B/h). Maximize exact profit among subsets of scaled weight at most B′. Prove profit at least OPT and original weight at most (1+δ)B. Contrast this bicriteria guarantee with a feasible FPTAS.
guide: Every originally feasible subset has sum floor(w_i/h)≤floor(sum w_i/h)≤B′, so the rounded optimum contains an originally optimal candidate. For the returned set S, sum w_i<h sum w′_i+|S|h≤B+n h=(1+δ)B. This is an upper capacity bound, while profit is compared in the favorable direction.

After filtering w_i>B when benchmarking the original problem, B′=O(n/δ), so an exact-profit DP over rounded weight is polynomial in n and 1/δ with binary profit arithmetic. The output may exceed B, and no multiplicative profit statement repairs that violation. A one-item example with weight just above B demonstrates why original feasibility must be reported separately.
questions.followup: What guarantee follows if ceilings replace floors and the capacity remains B′?
questions.deliverable: A bicriteria theorem with a precise feasibility limitation.

questions.title: Rational data and exact scaling comparisons
questions.prompt: Assume all weights, profits, B and ε are positive binary-encoded rationals of total encoding length L. Show that profit scaling can be implemented in time polynomial in L,n,1/ε without expanding a DP indexed by a common denominator. Bound the bit lengths of sums and floor computations.
guide: A sum of at most n input rationals can be represented over the product of their denominators. The product has bit length at most the sum of input denominator lengths, hence O(L); numerator growth adds only polynomially many bits. Reduced fractions can be used, but reduction is not needed to obtain this upper bound.

Compute floor(p_i/K) by integer multiplication and division of rational numerators and denominators. This operation has polynomial bit complexity, and the scaled-profit range remains O(n²/ε) after infeasible items are discarded. Store exact rational weights in the DP and compare them by cross multiplication. Clearing denominators is safe arithmetic, but a weight DP of numerical capacity equal to that denominator product may be exponentially long.

questions.deliverable: A bit-complexity audit of the scaling algorithm.

questions.title: Research exercise: an approximate Pareto frontier
questions.prompt: Construct a prefix algorithm that trims positive-profit states into intervals [(1+δ)^j,(1+δ)^(j+1)), retaining minimum weight in each interval and keeping the empty state. With δ=ε/(2n), prove a (1−ε) guarantee. Compare frontier sizes with exact dominance pruning on instances n≤24; exact enumeration is the baseline.
guide: After adding an item from the previous prefix, trimming replaces a state by one with no greater weight and profit greater than its profit divided by 1+δ. Inductively each exact prefix witness has a retained witness of no larger weight and at least its profit divided by (1+δ)^i. At i=n, (1+δ)^n≤e^(ε/2)≤1/(1−ε) for 0<ε<1.

The number of occupied profit intervals is O((n/ε) log(nPmax/Pmin)), polynomial in the rational encoding length and 1/ε. Generate interval boundaries with exact rational arithmetic and preserve a separate zero-profit state. Report frontier counts and returned value against enumeration; any weight violation or ratio below 1−ε is a failure. This is a study of a specified approximation technique, not a claim of novelty.
questions.followup: Can one use one final trimming step instead of n stages without losing polynomial space?

questions.title: Research exercise: quantify worst-case rounding loss
questions.prompt: Fix n≤20 and rational ε. Investigate floor-profit scaling with K=εPmax/n under adversarial tie breaking. Enumerate all feasible subsets for integer instances with weights≤12 and profits≤30, then compare its actual loss with nK and |O|K. Prove a universal bound using the smaller cardinality of an optimal witness.
guide: For any optimal O, scaled optimality gives p(S)≥Kp′(S)≥Kp′(O)>OPT−|O|K, with a non-strict bound covering integral rounding boundaries. If several original optima exist, choose one with minimum cardinality to sharpen the certificate. The bound concerns the witness O and does not require the returned solution to have the same count.

Group subsets by scaled profit and keep the least original profit among feasible scaled maximizers to model worst tie breaking. Record the ratio loss/(|O|K), rather than expecting a random solver to find bad ties. The baseline is exhaustive optimization in both objectives. A counterexample to the proved inequality is a failed implementation or proof; absence of a near-tight example is reported as inconclusive rather than a new theorem.

questions.title: The list-scheduling barrier before rounding
questions.prompt: For m≥2 identical machines, prove list scheduling has ratio at most 2−1/m. Then give a job order attaining that ratio using m(m−1) unit jobs followed by one job of length m. Explain why a PTAS must exploit more information than the next least-loaded machine.
guide: Let j be the last completing job and s its start time. At its assignment every machine has load at least s, so ms≤sum p_i−p_j. Consequently Cmax≤sum p_i/m+(1−1/m)p_j≤(2−1/m)OPT, using both total-load and largest-job lower bounds.

The unit jobs leave every machine at load m−1. The final job creates makespan 2m−1. An optimum places the long job alone and distributes the m(m−1) unit jobs as m units on each of the remaining m−1 machines, so OPT=m. The family is exact for every m, rather than an asymptotic assertion hiding an ordering condition.
questions.followup: Why does ordering jobs by nonincreasing size invalidate this particular bad example?
questions.deliverable: A sharp proof and a matching parameterized instance.

questions.title: A fixed-machine approximation scheme by load states
questions.prompt: For fixed m and positive integer processing times, let L=max(max p_j,sum p_j/m), h=εL/n, and round each job down to multiples of h. Build an exact DP over m−1 rounded machine loads and prove the reconstructed schedule has makespan at most (1+ε)OPT.
guide: Use states recording the first m−1 loads after a job prefix; the final machine load is determined by the rounded prefix total. A transition assigns the next rounded job to any machine. All rounded loads are at most sum p_j/h≤mn/ε, so the number of states is polynomial for fixed m.

An optimum original schedule remains a rounded schedule of makespan at most OPT. The DP finds a rounded optimum no worse than this. Restoring original times increases any one machine by less than nh=εL≤εOPT. The exponent depends on m, so this construction alone does not give a uniform PTAS when m belongs to the input.
questions.followup: How does symmetry reduction by sorting machine loads affect reconstruction?
questions.deliverable: An explicit recurrence and the dependence of its exponent on m.

questions.title: A separating certificate for rounded configurations
questions.prompt: At target T=1, suppose jobs have sizes 2/5 and 3/5, with counts a and b and m machines. Enumerate maximal feasible configurations and derive necessary and sufficient inequalities on a,b,m for a packing. Include an explicit reconstruction and compare with the total-load bound.
guide: A machine can hold either two 2/5 jobs or one of each type or one 3/5 job; no machine holds two 3/5 jobs. Thus b≤m is necessary. Use b bins for the larger jobs, put min(a,b) smaller jobs beside them, then pair any remaining smaller jobs in unused bins. Feasibility is equivalent to b+ceil(max(0,a−b)/2)≤m.

Equivalently b≤m and a+b≤2m, for integer a,b. These conditions are also sufficient by the construction. Total load alone is weaker: m=2,a=0,b=3 has load 9/5≤2 but needs three bins. The count inequalities are certificates tied to the feasible configuration set, rather than an unexplained LP feasibility claim.
questions.followup: Add jobs of size 1/5 and derive the new residual-capacity conditions.
questions.deliverable: All maximal configurations, an exact characterization, and a counterexample to volume sufficiency.

questions.title: Why the makespan PTAS need not be fully polynomial
questions.prompt: Assume the standard strong NP-completeness of 3-PARTITION with 3m integer values in (B/4,B/2) summing to mB, where B is polynomially bounded. Prove that an FPTAS for makespan on an input number m of identical machines would imply P=NP. Choose ε explicitly.
guide: Map each value to a job and use m machines. The total-load lower bound is B. A makespan-B schedule exists exactly when each machine receives a triple summing to B, because the strict size bounds force three jobs per machine. In a NO instance every schedule has integral makespan at least B+1.

Run an assumed FPTAS with ε=1/(2B). In a YES instance it returns makespan at most B+1/2, hence at most B by integrality; in a NO instance no such schedule exists. Since B is polynomially bounded on the strongly hard family, 1/ε is polynomial. The argument uses strong hardness essentially and does not contradict the fixed-m construction.
questions.followup: Why does the same ε choice fail to contradict an FPTAS for ordinary binary-encoded knapsack?
questions.deliverable: A gap-preserving reduction and a runtime calculation.

questions.title: Geometric rounding and a bounded configuration universe
questions.prompt: Fix η∈(0,1/4), target T, and jobs in (ηT,T]. Round each job upward to the next value ηT(1+η)^q. Bound the number of types and configurations of load at most (1+η)T. Prove a T-schedule of the original large jobs induces a feasible rounded configuration multiset.
guide: Each rounded processing time is at most (1+η) times its original value, so a machine of original load at most T has rounded load at most (1+η)T. There are O(log(1/η)/η) types, with one additional endpoint type if necessary. Each configuration contains fewer than (1+η)/η jobs.

A coarse bound on the number of count vectors is (1+floor((1+η)/η))^d, where d is the type count. This is finite as a function of η alone. A DP over remaining counts of all d types and machine count can test integral configuration feasibility in n^O(d) time. State this exponent instead of inferring an FPTAS from the bounded universe.
questions.followup: Compare this type bound with additive rounding at spacing η²T.
questions.deliverable: An upward-rounding lemma and explicit enumeration bounds.

questions.title: Research exercise: audit a configuration relaxation
questions.prompt: For T=1, enumerate rational job sizes on the grid {1/6,…,1} and count vectors with at most 18 jobs. Compare the minimum integral number of configurations with the configuration LP optimum. Use exact subset assignment as a baseline; exhibit and verify a gap or report the searched domain without claiming equality.
guide: Create a variable for each feasible type-count vector and constraints that cover every job multiplicity. Fractional solutions provide lower bounds, but rounded variable counts do not automatically use at most m machines. Verify an integral packing by writing every configuration and its multiplicity, then reconstructing the original job identities.

For each reported fractional optimum, produce a dual feasible type-price vector with the same value: every configuration must have total price at most one. This supplies a check independent of solver status. Reject any claimed gap whose certificates disagree. The investigation targets the difference between fractional and integral configurations; a finite search cannot establish that the gap is universally absent.

questions.title: Research exercise: round a sparse configuration solution
questions.prompt: For d rounded large-job types and a feasible configuration covering LP of value M, prove there is an optimal basic solution with at most d positive variables. Show that opening ceilings of these configurations uses at most M+d machines. Test this additive bound against exact integer optima for d≤4; explain why it is insufficient for a makespan PTAS with exactly m machines.
guide: The covering LP has d demand inequalities and nonnegative variables. At an extreme optimum at most d configuration variables are positive, by the standard linearly independent active-column argument. An extreme optimum exists because the positive all-one objective gives a bounded optimal face. Rounding each positive count up preserves coverage and adds less than d to the fractional objective.

Extra covered jobs can be discarded from configurations, yielding a valid assignment of every input job once. The resulting bound is on the number of machines, not the makespan on a prescribed m. For the experiment compare with an exact count-vector DP and check both coverage and machine count. Treat exceeding M+d, or silently using extra machines in an m-machine schedule, as failure.
questions.followup: Under what lower bound on M does M+d become a multiplicative (1+η) bound?
questions.deliverable: A sparse-support lemma, additive rounding theorem, and a controlled comparison.

questions.title: An additive d bound from the configuration LP
questions.prompt: Suppose bin-packing items take d distinct rational sizes in (0,1]. Enumerate all feasible configurations and prove that rounding an optimal basic configuration-LP solution upward yields at most OPT+d bins. State the assumptions needed to compute the configuration set in polynomial time.
guide: The LP minimizes the sum of configuration multiplicities subject to d coverage constraints. A basic optimum has at most d positive variables. Ceiling those variables covers all demands and uses less than LP+d≤OPT+d bins. Remove surplus copies of types and assign the actual items to obtain a valid packing.

For fixed d alone, tiny binary-encoded item sizes can permit exponentially large configuration coordinates. In the large-item setting where every size is at least η, each bin contains at most 1/η items and enumeration is bounded by (1+1/η)^d. Distinguish a proof with an explicitly supplied configuration set from an algorithm that must construct that set.
questions.followup: Can one replace strict <LP+d by an integral bound involving floor(LP)?
questions.deliverable: A rounding proof plus a precise configuration-enumeration condition.

questions.title: Volume and threshold-count bounds are complementary
questions.prompt: For every integer q≥1, prove that items larger than 1/(q+1) give the lower bound ceil(N_q/q) on bin count. Construct instances where this beats volume by a factor approaching (q+1)/q, and explain why finitely many such threshold tests still do not fully characterize feasible bins.
guide: A bin cannot contain q+1 items each strictly larger than 1/(q+1), so q·OPT≥N_q. Take N items of size 1/(q+1)+δ with δ sufficiently small that q items fit. The count bound is approximately N/q, while total volume is approximately N/(q+1), giving the claimed factor as N grows and δ decreases.

These bounds price items only through threshold counts. Three items of size 0.6 and three of size 0.4 pack in three bins. Replace the small sizes by 0.39,0.39,0.42. Volume remains three and every count N_q is unchanged, but three bins are impossible: each must hold one 0.6 item and none can hold 0.42. Four bins suffice. Even volume together with all these reciprocal-threshold counts misses this mixed-size obstruction.
questions.followup: Derive a valid dual type-price vector for sizes 0.51 and 0.26 that improves a selected single threshold bound.
questions.deliverable: The family of inequalities and an asymptotically sharp comparison.

questions.title: A complete Next-Fit analysis and sharp family
questions.prompt: Next Fit keeps only the current open bin. Prove that it uses at most 2OPT−1 bins for nonempty instances. Give an input family whose ratio tends to 2, and identify why allowing access to earlier bins changes the example.
guide: Whenever a new bin opens, its first item did not fit in the preceding bin. Hence every consecutive pair of bins has combined final load greater than one. Pair bins (1,2),(3,4),… to obtain total volume>floor(A/2), so OPT≥floor(A/2)+1. This implies A≤2OPT−1.

Use alternating items ε and 1−ε+ε², with ε chosen so each pair exceeds one but many ε items fit together. Next Fit separates nearly every item, while an optimum puts each large item in its own bin and packs all small items in o(N) additional bins when ε tends to zero sufficiently quickly. Choose ε=1/N² for N pairs to make the calculation explicit.
questions.followup: Compute the exact bin count on this family under First Fit.
questions.deliverable: A finite-instance inequality and a parameterized lower-bound family.

questions.title: Size rounding as resource augmentation
questions.prompt: Let δ∈(0,1). Suppose each item is rounded upward to a size at most (1+δ) times its original size. Prove that an optimum original packing fits in OPT bins of capacity 1+δ after rounding. Construct a family showing that the same statement with unit capacity can fail by a constant factor.
guide: Within an original bin, the rounded total is at most (1+δ) times its original total, hence at most 1+δ. This proves a capacity-augmentation result with unchanged bin count. It does not say the rounded items fit in unit bins, and scaling the rounded solution down changes the physical sizes of the original input.

Take pairs of items of original size exactly 1/2 and round them to 1/2+γ with 0<γ≤δ/2. Original OPT is n/2 for even n, while rounded OPT at unit capacity is n. Thus even arbitrarily small multiplicative size increases may double bin count. Grouping arguments avoid this discontinuity through an injection into different item identities.
questions.followup: What additional promise on bin slack would make unit-capacity rounding safe?
questions.deliverable: A bicriteria proof and a discontinuity example.

questions.title: Convert an additive guarantee into a threshold guarantee
questions.prompt: Suppose an algorithm satisfies A(I)≤(1+η)OPT(I)+C(η), with explicit positive C. For a requested ε∈(0,1), choose η and a threshold N_ε so that OPT≥N_ε implies A≤(1+ε)OPT. Explain why solving all smaller-optimum instances exactly is not an automatic polynomial repair.
guide: Set η=ε/2 and choose N_ε≥2C(ε/2)/ε. For OPT above this threshold, the additive term is at most εOPT/2. This derives the asymptotic ratio with the dependence of the large-instance threshold on ε made explicit. Rounding an integer N_ε upward causes no difficulty.

The remaining inputs can have arbitrarily many items with tiny sizes, even when OPT=2. Moreover deciding whether such a binary-encoded instance fits in two bins contains PARTITION. A threshold on optimum value is not a threshold on input length, so brute force on all small-optimum cases is not justified.
questions.followup: Under a fixed lower bound η0 on every item size, how many items can a small-optimum instance contain?

questions.title: Research exercise: optimize a grouping budget
questions.prompt: For items of size at least η, sort decreasingly and form groups of g=ceil(η²n) items. Set aside the first group and round later groups to their maxima. Prove an OPT+ceil(η²n) bound for the large-item stage using the inter-group injection, then convert it to (1+η)OPT+1. Compare group sizes with an exact packing baseline for n≤22.
guide: Match the rounded items of group j≥2 positionwise to original items in group j−1, padding the last group only by deleting unused witnesses. Every matched original item is at least as large as the rounded replacement, so the later rounded groups can be packed into the bins of an optimum original packing. The first group needs at most g extra bins.

Since all n items have size at least η, nη≤OPT. Thus g≤η²n+1≤ηOPT+1. The experiment should vary g around the theoretical value and report the distinct-type count, extra bins, and exact optimum. Failure means an invalid injection, a rounded item exceeding its matched witness, or a claimed bound violated by a certified packing instance.

questions.title: Research exercise: search for valid bin prices
questions.prompt: For sizes {1/5,2/5,3/5,4/5}, enumerate all configurations. Find nonnegative type prices λ maximizing a given count vector’s lower bound subject to every configuration having price at most one. Compare this dual bound, volume, and exact packing for count vectors of total size at most 24 items.
guide: The constraints are finite: for each count vector a with sum a_i s_i≤1, impose sum a_i λ_i≤1. Summing the price constraint over every bin proves OPT≥sum n_i λ_i. Volume is the special feasible choice λ_i=s_i, so an optimized dual must be at least as strong when computed exactly.

Use exact rational certificates and an integer count-vector DP as the baseline. Record any integrality gap as OPT/dual, retaining ceiling effects separately. A purported lower bound greater than the certified optimum, or an unenumerated feasible configuration with price above one, is a failure. This is a reproducible investigation of a known LP, with no claim that finite grid behavior settles general bin packing.

questions.title: How much independence does clause evaluation require?
questions.prompt: For a weighted CNF whose normalized clauses have width at most k, prove that k-wise independent fair bits give the same expected satisfied weight as fully independent bits. Show that pairwise independence is insufficient for width three by using a uniform even-parity triple.
guide: Each clause’s truth indicator depends on at most k distinct coordinates. A k-wise independent fair distribution has exactly the uniform distribution on that coordinate set, so its failure probability is 2^−width. Sum the expectations with nonnegative weights; independence among different clauses is not required.

For a uniform distribution on {000,011,101,110}, every pair is uniform, but Pr[x∨y∨z is false]=1/4 rather than 1/8. Thus this particular clause has expected satisfaction 3/4. The example isolates the missing third-order independence without changing any one-bit or two-bit marginal.
questions.followup: Can a k-wise independent distribution be enumerated efficiently if its support is explicitly supplied?
questions.deliverable: A locality lemma and a pairwise-independent counterexample.

questions.title: Optimize a common bias on a signed formula
questions.prompt: Consider weights A,B,C≥0 on clauses x, ¬y, and x∨y respectively, with x,y independently true with common probability p. Derive the expected value as a polynomial in p, maximize it on [0,1], and compare with choosing a deterministic assignment separately for each instance.
guide: The expectation is Ap+B(1−p)+C(2p−p²)=B+(A−B+2C)p−Cp². If C>0, the maximizing bias is the projection of (A−B+2C)/(2C) onto [0,1]. If C=0, choose an endpoint according to the sign of A−B. Include boundary cases rather than dividing by C silently.

The four deterministic assignments have values B, A+B+C, C, and A+C respectively for (0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1). Therefore the optimum is A+B+C, attained by x=1,y=0. A common bias constrains both marginals equally and can lose value even though independent variable-specific marginals can attain the optimum.
questions.followup: For A=B and C>0, quantify the common-bias loss exactly.
questions.deliverable: The optimizer formula and a correctly evaluated four-assignment table.

questions.title: A concentration bound from variable influence
questions.prompt: Let F be satisfied clause weight under independent fair variables, and let D_i be total weight of clauses containing variable i. Prove Pr[F≤E F−t]≤exp(−2t²/sum D_i²) using bounded differences. Explain why unbounded clause overlap can make expectation alone a weak high-probability certificate.
guide: Changing bit i changes only clauses incident to i, and their total possible objective change is at most D_i. Apply the bounded-differences inequality to the independent bit coordinates; no clause-indicator independence is assumed. If all D_i vanish, F is constant and the nontrivial tail probability is zero.

For M identical unit clauses x of weight one, F is either 0 or M with equal probability. Its expectation is M/2, but it does not concentrate around that value on a sublinear scale. Here D_x=M, so the denominator correctly records the large dependency. Normalization may merge duplicates into one weight-M clause without changing the phenomenon.
questions.followup: What exponent follows if every clause has weight one and every variable occurs at most d times?
questions.deliverable: An influence calculation and an overlap counterexample.

questions.title: Derandomize a correlated finite distribution
questions.prompt: You are given M Boolean assignments with rational probabilities summing to one. Their distribution need not be independent. Design a conditional-expectation procedure that fixes variables one at a time and returns satisfied weight at least the distributional mean. Give runtime and specify how zero-probability branches are handled.
guide: Maintain the surviving assignments and their original probability masses. For each next bit value with positive surviving mass, compute the weighted average objective among that child’s assignments. The parent conditional mean is the mass-weighted average of the positive children, so one child has value at least the parent. Discard a zero-mass child rather than defining a conditional expectation there.

After all coordinates are fixed, every surviving assignment is the same word and the conditional mean equals its actual objective. Evaluating all M objectives once and aggregating by prefixes gives a polynomial implementation, for example O(Mn+M·formula size) arithmetic operations. This construction preserves the supplied expectation but does not justify a full-independence clause formula for the starting distribution.
questions.followup: When is simply taking the best support assignment faster than this prefix procedure?
questions.deliverable: A distribution-independent derandomization invariant and a finite-support implementation.

questions.title: Encode a cut objective as two-literal satisfaction
questions.prompt: For each nonnegative weighted graph edge uv create the two clauses (x_u∨x_v) and (¬x_u∨¬x_v), each of weight w_uv. Prove satisfied clause weight equals total edge weight plus cut weight. Derive what a 3/4 clause-weight guarantee implies for cut weight, and explain the effect of the additive baseline.
guide: If the endpoints receive different bits, both clauses are true; if equal, exactly one is true. Summing yields SAT(x)=W+CUT(x), and OPT_SAT=W+OPT_CUT. A guarantee SAT(x)≥(3/4)(W+OPT_CUT) gives CUT(x)≥(3/4)OPT_CUT−W/4.

Since OPT_CUT≤W, this expression does not imply a 3/4 cut approximation; at OPT_CUT=W it gives only W/2. Fair assignments have expected cut W/2 and expected satisfaction 3W/2, consistent with the identity. An affine objective shift must be tracked in a reduction rather than cancelling ratios as though objectives were proportional.
questions.followup: Using OPT_CUT≥W/2, what is the weakest multiplicative ratio certified by the displayed inequality?
questions.deliverable: An exact objective identity and a ratio-transfer calculation.

questions.title: Research exercise: finite support versus clause locality
questions.prompt: For n≤8, enumerate uniform linear subspaces of F₂^n given by generator matrices of rank at most four. For clause widths k≤4, compare their worst clause-failure probability with 2^−k. The baseline is full-cube enumeration. Prove a rank criterion characterizing when every width-k marginal is uniform.
guide: Sampling a uniform generator seed gives a uniform image under any chosen set of output coordinates. That marginal is uniform on all k bits exactly when the corresponding k columns of the generator matrix have rank k. Consequently every width-at-most-k marginal is fair and independent exactly when every such column subset is linearly independent.

Enumerate both positive and negative literal patterns; checking only all-positive clauses can miss a nonuniform marginal whose missing or heavy atom lies elsewhere. Report the smallest dependent column sets and their exact violating probabilities. A rank-certified k-wise independent family with a wrong clause probability is a failure. The target is a finite characterization and experiment, not a new pseudorandom construction.

questions.title: Research exercise: certify a grid search for biases
questions.prompt: For a weighted CNF of total weight W and normalized width at most k, let f(p_1,…,p_n) be expected satisfaction under independent marginals. Thus exact Boolean optimization is the baseline and the grid should never beat it beyond numerical tolerance. Record the cost of the grid and its certified error; exceeding OPT or missing the additive bound is failure. The exercise studies certification, not a polynomial-time solution for arbitrary n.

questions.title: An exact integrality gap on all sign patterns
questions.prompt: For k≥2 take all 2^k clauses containing each of x_1,…,x_k exactly once, with every sign pattern and unit weight. Compute the Boolean optimum, the clause-LP optimum, and the value of independent rounding at y_i=1/2. Explain which k gives the strongest gap.
guide: Every assignment falsifies precisely the clause whose literals all oppose that assignment, so its value is exactly 2^k−1. The LP setting y_i=1/2,z_C=1 is feasible because each clause has literal-marginal sum k/2≥1, and it reaches the trivial upper bound 2^k.

questions.title: The extremal marginal distribution for one clause
questions.prompt: Fix a normalized clause with k≥2 literals and literal-truth marginals q_i∈[0,1] summing to z∈[0,1]. Minimize its independent-rounding success probability over these marginals. Prove the resulting function lies above its chord from z=0 to z=1, and characterize equality.
guide: Failure is product(1−q_i). At fixed sum z, AM–GM makes this product largest when all q_i=z/k; hence the minimum success is g_k(z)=1−(1−z/k)^k. For k≥2, g_k is strictly concave on (0,1), as its second derivative is negative.

Since g_k(0)=0, concavity yields g_k(z)≥z g_k(1), with strict inequality for 0<z<1. Equality in the marginal step requires equal q_i, except at the trivial zero endpoint. The two inequalities have different equality conditions, which matter when diagnosing whether an LP-rounding analysis can be tight.
questions.followup: What changes if the marginal sum exceeds one but z_C is capped at one?

references.title: Williamson–Shmoys · The Design of Approximation Algorithms · §§5.4–5.6

questions.title: Prove a concrete transformed-marginal rounding rule
questions.prompt: Set each variable true independently with probability f(y)=1/4+y/2. Prove this produces expected clause weight at least 3/4 of the standard MAX-SAT LP value. Treat unit clauses separately and give an elementary verification for all clause widths.
guide: A literal with LP truth marginal q has rounded truth probability 1/4+q/2, for either sign. For width k and LP value z, failure is at most (3/4−z/(2k))^k. The corresponding success function is concave in z, so it suffices to check z=0 and z=1 for a lower bound 3z/4.

For k=1, success is 1/4+z/2≥3z/4. At z=1, width two gives failure 1/4; widths three and four give respectively (7/12)^3 and (5/8)^4, both below 1/4; for k≥5 use failure≤(3/4)^5<1/4. Sum the resulting inequalities with nonnegative weights.
questions.followup: Why is the identity f(1−y)=1−f(y) necessary to use the same literal calculation for both signs?
questions.deliverable: A complete 3/4 proof for the specified rounding function.

questions.title: LP-optimal marginals can have different rounding values

The LP objective is identically one across this face, yet rounding values vary. An arbitrary optimal solver output therefore supports the worst-face guarantee, while a favorable integral optimum gives exact satisfaction. A secondary objective or perturbation can select a face point, but its effect on global rounding must be analyzed rather than inferred from unchanged LP value.

questions.title: Perturb a tight two-variable gap

Because min weight≤W/4, the ratio is at least 3/4, with equality exactly when all weights coincide. If one weight decreases while the others are fixed, the cheapest clause becomes easier to sacrifice and the ratio increases. questions.title: Separate exponentially many prize-collecting cuts

If every minimum cut is at least its corresponding y_v, then every admissible cut containing v has capacity at least y_v. Check variable bounds separately. Polynomial rational min-cut algorithms and exact comparisons give polynomial separation complexity even though the relaxation has exponentially many written constraints. questions.title: A gap witness without infinite penalties

Set every y_v=1 and every x_e=1/2. Every nonempty proper vertex subset of a cycle has at least two boundary edges, so every required cut has fractional capacity at least one. The fractional objective is n/2 and no penalty is paid. Hence OPT_int/OPT_LP≥2−2/n; an upper bound or exact LP optimum is unnecessary for this lower-bound certificate.

questions.title: Optimize the threshold for a particular LP objective
questions.prompt: Let A>0 be fractional edge cost and B>0 fractional penalty. A threshold uniform on [γ,1] has analysis bound F(γ)=[2A ln(1/γ)+B]/(1−γ). Derive its unique minimizer in (0,1), prove uniqueness, and analyze the limiting cases B→0 and A→0.
guide: Differentiation gives the stationary equation B/(2A)=1/γ−1−ln(1/γ). Put u=1/γ>1. The function u−1−ln u increases strictly from zero to infinity, since its derivative is 1−1/u. Thus exactly one stationary point exists, and the derivative changes from negative to positive there.

As B→0 with A fixed, u→1 and γ→1, approaching bound 2A. As A→0 with B fixed, u grows and γ→0, approaching B. A fixed worst-case threshold balances coefficients, whereas this objective-sensitive choice optimizes the actual certified combination; it need not improve the universal worst-case ratio.

questions.title: Why the prize-collecting LP is exact on a rooted star
questions.prompt: On a star rooted at its center, leaf i has incident edge cost c_i≥0 and penalty π_i≥0. Solve the integral problem and the cut relaxation exactly, characterize all optimal fractional solutions, and explain how arbitrary thresholds behave when ties c_i=π_i occur.
guide: For each leaf the singleton cut requires x_i≥y_i. Setting x_i=y_i is cheapest, so its LP contribution is c_i y_i+π_i(1−y_i), minimized by y_i=1 if c_i<π_i, by zero if c_i>π_i, and by every y_i∈[0,1] in a tie. The optimum is sum min(c_i,π_i).

The integral solution makes the same independent leaf decisions, proving LP exactness. Thresholding any optimal y changes only tied leaves, each of which costs the same whether included or omitted. Connecting the retained leaves by their actual star edges is therefore optimal at every positive threshold. A generic factor-β rounding bound can be much looser than this instance geometry.

questions.deliverable: A full optimum characterization and a threshold-level argument.

questions.title: Research exercise: optimize over all threshold laws
questions.prompt: For β≥1, analyze every distribution of α∈(0,1]. Suppose the proof uses only edge coefficient βE[1/α] and uniform penalty coefficient sup_{0≤y<1} Pr[α>y]/(1−y). Prove their maximum is at least 1/(1−e^(−1/β)), attained by a uniform law on [e^(−1/β),1].

questions.title: Eliminate the dual contribution variables
questions.prompt: Starting with dual constraints sum_j w_ij≤f_i, v_j−w_ij≤c_ij, w_ij≥0, eliminate w to characterize feasible v by sum_j max(0,v_j−c_ij)≤f_i. Derive c_ij≤v_j on positive assignments of an optimal primal-dual pair.

questions.title: Why the same cluster opening violates hard capacities

The rule opens one supported facility and assigns all n clients there, producing load n although its capacity is one. Costs can come from coincident or arbitrarily close metric points and do not affect this infeasibility. A capacitated relaxation may be perfectly feasible while an uncapacitated rounding rule fails outcome by outcome.

Support complementary slackness implies C_j≤v_j, and the new priority gives v_j≤v_l. Hence the connection is at most 3v_l. questions.title: Derandomize after the client groups are fixed

The representative selection depends on LP values and support intersections, not on earlier random opening outcomes. questions.title: Integral processing slots do not enforce nonpreemption

Sending total flow sum p_j corresponds to a feasible processing table. Integer capacities and a linear min-cost-flow objective give an integral optimum, so each slot can be assigned wholly to one job.

Integral slots for a job need not be consecutive. Its LP completion surrogate is mean occupied slot midpoint plus p_j/2, rather than its last occupied slot endpoint. questions.title: Exactly measure the completion surrogate’s slack
questions.prompt: A job of integer size p occupies distinct unit slots with endpoints t_1<…<t_p=D. Define Cbar=(1/p)sum(t_i−1/2)+p/2. Prove D−Cbar equals the mean backward displacement from the final p consecutive slots, and characterize when equality Cbar=D holds.
guide: The final p consecutive endpoints are D−p+1,…,D. Their mean midpoint is D−p/2. Therefore D−Cbar=(1/p)sum_{i=1}^p[(D−p+i)−t_i]. Each summand is nonnegative because p−i occupied slots must occur after t_i before or at D.

Equality holds exactly when t_i=D−p+i for every i, meaning the job runs without an internal gap over its final p slots. The identity quantifies precisely how preemption can lower the relaxation objective. Release dates restrict eligible slots but do not alter the displacement argument.

questions.title: Handle ties in independently sampled processing times

The upper bound deliberately includes all equal-time samples and is safe under any fixed tie rule. Machine capacity then bounds the prefix sum by x+1/2 in unit slots. It is an inequality, not the equality obtained by assuming no ties; rational discrete sampling can produce ties unless the LP processing table is integral.

questions.title: A common quantile destroys the prefix calculation

Before time endpoint two the fractional processing volume of A is only one. Thus the independent-sampling identity would give one while the common-quantile conditional workload is two. questions.title: Analyze intentional idle time in a priority schedule
questions.prompt: For a fixed priority order j_1,…,j_n, define S_l=max(C_{l−1},r_{j_l}) and C_l=S_l+p_{j_l}. Prove C_l=max_{h≤l}[r_{j_h}+sum_{q=h}^l p_{j_q}]. Give a two-job instance showing that this ordered schedule may idle while a later-priority job is available.

Let the first-priority job have release ten and processing one, and the second have release zero and processing one. The schedule idles to ten even though the second job is available. Such idling is consistent with preserving a sampled priority order. Replacing it with a work-conserving dispatch rule defines another algorithm whose weighted-cost proof must be checked separately.

questions.title: Research exercise: implement the relaxation without its horizon

The chosen job changes only at a release or completion event, so there are at most 2n nonidle intervals, with polynomial-bit endpoints. Integrate t over each interval exactly and sample a job’s processing position from its interval lengths. The explicit finite-horizon flow optimum is the baseline; objective disagreement or more than O(n) genuine event intervals is failure. questions.title: Why logarithmic-over-loglog congestion can be necessary
questions.prompt: Send n unit commodities independently and uniformly onto n parallel routes, each with its own bottleneck edge. For fixed δ∈(0,1), let k=floor((1−δ)ln n/ln ln n). Prove that with probability tending to one some edge has load at least k, despite fractional load one.

For distinct bins the exact joint probability is n!/[k!²(n−2k)!]·n^(−2k)(1−2/n)^(n−2k). Its ratio to the squared one-bin probability is 1+O(k²/n), tending to one. Hence Var Z/(E Z)²→0 and Chebyshev implies Pr[Z=0]→0. This lower bound concerns independent rounding, not the existence of a congestion-one integral assignment.

questions.title: A concentration bound for bounded commodity sizes

Markov’s inequality followed by t=ln(a/μ) gives exp[−(a/b)ln(a/μ)+a/b−μ/b], which is at most (eμ/a)^(a/b). For μ=0 and nonnegative loads, L=0 almost surely. The effective concentration parameter is μ/b, so a large maximum demand weakens the guarantee even at fixed expected load.

questions.title: Extract and sample rational path flows exactly

Express the rational path probabilities with a common integer denominator D whose bit length is polynomial in the input arithmetic length. Draw a uniform integer in [0,D−1] by rejection from ceil(log₂D) fair bits; acceptance probability exceeds one half. This gives expected polynomial time, but exact sampling of a probability such as 1/3 cannot use a uniformly bounded number of fair bits because bounded-bit outcome probabilities are dyadic.

questions.title: One bound covering large and small expected edge loads

When μ≫H the excess is o(μ), giving near-relative preservation; when μ=O(1), this additive estimate is O(log m), weaker than the sharper log m/log log m Chernoff optimization. Different bounds are useful in different load regimes.

questions.title: Derandomize routing with an exponential potential
questions.prompt: For explicit polynomial path supports, choose t>0 and a threshold a such that E Ψ<1 for Ψ=sum_e exp[t(L_e−a)]. Show how to fix one commodity path at a time without increasing its conditional expectation, obtaining every edge load strictly below a.

Evaluate the sum for each supported path of the next commodity. Their probability-weighted average equals the current conditional expectation, so one candidate does not increase it.

At the end Ψ is deterministic and below one. If any edge had L_e≥a its single summand would be at least one, a contradiction. Account for numerical precision or use a rational base q=e^t>1 and potential sum q^(L_e−a) with a strict initial margin. A symbolic expression is not automatically a polynomial-bit exact implementation.

questions.title: Research exercise: trade congestion for accepted commodities

Those choices remain independent and have total mean at most b, so the Chernoff bound is at most (eb/c)^c. Union-bound over at most ℓ path edges, then average over i’s path.

Every retained commodity avoids all originally overloaded edges, while all other originally nonoverloaded edges had load at most c; deleting commodities cannot increase loads. Sum retention probabilities to get the expected throughput. For the experiment enumerate path choices and retained subsets for an exact baseline; a capacity violation or expectation below the formula is failure. Negative lower bounds are reported as vacuous.

questions.title: Global edge density is not minimum-degree density

Every isolated vertex has empty open neighborhood, making open domination impossible even for S=V. An average-edge-density hypothesis therefore does not imply the minimum-degree assumption used by the algorithm.

For a vertex of degree d, the miss bound is exp(−sd/n), so only vertices with d≥δn receive the uniform exp(−δs) guarantee. Isolated vertices can be colored separately, but arbitrary low-degree residual subgraphs need an additional argument. Merely replacing minimum degree by average degree leaves that structural gap unresolved.

The uncovered count shrinks by factor at most 1−δ until it is below one, using at most ceil(ln n/δ)+1 steps. Repeatedly chosen vertices cannot improve coverage and may be skipped.

Each remaining vertex loses at least one color to a sampled neighbor, leaving lists of size at most two; test the resulting list constraints by 2SAT. The restriction of a genuine global coloring appears among the candidates. Runtime is n^O(1/δ), polynomial for fixed δ.

questions.title: A proper sample coloring that cannot extend
questions.prompt: Let a,b,c form a triangle and attach independent leaves s_a,s_b,s_c to the respective triangle vertices. Use S={s_a,s_b,s_c}. Show that coloring every sample vertex color three is proper but has no extension, although the full graph is 3-colorable. Give the resulting 2SAT contradiction.
guide: The leaves are mutually nonadjacent, so the all-three restriction is proper. It forbids color three at each triangle vertex, leaving a triangle with only colors one and two. This has no proper coloring. The full graph is easily 3-colored by coloring the triangle distinctly and giving each leaf any color different from its neighbor.

With a Boolean variable for each triangle vertex’s two-color choice, every triangle edge requires unequal bits. Along the three-edge cycle, implications force a bit to its negation and conversely, producing an unsatisfiable 2SAT component. The certificate disproves extension of this restriction; it does not certify global non-3-colorability.

The sample {s} dominates every vertex outside it, but residual lists have size three, which already encode NP-hard 3-coloring. The three-color algorithm succeeds because one forbidden color leaves at most two choices, allowing a 2SAT representation. The four-color case requires additional structure or a different algorithmic idea.

questions.title: Research exercise: replace minimum degree by fractional domination

Expected size is at most 3τ ln n; Markov bounds exceeding a sufficiently large constant multiple with probability below one half. Handle n≤2 separately.

Enumerating sample colorings and solving two-list extensions gives exp(O(τ ln n)) time under the 3-colorability promise. Minimum degree δn permits z_v=1/(δn), truncated appropriately in small cases, so τ≤1/δ. For a finite audit use exact fractional domination LPs and exact dominating-set enumeration on n≤14. questions.title: Research exercise: a logarithmic sample can be necessary
questions.prompt: In a random balanced bipartite graph on n vertices, include each cross-edge independently with probability 1/2. questions.title: Solve the triangle relaxation exactly

An integral cut has at most two triangle edges, and two are attainable. Each vector pair is separated with probability 2/3, so the expected rounded cut is two, giving integral-to-SDP ratio 8/9. Since the vector sum is zero, a nondegenerate hyperplane cannot put all three on the same side; every rounded cut actually has value two.

questions.title: Build a spectral dual certificate for MAX-CUT

guide: For PSD A,X, tr(AX)≥0, since tr(AX)=tr(A^(1/2)XA^(1/2)) and the latter matrix is PSD. Apply this to A=Diag(λ)−L/4. Because X_ii=1, the inequality rearranges to tr(LX)/4≤sum λ_i.

Taking every λ_i=λ_max(L)/4 makes A=(λ_max(L)I−L)/4 PSD by the spectral theorem. This bounds the SDP by nλ_max(L)/4 and hence bounds every integral cut. For a triangle λ_max=3, recovering 9/4. Equality requires the range of X to lie in the top-eigenspace for this uniform certificate.

questions.title: Characterize when the SDP reaches total edge weight
questions.prompt: Assume every graph edge has positive weight. Prove the MAX-CUT SDP value equals total edge weight W if and only if the graph is bipartite. Show that hyperplane rounding is exact on every SDP optimum attaining W.
guide: Every edge contribution is at most its weight. A bipartition assigns antipodal unit vectors to its sides, attaining W. Conversely attaining W forces v_u·v_v=−1 on every edge because all weights are positive; equality for unit vectors implies v_v=−v_u.

Along an odd cycle successive sign reversals would give v=−v, impossible for a unit vector. Thus the graph is bipartite. A random hyperplane separates every antipodal edge except on a probability-zero orthogonality event, so it returns value W. Zero-weight edges must be omitted from the converse graph characterization.

questions.title: Research exercise: transfer rounding to signed edge rewards
questions.prompt: For each edge give a nonnegative reward for either equality or inequality of endpoint signs. Formulate a Gram SDP and prove the same α_GW edgewise guarantee for total reward. Then translate it to a signed MAX-CUT objective with negative weights, retaining the additive shift. Compare with exact enumeration for n≤12.
guide: An inequality edge has reward probability θ/π and SDP contribution (1−cos θ)/2. An equality edge has probability 1−θ/π and contribution (1+cos θ)/2; apply the same angular inequality at angle π−θ. All reward weights are nonnegative, so the inequalities sum safely.

For signed cut weights w, replace each negative edge by an equality reward |w|. The reward objective is signed-cut value plus W_−=sum_{w<0}|w|. Hence the guarantee becomes ALG_signed≥α OPT_signed−(1−α)W_−, rather than a pure α ratio. Exact sign enumeration is the baseline; dropping this additive term or obtaining an incompatible reward expectation is failure.
questions.followup: Why can the resulting signed objective be negative even though reward is always nonnegative?
questions.deliverable: A correct signed-reward formulation and a shift-aware comparison.

questions.title: Exploit a high-degree neighborhood without knowing a coloring
questions.prompt: In a promised 3-colorable graph, prove every open neighborhood is bipartite. Give an algorithm that repeatedly two-colors and removes a neighborhood of size at least σ, using at most 2n/σ fresh colors before the residual maximum degree drops below σ.

Every iteration removes at least σ vertices, so there are at most floor(n/σ) iterations. Assign a new two-color palette each time; edges across removed groups then cannot be monochromatic. The surviving graph is still 3-colorable and has maximum degree below σ, making it suitable for a low-degree semicoloring routine.

questions.title: Triangles force rigidity in a vector 3-coloring
questions.prompt: Suppose unit vectors satisfy v_u·v_v≤−1/2 on edges. Prove that on a triangle all three edge products equal −1/2 and the vector sum is zero. Deduce that the two nonadjacent tips of a diamond formed by two triangles sharing an edge must receive the same vector.

If triangles abc and abd share edge ab, the identities give c=−a−b=d. Thus local triangle structure propagates exact vector equalities across a graph. It does not force those tips to be adjacent or distinctly colored, and a vector solution still need not encode a discrete global three-color partition.

questions.title: Track numerical angular slack through the color exponent
questions.prompt: Assume every edge product is at most −1/2+η with 0≤η<1/2. Define p(η)=1−arccos(−1/2+η)/π. Derive a hyperplane semicoloring using O(Δ^{ln 2/ln(1/p(η))}) colors, and quantify how η=O(1/ln n) affects the color count when Δ≤n.

On a fixed interval η∈[0,η0] below 1/2, arccos and the exponent a(η) are differentiable with bounded derivatives. Hence a(η)=a(0)+O(η), and Δ^{a(η)−a(0)}≤exp(O(η ln n)). An inverse-logarithmic edge error changes the bound by a constant factor; a fixed positive error changes its polynomial exponent.

questions.title: When recursion avoids an extra logarithmic factor
questions.prompt: Assume every s-vertex induced subgraph admits a semicoloring of at least (1−ρ)s vertices using at most A s^b colors, with fixed 0<ρ<1 and b>0. Prove full coloring uses at most A n^b/(1−ρ^b) colors. Contrast with a semicoloring bound depending only on a fixed global Δ.
guide: After r successful rounds at most ρ^r n vertices remain. With disjoint palettes, the total color count is bounded by sum_r A(ρ^r n)^b=A n^b/(1−ρ^b), extending the finite sum to an infinite one. Integer rounding contributes at most O(log n) additional colors if the assumed bound is rounded up.

If the only available guarantee is AΔ^a per round with Δ fixed from the original graph, that quantity need not shrink, and O(log n) rounds can cost O(Δ^a log n). The improved geometric conclusion is conditional on an s-dependent guarantee for every residual graph; it must not be silently applied to a routine that provides only the global-degree bound.
questions.followup: What changes when b=0, or when ρ tends to one with n?

questions.title: Repeated planes do not create independent signatures
questions.prompt: Suppose t nominal hyperplanes consist of r independent planes, each duplicated any positive number of times, with t≥r. For an edge of angle θ, compute its signature-collision probability and the maximum number of distinct signatures. Explain why counting 2^t colors and using (1−θ/π)^t are both misleading.
guide: Duplicating a plane repeats an existing sign bit and adds no new constraint to signature equality. The edge collides exactly when all r independent original planes fail to separate it, giving probability (1−θ/π)^r. There are at most 2^r realized signatures regardless of t.

In the extreme r=1, arbitrarily many duplicate bits still yield only two labels and edge collision probability 1−θ/π. The independence parameter is the number of independent geometric tests, not the length of a stored bit string. A shared pseudorandom generator needs a proved replacement property before a product bound can be asserted.

questions.title: Research exercise: a vector 3-coloring with chromatic number four
questions.prompt: Let vertices be the 15 two-element subsets of {1,…,6}, adjacent when disjoint. Set v_A=(1_A−(1/3)1)/sqrt(4/3). Prove these form a vector 3-coloring but the graph has chromatic number four. You may first prove that every pairwise-intersecting family of two-subsets is a star or a triangle.
guide: The squared centered norm is 2−4/6=4/3. For disjoint A,B the centered dot product is −4/6, so normalized product is −1/2. A color class is a pairwise-intersecting edge family in K6: if it has no common vertex, choosing two intersecting edges forces all others into their triangle.

A triangle class has at most three members and a star at most five, so three classes covering 15 pairs would all have to be disjoint full stars; distinct full stars intersect, which is impossible. Four colors suffice by assigning pairs first containing 1, then 2, then 3, and the remaining pairs inside {4,5,6}. Exhaustive coloring on 15 vertices is an optional baseline; any Gram or coloring-certificate mismatch is failure.

questions.title: Prove the Gaussian tail bounds with their prefactors
questions.prompt: For standard normal density φ and upper tail Q(t), prove tφ(t)/(1+t²)≤Q(t)≤φ(t)/t for t>0. Use the proof to state a uniform two-sided asymptotic bound Q(t)=Θ(e^(−t²/2)/t) for t≥1, with explicit constants.
guide: Since s≥t, Q(t)=∫_t^∞φ(s)ds≤(1/t)∫_t^∞sφ(s)ds=φ(t)/t. Integration by parts gives Q(t)=φ(t)/t−∫_t^∞φ(s)/s² ds≥φ(t)/t−Q(t)/t², which rearranges to the lower bound.

For t≥1, t/(1+t²)≥1/(2t), so φ(t)/(2t)≤Q(t)≤φ(t)/t. The constants are therefore 1/(2sqrt(2π)) and 1/sqrt(2π) in front of e^(−t²/2)/t. The prefactor cannot be discarded when optimizing logarithmic corrections in a rounding threshold.

questions.title: A conditional tail estimate for negatively correlated projections
questions.prompt: Let U,V be standard normals with correlation ρ≤−a for fixed 0<a<1. Prove Pr[V≥t | U≥t]≤Q(t sqrt((1+a)/(1−a))) for t≥0. Treat the degenerate case ρ=−1 separately.

Independence lets one bound the conditional Z-tail by its unconditional Q value. Since (1−ρ)/(1+ρ) increases as ρ decreases, replacing ρ by −a weakens the bound safely. For ρ=−1, V=−U and simultaneous positive-threshold selection has probability zero; at t=0 the joint event also has probability zero.

questions.title: Convert expected independent-set size into success probability
questions.prompt: Let a randomized independent-set algorithm output X∈[0,n] with E X≥γn, 0<γ≤1. Prove Pr[X≥γn/2]≥γ/(2−γ), give a distribution attaining the limiting bound, and bound independent repetitions needed for failure probability at most η.
guide: Writing p=Pr[X≥γn/2], bound E X≤p n+(1−p)γn/2, with a limiting interpretation for strict failure. Rearranging gives p≥γ/(2−γ). A distribution concentrated at n and just below γn/2 approaches equality, so constant success probability independent of γ cannot follow from expectation alone.

Independent repetitions miss with probability at most (1−p)^R≤e^(−pR). Thus R≥((2−γ)/γ)ln(1/η) suffices. Keeping the largest valid output never lowers success. The repetition factor depends on the extraction fraction γ, which is polynomially small in Δ for Gaussian rounding.

questions.title: An explicit frequency-two integrality gap
questions.prompt: Let universe elements be edges of K_m and let each vertex define the set of its incident edges, with cost one. Prove the integral cover optimum is m−1 and the LP optimum is m/2. Give matching primal and dual fractional certificates.

questions.title: Compare sequential and simultaneous dual growth

questions.title: A directed potential certificate with negative arcs
questions.prompt: In a directed graph with no reachable negative cycle and a reachable target, let d(v) be shortest-walk distance from s. Prove d(v)−d(u)≤c_uv on each reachable arc and show telescoping certifies every s–t path cost at least d(t). Explain why the undirected absolute-value inequality is inappropriate.

A directed arc constrains only one potential difference. It does not imply d(u)−d(v)≤c_uv because a reverse arc may not exist. Restrict attention to vertices reachable from s, or specify finite potentials on the relevant subgraph, so no subtraction of infinite distances is hidden.

questions.title: Handle zero-cost edges without infinitesimal growth
questions.prompt: Specify a one-sided cut-growing shortest-path algorithm when edge costs may be zero. Before each positive dual increase, close the reachable region under all tight edges. Prove progress, dual feasibility, and correct detection when t is unreachable.
guide: Given the current tight-edge graph, add every vertex reachable from s before choosing a new growth cut S. If t is absent, every edge leaving S has positive slack; otherwise closure would have traversed it. Increase y_S to the minimum boundary slack and then close again.

Every finite growth event makes at least one new boundary edge tight and adds a vertex, so at most n−1 positive-growth events occur. If no boundary edge exists while t is outside, the original graph separates s from t and no feasible path exists. Zero-growth closure prevents cycling on already tight edges while preserving the standard nested-cut certificate.

questions.title: Negative undirected costs change the optimization model

Give examples showing that the walk objective and cut LP can be unbounded, and explain the relation of all-negative simple paths to LONGEST PATH.
guide: If a reachable negative edge can be traversed forward and backward on a route to t, each round trip decreases walk cost without limit. In the cut LP with x_e≥0 and no upper bound, increasing any negative-cost edge variable preserves all lower-bound cut constraints while sending the objective to negative infinity.

A simple path cannot repeat that edge, so its cost is bounded on a finite graph. Giving every edge cost −1 makes minimum simple-path cost the negative of the longest simple-path length; this is NP-hard. Thus nonnegativity in the primal–dual shortest-path formulation cannot be removed by an informal sign change.

questions.title: Decompose the entire path–dual gap
questions.prompt: For an undirected s–t path P and feasible nonnegative cut dual y, define edge slack r_e=c_e−sum_{S:e∈δ(S)}y_S. Prove c(P)−sum_S y_S=sum_{e∈P}r_e+sum_S y_S(|P∩δ(S)|−1). Characterize equality term by term.

Equality requires every path edge to be tight and every positive-dual separating cut to be crossed exactly once. Conversely these conditions make both sums vanish and certify path optimality by weak duality. The identity quantifies two independent causes of a loose certificate: unused edge slack and repeated charging across a cut.

A minimum of affine functions is concave, and its active slopes decrease as λ grows. questions.title: Research exercise: remove zero-cost degeneracy lexicographically

All perturbed edges are positive, so minimum walks are simple and zero-cycle degeneracy disappears. The integer multiplier uses O(log n) extra bits. Replace all demands inside each component by any spanning tree and prove that the separating-cut LP is unchanged.

Conversely connecting that component satisfies every listed pair. A spanning tree of its demand graph generates the same equivalence relation with only k−1 pairs for k terminals.

A cut separates some original demand exactly when it splits a demand component. Every spanning tree of that component has an edge crossing each nontrivial split, so the family of required cuts is identical after compression. questions.title: Prove the contracted-forest degree inequality precisely

Partition its nodes into active A and inactive I, with every inactive node having degree at least two. Prove sum_{v∈A}deg(v)≤2|A|−2c, where c is the number of nonempty components. Explain how pruning supplies the inactive-leaf hypothesis.

An inactive leaf would attach through one crossing edge although no required demand leaves that current component. In the pruned feasible forest that edge can be deleted: any demand path using it would require a terminal demand to cross the component boundary, contradicting inactivity after accounting for already isolated feasible pieces. The needed structural input is acyclicity of the purchased forest and feasibility-preserving pruning, not a pointwise bound on active degrees.

questions.title: Connecting every terminal can be arbitrarily too expensive

The s,t component has no crossing demand, while a and b are active. Growth from a can make as tight and merge the inactive region into a’s component.

The merged set {s,t,a} still separates a from b, so its cut variable is eligible to grow. This is a new dual variable associated with a larger set; the old y_{s,t} remains frozen. questions.title: Pruning a purchased forest is order independent

guide: Every feasible subforest must contain the entire unique F-path of each required pair; deleting any edge of such a path disconnects that pair because F has no alternative route. Therefore the union U of all those paths is contained in every feasible subforest.

U itself satisfies every demand and is thus feasible. It is the unique minimum-by-inclusion subforest, so reverse deletion or arbitrary legal deletion must finish at U. This uniqueness depends on F being a forest; a cyclic purchased graph can have several different minimal feasible subgraphs.

questions.title: Research exercise: adapt moat growth to even terminal components

After pruning, an inactive contracted leaf would have even terminal parity on its attached part, so deleting its unique crossing edge preserves even parity on both sides; this contradicts minimality. questions.title: Research exercise: test nonuniform moat growth rates
questions.prompt: Consider a unit-edge star with k≥3 leaves and demands joining its center to every leaf. Give the center moat growth rate M and every leaf rate one. The local rate-weighted crossing sum is kM+k, while twice the dual growth rate is 2(M+k); the standard bound fails when (k−2)M>k. questions.title: Economies of scale are weaker than concavity
