Take f(x)=x on [0,1], f(x)=1 on [1,2], and f(x)=x/2 on [2,∞). It is continuous, nondecreasing, and its cost-per-unit ratio is nonincreasing. Its slope rises from zero to 1/2 at two, violating concavity. Route merging needs subadditivity, while comparison of capacity vectors needs monotonicity.

For the four-cycle in cyclic order, opposite-pair distances sum to four, while each adjacent-pair matching sums to two. The unique largest sum violates the tree condition. Thus every feasible capacity vector has capacity at least u_e. Routing each commodity along its unique path attains these lower bounds simultaneously.

Monotonicity of f then proves cost optimality without needing concavity or subadditivity. Under the model where undirected capacity bounds total path usage, two opposite demands D on the same edge require 2D, not net flow zero. questions.title: Planar grids require growing bag width

guide: The decomposition nodes whose bags meet a connected graph set form a subtree: unite the connected occurrence subtrees of its vertices along its edges. Any two crosses intersect, so their bag-occurrence subtrees pairwise intersect. Finite pairwise-intersecting subtrees of a tree have a common node; root the tree and choose the subtree whose closest-to-root vertex is deepest to prove this Helly fact.

The common bag meets every cross. A set of fewer than r grid vertices misses some row and some column, hence misses their union cross, a contradiction. Therefore the bag has at least r vertices and treewidth is at least r−1. Planarity alone does not bound the width required by an exact independent-set DP.

questions.title: Prove the structural separation behind a join recurrence
questions.prompt: In a rooted tree decomposition, let a join node and both children have the same bag B. Prove the vertex sets appearing strictly below the two children intersect only in B and have no edge between their interiors. Use this to justify combining two independent sets agreeing on B.
guide: If a vertex appeared in both child subtrees, connectedness of its bag occurrences would force it into the join bag B. If an edge joined vertices exclusive to the two interiors, some bag would have to contain both endpoints; connectedness would again force an endpoint through B, contradicting exclusivity.

Thus the two interior solutions interact only through their common chosen subset of B. Agreement on that subset and independence within each child imply independence of their union. The objective subtracts the common selected bag weight once. This derives the recurrence from the decomposition axioms rather than treating the subtraction as an isolated accounting rule.

questions.title: Research exercise: make the shifting loss exact

The outer cycle shields all inner cycles from the unbounded face; after its vertices are removed the next cycle is exposed, giving one cycle per layer. Choose the two bridge-attachment vertices to be the zero-weight opposite pair on each cycle.

questions.title: Reduce a nonuniform verifier without exponential duplication

A global proof assignment induces exactly the verifier’s answer behavior, so weighted satisfied fraction equals sum_r p_r·accept_r. A common denominator has polynomial bit length but can have exponentially large numerical value. questions.title: Compute covariance from signed clause overlap

questions.title: Quantify numerical error during derandomization

Each job’s sample distribution has one point, so ordering samples is deterministic. Scheduling that order as early as releases allow can only improve completion times; because the LP is a lower bound it must preserve optimal objective. questions.title: A union bound can be asymptotically sharp

questions.title: A structured dense family needs only a constant sample

Taking s≥ln(3/η)/(2δ−1) hits every part by a union bound. A sample hitting three parts contains a triangle and determines the three parts’ color identities up to permutation; outside vertices are forced by their neighbors in two other parts. General dense graphs lack this complete multipartite structure, so their logarithmic domination lower bounds remain compatible.

questions.title: Cheapest boundary edge is not reduced-slack growth

Cut-dual growth repeatedly charges the direct edge whenever it crosses the growing reachable cut. Its remaining slack decreases across earlier stages, so it can become tight after total growth two even while its original cost stays two. questions.title: Classify bridges before moat growth

Every feasible solution includes each mandatory bridge. Removing an edge yields a terminal spanning tree, so the terminal MST is at most 2OPT. Expanding MST edges and taking their union cannot increase the summed path cost.

questions.title: Determine optimal worst-case tree distortion for a four-cycle

guide: The opposite-pair sum in any dominating tree metric is at least four. If all adjacent distances were strictly below two, both adjacent-pair sums would be below four, leaving a unique largest sum and violating the four-point condition. Thus some adjacent pair has stretch at least two.

A four-leaf star with unit leaf edges gives every distinct distance two, attaining worst stretch two. Uniformly deleting a cycle edge gives adjacent expected distance (3+1+1+1)/4=3/2 and opposite distance always two, so maximum pairwise expected stretch is 3/2. questions.title: Balance the minor-compression tree

questions.title: Replace coefficient messages by evaluation messages
questions.prompt: A merge requires a polynomial of degree at most d over F_q, with q>d+2. Specify a protocol in which the prover sends d+1 values at fixed distinct public nodes instead of coefficients. Give the verifier’s interpolation formula, endpoint and random-point checks, and a direct polynomial bound on arithmetic and bit costs.
guide: Fix distinct nodes α₀,…,α_d before interaction. Every received value vector determines one polynomial g(t)=∑v_i∏_{j≠i}(t−α_j)/(α_i−α_j). Thus a bounded-length value message enforces the degree cap just as a bounded coefficient message does. Check g(0) and g(1) against the two current claims, then choose a fresh uniform r and continue with g(r).

Using direct Lagrange evaluation costs O(d²) field operations per evaluated point, with denominator inverses precomputed once for fixed nodes. Each message contains (d+1)ceil(log₂ q) bits, apart from framing; field operations are polynomial in log q under an explicit field representation. Soundness is basis-independent because a false endpoint forces this uniquely determined g to differ from the truthful degree-d restriction.
questions.followup: Why must a verifier reject duplicate interpolation nodes rather than treating the resulting system as another representation?
questions.deliverable: Complete message specification and a resource bound in d and log q.

questions.title: Soundness with imperfect random challenges
questions.prompt: At each compression, suppose the challenge distribution D_h, conditioned on the entire prior public history h and the current prover polynomial, satisfies max_a D_h(a)≤2^(−H). Prove a soundness bound for discrepancy degrees d₁,…,d_L. Give a matching one-step example when the challenge support has at most d points, and audit reduction modulo q of a uniformly sampled b-bit integer.
guide: A fixed nonzero discrepancy of degree d has at most d roots, so its collision probability is at most min(1,d·2^(−H)). Sum these conditional bounds at the first loss of a false-claim invariant. The entropy requirement must hold after the polynomial message; a marginally uniform challenge correlated with that message supplies no such guarantee.

If the support S has size at most d, a discrepancy containing ∏_{a∈S}(X−a) can vanish at every possible challenge. For U mod q with U uniform on b bits, each atom is at most ceil(2^b/q)/2^b, giving the corresponding d-times-largest-atom bound. Rejection sampling restores uniformity; a truncation event needs its own error budget.
questions.followup: Is a large Shannon entropy sufficient to substitute H in the bound?
questions.deliverable: Conditional theorem, support attack and an explicit biased-sampling bound.

questions.title: Interpolation nodes in small characteristic
questions.prompt: A proposed batched compression uses the integer labels 0,1,…,k−1 as interpolation nodes over F_(2^ℓ), claiming that 2^ℓ>k makes them distinct. Exhibit the error and repair the protocol using an explicit representation F_2[T]/(f). State the matrix-curve degree, permanent degree and communication cost for k claims about d×d matrices.
guide: Integer embedding into a characteristic-two field sends every even integer to 0 and every odd integer to 1. Cardinality does not make those particular field elements distinct. Instead fix an irreducible degree-ℓ polynomial f and enumerate k distinct ℓ-bit coefficient vectors representing residue classes, with 2^ℓ≥k.

Lagrange interpolation through matrices B₁,…,B_k produces a matrix curve C(t) with entry degree at most k−1. Its d-dimensional permanent has degree at most d(k−1), so send d(k−1)+1 coefficients and test all prescribed nodes before the fresh challenge. Communication is O(dkℓ) bits for this polynomial message, plus the initial scalar claims. Field construction and arithmetic must use the agreed representation.
questions.followup: Does increasing ℓ also increase the characteristic relevant to reconstructing an integer permanent?
questions.deliverable: A characteristic-two counterexample and a fully specified repaired interpolation scheme.

questions.title: Batch independent permanent assertions safely
questions.prompt: You are given k unrelated d×d matrices A_i over F_q and claimed permanents s_i, with q≥k. Audit the proposal to verify only ∏s_i using a block-diagonal permanent. Then design one random-point interpolation reduction that retains an incorrect-claim invariant whenever at least one s_i is false. Quantify degree, messages and error.
guide: A product equality does not certify every factor. For example A₁=[0], A₂=[1] and claims (0,2) over a field of characteristic greater than two pass the product check. Zero factors can mask arbitrary false assertions, and even nonzero factors can compensate multiplicatively.

Choose distinct α_i and interpolate a degree-(k−1) matrix curve through the A_i. Ask for a polynomial g of degree at most d(k−1), check g(α_i)=s_i for every i, and sample uniform r. Any incorrect s_i implies g differs from per(C(t)); the reduced assertion at C(r) remains false except with probability at most d(k−1)/q. Follow it by the ordinary dimension-reducing protocol and add the two error budgets.
questions.followup: For k=1, what reduction is necessary, and how should the degree-zero edge case be handled?
questions.deliverable: A masking example and a protocol for batching k same-dimension assertions.

questions.title: Separate field size from integer information
questions.prompt: A verifier uses F_(p^ℓ) with enormous p^ℓ to obtain a tiny root-bound error, then claims that one verified field value uniquely determines the integer permanent of a 0–1 matrix. Refute the inference even when the field contains more than n! elements. Explain the special role of characteristic two and give separate conditions for algebraic soundness and integer reconstruction.
guide: The homomorphism from integers into F_(p^ℓ) has kernel pZ regardless of ℓ. An extension field enlarges the challenge space but does not reveal more than the residue modulo p of an integer permanent. For the 2×2 all-ones matrix the permanent is 2, which maps to zero in every characteristic-two extension, however large that extension is.

In characteristic two, determinant and permanent coincide because the signs in the determinant disappear. Computing that residue is therefore much weaker than recovering the integer count. Root-bound soundness depends on q=p^ℓ relative to discrepancy degrees; unique integer reconstruction depends on a bound for the integer range and on the characteristic modulus, or on the product of distinct characteristic primes.
questions.followup: Can several fields of characteristics p,p,p supply three independent CRT moduli?
questions.deliverable: A numerical counterexample and two explicitly different parameter requirements.

questions.title: Audit selective restart policies
questions.prompt: Modify a degree-d compression so that the prover may abort after seeing r and request another fresh challenge, with at most T attempts. Analyze both unconditional false acceptance and false acceptance conditioned on eventual completion. Give a policy attaining the qualitative gap, and design a verifier rule that preserves a stated error budget η.
guide: If each polynomial is fixed before its attempt’s fresh challenge, a false assertion can escape in at most d/q probability per attempt. A union bound gives unconditional false acceptance at most Td/q, even if later polynomials depend on earlier failed challenges. Choosing q≥Td/η preserves an η budget for this step.

The prover can abort precisely when the challenge is not a root of a chosen discrepancy. Then every completed execution can be a false acceptance, although completion is rare; conditional soundness is not the original soundness definition. Count an abort as rejection, cap retries globally and report acceptance probability over all verifier randomness. An unbounded restart policy can eventually hit a root with probability one.
questions.followup: What changes if the application retries an aborted proof outside the verifier’s recorded attempt counter?
questions.deliverable: A stopping-policy attack, a repaired verifier specification and a theorem distinguishing conditional from unconditional error.

questions.title: Recover a permanent from a corrupted evaluation oracle
questions.prompt: Let O agree with permanent on at least 1−ρ of all d×d matrices over F_q. For a target A choose a uniform matrix R and query O(A+tR) at L distinct nonzero t, where q>L and L>d. Use univariate error correction to recover per(A), stating a sufficient success bound without independence assumptions on the queried errors. Compare this fixed-oracle model with an interactive cheating prover.
guide: For every nonzero t, A+tR is uniform, so the expected number Z of corrupted answers is at most Lρ. The restriction t↦per(A+tR) has degree at most d. A unique decoder corrects t₀=floor((L−d−1)/2) errors, and Markov gives failure probability at most Lρ/(t₀+1). Choose L and ρ so this is below one, then amplify with independent choices of R.

Queries on one affine line are correlated; the expectation and Markov argument deliberately avoid a binomial-tail claim. The oracle must be one fixed function with the stated global agreement. An adaptive prover allowed to see the entire line can corrupt every queried point while having no meaningful pre-existing distance from permanent, so the same premise does not follow from interactive access alone.
questions.followup: Can a quadratic matrix curve give pairwise-independent query locations while retaining a polynomial restriction degree?
questions.deliverable: A decoder algorithm, a parameter inequality for success, and a precise comparison of oracle and interactive models.

questions.title: Compose counting verification with an outer randomized computation
questions.prompt: An outer polynomial-time randomized oracle machine makes at most Q(n) adaptive counting queries and has error α(n). Each answer-verification subprotocol has honest rejection probability at most β and false-answer acceptance probability at most δ, conditionally on every prior history. Derive completeness and soundness of the composite verifier, including randomness, bit lengths and amplification costs.
guide: Couple the honest execution with the ideal outer oracle computation using the same outer random tape. With probability at least 1−α it takes an accepting ideal path; at most Qβ additional probability is lost to honest subprotocol failures. Thus completeness is at least 1−α−Qβ, assuming correctly encoded answers and a verifier that rejects malformed or out-of-range counts.

For a NO input, if no false oracle answer is accepted, every completed path agrees with an ideal outer path, whose acceptance probability is at most α. A first-incorrect-answer argument adds at most Qδ. Fresh verification randomness must remain valid conditional on the outer history. Count the polynomial output bits of each #P query and the polynomial overhead needed to achieve β,δ of order η/Q.
questions.followup: Which term vanishes when the counting protocol has perfect completeness?
questions.deliverable: Two explicit probability bounds and a polynomial-resource composition theorem.

questions.title: Verify weighted counts and signed gaps
questions.prompt: For a polynomial-time predicate R(x,y), |y|=p(n), and a polynomial-time nonnegative integer weight W(x,y)<2^b(n), construct a #P representation of ∑_y R(x,y)W(x,y). Then design an interactive verifier for a claimed difference of two such sums. Give range bounds, witness lengths, number of counting checks and the total error.
guide: Use accepting witnesses (y,z) with |z|=b(n), requiring R(x,y) and the integer z<W(x,y). Exactly W(x,y) choices of z accept for each eligible y. The resulting count is below 2^(p+b), and the construction runs in polynomial time in the original input length.

For a signed gap g=f₀−f₁, request and verify both nonnegative counts, range-check them, and subtract using p+b+O(1) bits. At least one false count must have passed whenever the verified difference is wrong, so two checks of error δ give error at most 2δ. A negative gap is not itself a #P count merely because its two summands are; name the signed-function model separately.
questions.followup: How do you encode a signed weight without permitting a negative number of accepting paths?
questions.deliverable: An explicit counting machine and a signed-value verification protocol.

questions.title: Sample a witness using certified branch counts
questions.prompt: Assume R(x,y) has a positive total count C of witnesses y∈{0,1}^p, and exact prefix-count verification has perfect completeness for the honest prover. Design an honest-prover procedure that samples a uniformly random witness using at most 2p+1 count claims and fresh branch-sampling coins. Analyze exact rational sampling, zero-count branches and malicious selective aborts.
guide: First certify the positive total count C. At a reached prefix u certify extension counts c₀,c₁, check their sum against the previous positive count, and use fresh independent coins to choose branch b with probability c_b/(c₀+c₁). The probabilities along every witness path telescope to 1/C. Perfect completeness ensures honest verification never rejects and thus introduces no prefix-dependent selection; zero-count branches are never taken.

Sample an integer uniformly below c₀+c₁ by rejection from enough fair bits; expected trials are below two and arithmetic uses O(p) count bits. This exact sampler has expected polynomial time. If a separate instance has C=0, it can report no witness after certification rather than sample. False accepted counts have a conditional union-bound budget, but a malicious prover can abort on selected prefixes even while claiming true counts. Uniformity conditioned on completion therefore does not follow from soundness.
questions.followup: What output convention permits a clean coupling statement without conditioning away malicious aborts?
questions.deliverable: Sampling pseudocode, a telescoping uniformity proof and an abort-bias example.

questions.title: Why flipping the verifier’s output is insufficient
questions.prompt: Write the prover and probability quantifiers for an interactive proof of L, and audit the proposed proof of its complement obtained by flipping acceptance and rejection. Give a one-message counterexample. Then explain how a verified exact count can support both the predicates f(x)=0 and f(x)>0 without using that invalid transformation.
guide: Completeness asserts existence of an accepting prover on YES inputs; it does not say every prover accepts. A verifier that accepts when its single received bit is 1 and rejects when it is 0 has a perfectly successful prover, yet its flipped verifier also has one. Replacing existentially successful behavior by the opposite output does not produce a universal soundness guarantee.

For an exactly verifiable nonnegative f, request one bounded-range value a, verify it, and then evaluate either a=0 or a>0 deterministically. A wrong decision requires an incorrectly certified value. The special function-verification structure supplies both predicates; it does not justify a general syntactic complementation rule for arbitrary interactive protocols.
questions.followup: What stronger condition on all prover strategies would make output flipping safe?
questions.deliverable: Formal quantifiers, a minimal counterexample and two counting-based decision verifiers.

questions.title: A low-degree oracle extension need not be cheaply evaluable
questions.prompt: Let O:{0,1}^m→{0,1} be an arbitrary black-box oracle and let Õ be its unique multilinear extension over an odd-characteristic field. Evaluate Õ at (1/2,…,1/2). Prove a deterministic black-box query lower bound for exact evaluation and explain what this obstruction does, and does not, establish about relativizing algebraic protocols.
guide: The interpolation weights at this point are all 2^(−m), so Õ(1/2,…,1/2)=2^(−m)∑_b O(b) in the field. Any deterministic evaluator that leaves an address unqueried has identical observations on two oracles differing only there, yet their extension values differ by the nonzero field element 2^(−m). Exact evaluation therefore requires all 2^m queries in the worst case.

The extension still has individual degree one and total degree at most m. Thus the problem is not absence of a low-degree formal extension but lack of an efficient black-box evaluation procedure at non-Boolean points. This explains a concrete obstacle to inserting arbitrary oracle gates into an algebraic verifier; it is not by itself a complete oracle separation between complexity classes.
questions.followup: How does the argument change in characteristic two, where 1/2 is unavailable?
questions.deliverable: Interpolation calculation, query lower bound and a carefully delimited relativization conclusion.

questions.title: Turn a permanent program into a checker’s prover
questions.prompt: A program P answers permanent queries over F_q and may retain state. Specify how a checker can use evaluation queries to P to generate every bounded-degree polynomial message in an LFKN execution for the initial answer P(A). Prove the checker’s two guarantees and state exactly what a rejection certifies about P.
guide: For a degree-d matrix restriction, ask P for its permanent at d+1 distinct interpolation nodes and interpolate the polynomial message. Expansion claims are likewise obtained by querying the minors. If every answer P gives is correct, these messages are truthful and the checker accepts the initial answer with perfect completeness, apart from any explicitly introduced sampling cutoff.

If P(A) is wrong, all subsequent stateful answers constitute a legal adaptive cheating prover, so LFKN soundness still bounds acceptance. A rejection proves that at least one answer in the executed collection was incorrect; it need not identify which query was wrong or provide an efficiently checkable counterexample with a known correct permanent. Specify whether correctness refers to a fixed function or to every response in a stateful run.
questions.followup: Why does interpolation require a trusted degree bound on the true restriction rather than a promise that P is a low-degree program?
questions.deliverable: Checker pseudocode and logically exact accept/reject guarantees.

questions.title: Certify zero through several possible characteristics
questions.prompt: Let g be an integer gap with |g|<2^b. The verifier samples uniformly from a public list of K distinct primes and interactively verifies a claimed residue g mod p using a subprotocol of soundness δ. Design a test for g=0, bound its error when g≠0, and distinguish this test from reconstructing the integer g.
guide: A nonzero integer of magnitude below 2^b has fewer than b distinct prime divisors, since the product of b distinct primes is at least 2^b. Thus at most b entries of any distinct-prime list divide g. Accept only after a residue-zero claim is verified; for g≠0, acceptance is at most b/K+δ.

Choosing K≥2b/η and δ≤η/2 gives error at most η, assuming the supplied list and modular-verification reductions have polynomial total size and cost. On g=0 every prime gives a true zero residue. No integer reconstruction occurs: the random choice limits the chance of choosing a characteristic that annihilates this particular nonzero gap. A prover-selected prime would not provide that guarantee.
questions.followup: Give a sharper bound when every prime in the list is at least P_min.
questions.deliverable: A zero-test protocol and an explicit error and resource budget.

questions.title: Allocate verification error under an adaptive query schedule
questions.prompt: A computation may make an initially unknown polynomial number of oracle queries. Give an error schedule δ_i that guarantees total false acceptance at most η for every stopping time. Then, for known query costs a_i>0 and verification work modeled by a_i log(1/δ_i), solve the continuous optimal budget allocation and explain its limitations for adaptive queries.
guide: Use δ_i=η/[i(i+1)]. Its sum over all i≥1 is η, so every finite or adaptively stopped execution has the same first-error bound, without knowing its final query count. For polynomially many queries, log(1/δ_i)=O(log i+log(1/η)), preserving polynomial overhead under the stated cost model.

For a fixed finite cost list, Lagrange multipliers give δ_i=ηa_i/∑_j a_j, subject to any extra upper bounds on admissible error. The objective and constraint show why expensive checks receive larger budgets. This optimization is an offline model, not automatically an implementable rule when future costs are unknown or depend on unverified answers; compare it against the valid anytime schedule on a specified adversarial query family.
questions.followup: How should the allocation change if a subprotocol requires δ_i≤1/3 before amplification?
questions.deliverable: An anytime theorem, an optimized finite schedule and a concrete comparison instance.

questions.title: Audit reuse of a public algebraic challenge
questions.prompt: Consider a toy verifier for claims a=f(0), where the fixed polynomial f≡0 is directly evaluable. It receives a degree-one g, checks g(0)=a, reveals uniform r∈F_q, and checks g(r)=f(r). Show why reusing r after one honest invocation breaks a later false-claim check. Generalize the audit to adaptive counting subprotocols and give a repair.
guide: An honest first invocation uses a=0,g=0 and reveals r. If r≠0, a later prover claiming a=1 can send g(X)=1−X/r, which passes both checks at the reused point. The second false assertion is accepted with probability at least 1−1/q, whereas an independently sampled challenge would collide with this fixed nonzero degree-one discrepancy at only one point.

The toy language is deliberately easy: it isolates a failure in the conditional soundness argument rather than establishing hardness. In a composed verifier, check whether each challenge retains its required distribution after all previous transcripts and the current polynomial are fixed. Allocate fresh independent samples, or prove a replacement randomness property strong enough for that conditional statement; marginal uniformity alone is insufficient.
questions.followup: Can challenge reuse be safe for genuinely simultaneous, nonadaptive polynomial messages fixed before any challenge is revealed?
questions.deliverable: A complete cheating transcript and a reusable conditional-randomness audit criterion.

questions.title: Degree reduction as a quotient-ring normal form
questions.prompt: Work over a field F and the quotient F[x₁,…,x_m]/(x_i²−x_i : i∈[m]). Prove uniqueness of the multilinear representative of every Boolean-cube function. Using P(x,y)=x, show that coordinate reduction R_x and universal elimination of y need not commute as formal polynomials, while their Boolean values agree. Explain the operator-order obligation for a backward verifier.
guide: Repeated replacement of x_i^k by x_i for k≥1 produces a multilinear representative. Uniqueness follows by induction: a multilinear polynomial vanishing on the Boolean cube has both endpoint restrictions zero in the last coordinate, and hence all its coefficients vanish. Equivalently use the 2^m Boolean Lagrange basis polynomials.

Universal elimination sends P=x to x², whereas reducing x afterward sends x² to x. Reducing P first leaves x, so eliminating y afterward still yields x². These expressions agree on Boolean x but differ at general field points. A backward proof must verify the actual ordered operator identities, rather than replacing intermediate random-point evaluations by an unspecified Boolean-equivalent polynomial.
questions.followup: Which algebraic operations descend naturally to the quotient, and what changes when the verifier evaluates outside the Boolean cube?
questions.deliverable: A normal-form proof, a noncommutation calculation and a verifier invariant.

questions.title: Count every operation in a normalized QBF protocol
questions.prompt: An arithmetic formula of size s in n Boolean variables has individual degrees at most s. In the guide’s degree-reduction reformulation, first reduce all n coordinates, then eliminate quantifiers one at a time, reducing every surviving coordinate after each elimination. Bound operator count, individual degrees in every backward restriction, communication and a sufficient field size for total error η.
guide: Initial coordinate reductions need n operators. A stage with k surviving variables before elimination uses one quantifier operator and k−1 reductions. Thus n+n(n+1)/2 operators suffice. After initial normalization each surviving variable has degree at most one; a product or Boolean-OR elimination raises surviving individual degrees to at most two, and the following reductions restore degree one.

During the initial reductions the relevant univariate degrees are at most s; afterward they are at most two. A safe uniform discrepancy cap is D=max(s,2). With L operators, q≥LD/η gives the root-bound budget, and coefficient messages contain O(LD log q) bits. The verifier stores assignments and operator indices and finally evaluates the original size-s formula; it need not materialize an exponentially expanded polynomial. This is a reformulation, not the exact syntax of Shamir’s simple-QBF normalization.
questions.followup: Can the final reductions after eliminating the last variable be omitted from this count?
questions.deliverable: An indexed operator schedule and a bit-level polynomial resource proof.

questions.title: Compare Boolean-valued and nonzero-valued arithmetization
questions.prompt: Compare existential elimination a+b−ab with elimination by a+b in a negation-normal QBF arithmetization using products for universals. Evaluate ∀x∃y True in both conventions. State the correct invariant for each, and explain why a modular zero test can fail for the nonzero-valued convention even on a true formula.
guide: The Boolean-valued convention returns exactly 0 or 1 on Boolean assignments and makes ∀x∃y True evaluate to 1. The nonnegative sum/product convention returns 2 for each existential branch and then 4 for the universal product. Its invariant is zero for false and positive for true, rather than equality to the Boolean truth value.

Reducing the value 4 modulo 2 turns this true example into zero. More generally a characteristic dividing a positive arithmetized value can destroy the nonzero invariant. A proof using this convention must address prime selection and magnitude/divisibility; a Boolean-valued normalized protocol has a different invariant. Neither convention justifies mixing the other’s gate identities or final acceptance predicate without a new proof.
questions.followup: Why is pushing negations to literals useful for the nonnegative sum/product interpretation?
questions.deliverable: Two explicit evaluations and an invariant-and-characteristic comparison table.

questions.title: Use characteristic two without reducing the challenge space to two points
questions.prompt: Audit a normalized Boolean-valued QBF protocol over F_(2^ℓ). Verify the AND, OR and R_i identities on Boolean values, and explain why a large extension field can support the root-bound argument. Use X²−X to distinguish polynomial identities from equality of functions on F₂.
guide: AND is ab and OR is a+b−ab, with subtraction equal to addition in characteristic two; the four Boolean truth-table entries remain correct. The operator (1−x)P(0)+xP(1) still agrees at x=0,1 and is affine in x. Thus Boolean-valued gate correctness does not require odd characteristic.

The nonzero formal polynomial X²−X vanishes on all of F₂, illustrating why two available challenge points give no useful degree-two root estimate. On a larger characteristic-two extension it has only the roots 0 and 1, so uniform sampling from q=2^ℓ points restores a 2/q estimate. Keep the original degree cap below the field-size scale used in the error calculation and represent field elements explicitly.
questions.followup: Does this argument justify Shamir’s integer nonzero-valued convention in every characteristic?
questions.deliverable: Truth-table checks and a field-size argument with a formal-polynomial counterexample.

questions.title: Small circuits can have exponentially large formal degree
questions.prompt: Let P₀(x)=x and P_(j+1)(x)=P_j(x)², represented as a size-O(j) arithmetic circuit with shared subcomputations. Compare formal degree, Boolean-cube behavior and coefficient-message length with and without inserting R_x after every squaring. Explain which resource assertion a circuit-size bound alone fails to establish.
guide: Without reduction P_j=x^(2^j), although all these polynomials equal x on Boolean inputs. Circuit size and repeated-squaring evaluation time are polynomial in j, but a dense univariate coefficient message may require 2^j+1 entries. A verifier that assumes small circuit size implies small restriction degree has lost its polynomial communication guarantee.

Applying R_x after each squaring replaces x² by x, so every normalized stage is degree one. The intermediate operation being checked has degree at most two, and a backward protocol can verify O(j) such operations with constant-size polynomial messages. questions.title: Why Boolean branch sampling can miss one false leaf
questions.prompt: A proposed protocol verifies a universally quantified Boolean predicate by asking for its two child values, checking their product, and following a uniformly random Boolean child. Apply it to ∀x₁…∀x_n (x₁∨⋯∨x_n), falsely claimed true. Construct a consistent prover strategy and compute its exact acceptance probability. Compare with low-degree random-point reduction over F_q.
guide: The predicate has one false leaf, the all-zero assignment. A prover can announce value 1 at every internal node and both children 1. Every product check succeeds. The verifier rejects only when its n random branch choices lead to the all-zero leaf, so false acceptance is exactly 1−2^(−n).

The failure is quantitative: a false value can be concentrated on an exponentially small Boolean branch, so following one actual child does not preserve falsity with high probability. A polynomial restriction checked at a fresh field point instead keeps a false assertion except at its bounded number of roots. Degree reduction is required to make the sum of those root budgets polynomial rather than exponentially large.

questions.title: Remove the degree cap and build an almost-always escaping lie
questions.prompt: For odd q>2, the truthful restriction is f≡0 and a verifier checks a false universal value 1 using g(0)g(1)=1, then moves to g(r) at uniform r∈F_q. If no polynomial-degree cap is enforced, construct g that is 1 exactly at 0 and 1 and zero elsewhere. Compute the probability that the next claim becomes truthful and specify an enforceable repair.
guide: Take g(X)=1−(X(X−1))^(q−1). At X=0,1 it equals 1, and at every other field element the nonzero quantity X(X−1) has (q−1)-st power 1. Hence both endpoint values support the false product claim, while a random challenge erases the false assertion with probability 1−2/q.

The polynomial has degree 2(q−1), so the usual small-degree root estimate is unavailable. Enforce the announced degree bound by requiring exactly D+1 coefficients or D+1 evaluations at fixed nodes, interpreted as the uniquely determined degree-at-most-D polynomial. Reject overlong or malformed messages; merely evaluating a prover-supplied high-degree circuit at a few points does not enforce a degree promise.

questions.title: Reduce only coordinates whose degree budget needs repair
questions.prompt: Replace the all-surviving-coordinates normalization schedule by a syntactic degree tracker. For a specified QBF formula and threshold D≥2, insert R_i only when the tracked degree of surviving x_i would exceed D before a later verification step. Prove a safe tracker, give one family where it saves operations and one where it cannot omit reductions, and compare verifier communication.
guide: Maintain an upper bound for each individual degree: addition takes a maximum, multiplication adds bounds, substitution never increases a surviving bound, and R_i sets its own bound to at most one without increasing other coordinates. These rules provide a checkable sufficient schedule even when polynomial cancellations make the actual degree lower. Verify each inserted operation in its actual order.

For subformulas using disjoint surviving-variable sets, products need not double every coordinate, so normalizing all variables can waste checks. Repeated use of a surviving factor in both Boolean branches gives a contrasting squaring family. Report total checked degrees, rather than only the number of inserted operators: fewer checks with larger degrees can increase coefficient communication or the required field size. No optimality claim is needed for the scheduling heuristic.

questions.title: Which coordinate changes respect Boolean normalization?
questions.prompt: Over a field of characteristic different from two, classify invertible affine maps taking {0,1}^m onto itself and prove the classification. Then exhibit a characteristic-two Boolean-cube automorphism whose substitution into a multilinear polynomial produces a non-multilinear formal polynomial. State the consequence for reusing a degree-reduction schedule after changing coordinates.
guide: A scalar affine coordinate a₀+∑a_i x_i that is Boolean on every Boolean input can depend on at most one variable in odd characteristic. Comparing the values at 0, e_i and e_i+e_j proves this restriction; a nonconstant coordinate is x_i or 1−x_i. Invertibility then forces a permutation of coordinates followed by independent complements.

In characteristic two the invertible map (u,v)↦(u+v,v) preserves the Boolean cube. Substituting it into P(x,y)=xy gives uv+v², which has individual degree two in v even though its Boolean normal form is uv+v. Boolean-cube preservation alone therefore does not preserve the off-cube polynomial representation used by an interactive verifier. Recompute degree bounds and insert the relevant normalization identities after substitution.

questions.title: Solve an unequal posterior information-set game
questions.prompt: A verifier chooses independent uniform bits u,v, sends z=u∧v, receives one bit y and accepts iff y=u⊕v. Enumerate the private tapes compatible with each public history and compute an optimal legal strategy and its exact acceptance probability. Compare conditioning on z with giving the prover the full tape, and express the calculation using integer accepting-tape counts.
guide: For z=0 the compatible tapes are 00,01,10; their target parities are 0,1,1, so y=1 wins on two of three. For z=1 only tape 11 is possible and y=0 wins. The unconditional optimum is 2/4+1/4=3/4. Maximizing separately for each hidden tape would incorrectly give value one.

The posterior is uniform within a compatible-tape set here, but the two public messages have probabilities 3/4 and 1/4. Count two accepting tapes in the first cell and one in the second, then normalize once by four. This concrete calculation separates local conditional probabilities, public-message weights and the requirement that one action serve every tape in the same information set.
questions.followup: What is the optimum if the verifier instead sends u∨v?

questions.title: Eliminate the prover’s private randomization
questions.prompt: For a fixed input, normalize a polynomial-round private-coin verifier to a finite protocol tree with bounded messages. Prove that the maximum acceptance probability over randomized, computationally unbounded provers is attained by a deterministic function of the public transcript. Explain why this does not require storing the entire optimal strategy in polynomial space.
guide: A randomized prover induces a distribution over deterministic contingent policies: fix all of its random choices, including choices at histories not reached in the current execution. Its acceptance probability is the average value of these policies. Since the finite set of deterministic policies has a maximum, randomization cannot exceed that maximum. Equivalently choose maximizing actions recursively at transcript information sets.

The deterministic policy is constrained by observable history, not by the verifier’s hidden configuration. It may have an exponentially large table, but a polynomial-space algorithm can recompute the value of a history and enumerate its possible next messages whenever needed. Polynomial space concerns the workspace of this repeated computation, not the size of a simultaneously stored policy certificate.

questions.title: Recognize compatible private tapes by replay
questions.prompt: Fix a polynomial-time verifier V using at most R(n) fair bits, padded to a complete R-bit tape. For an encoded public history h, construct a polynomial-time predicate C(h,r) saying that tape r is compatible with h. Include malformed messages, early halting and unreachable histories. Show how this predicate supports counting compatible tapes without materializing their set.
guide: Replay V on input x and tape r, supplying exactly the prover messages written in h at their tagged turns. Compare each emitted verifier message with the corresponding entry of h, and reject a replay that halts too early, expects a different message type or encounters an invalid encoding. Use explicit terminal symbols and a fixed stage convention so partial histories have an unambiguous meaning.

For fixed h,r the replay takes polynomial time because V does. Hence |S(h)|=∑_r C(h,r) is the count of witnesses of a polynomial-time predicate, and can be computed by an exponential enumeration using an R-bit counter. A zero count means the public history is unreachable. The recurrence can invoke this membership test repeatedly; it does not need an exponential array of compatible tapes.

questions.title: Count unused random suffixes correctly
questions.prompt: A verifier has a three-bit tape. If its first bit is zero it accepts immediately; otherwise it reads the remaining two bits and accepts iff both are one. Compute acceptance by complete-tape counting, then generalize to a private-coin interaction with adaptive coin consumption and early termination. State a normal form in which verifier-message branches partition compatible tapes.
guide: The immediate-accept branch corresponds to four complete tapes, not one. The later-accept branch contributes only 111, so acceptance is 5/8. Treating each terminal execution path as one equally likely outcome would incorrectly assign probabilities, because paths consume different numbers of random bits.

Pad every execution to R fair bits even when suffix bits are unused. Add tagged visible terminal messages and, if necessary, fixed-length stages, so a verifier step partitions S(h) into compatible child sets. At a terminal child count all accepting compatible complete tapes; sum at verifier branches and maximize over one transcript-dependent prover action. Counts stay below 2^R, with O(R) bits, while replay and recursive storage remain polynomial.

questions.title: Equal-size posterior cells can have different values
questions.prompt: A verifier chooses r uniformly from {00,01,10,11}, reveals its first bit z and accepts a prover bit y iff y=f(r), where f(00)=f(01)=f(10)=0 and f(11)=1. Show why retaining only the number of compatible tapes loses information even though both histories have two tapes and the same public control state. Propose a sufficient representation.
guide: For z=0, y=0 succeeds on both compatible tapes, giving conditional value one. For z=1, either response succeeds on only one of the two tapes, giving conditional value one half. The two cells have equal size but different distributions of future acceptance behavior, so cardinality alone is not a sufficient state.

A sound implicit representation retains h and a replay predicate for S(h), together with the verifier description and stage. This permits enumerating each tape’s future behavior without exposing tape identity to the prover’s maximization. More aggressive compression needs an equivalence that preserves future observations and acceptance under every legal action, rather than an empirical match of cell sizes.

questions.title: Bound the bits needed for exact acceptance comparison
questions.prompt: A padded verifier uses R fair bits, and its optimal legal acceptance probability is K/2^R. Show how to compare it with 2/3 using polynomial-size integers, derive a lower bound on a nonzero difference from 2/3, and give a family showing why retaining only O(log n) fractional bits can be unsafe when R is polynomial in n.
guide: Compare 3K with 2^(R+1); no rational arithmetic is necessary. Since a power of two is not divisible by three, equality cannot occur and the probability gap is at least 1/(3·2^R). The recurrence’s counters and this final comparison use O(R) bits.

For a threshold such as one half, acceptance values (2^(R−1)±1)/2^R differ by only 2^(1−R), and a polynomial-time verifier can realize these values by comparing its random tape with an explicitly encoded threshold. A precision budget of O(log n) can round both to the same value when R grows faster than log n. Polynomially many precision bits are sufficient; a fixed coarse precision rule is not.

questions.title: Extract an optimal next action without storing its policy

The chosen action depends only on h and a fixed tie rule, so revisiting the same public history gives the same answer across all compatible hidden tapes. questions.title: Generalize the recurrence to succinct integer tape weights
questions.prompt: Replace a uniform R-bit tape by a distribution Pr[r]=w(r)/W, where w(r) is a nonnegative B-bit integer computable in polynomial time and W=∑_r w(r)>0. Use a weighted sum at terminal histories, a sum over disjoint visible verifier-message cells, and a maximum over legal prover messages. At the root the optimal acceptance probability is F(∅)/W. Both W and every continuation count are below 2^(R+B), so O(R+B) bits suffice.

Compute weights and compatibility on demand during tape enumeration; never store their entire list. This proof uses a single globally specified integer weight for each complete tape. It does not automatically cover an arbitrary collection of history-dependent rational transition probabilities by asserting that their common denominator is small: that separate representation requires its own bit bound or a justified approximation analysis.

questions.title: Quantify the power of leaking a few hidden bits

Acceptance together with this particular z has probability at most the original optimal value. Summing over the fixed set Z gives the factor |Z|≤2^ℓ.

The assumption bounds all observable leakage transcripts, not only payload bits: timing and length must be included in an actual bounded encoding or otherwise counted in Z. A Shannon-entropy or mutual-information bound alone does not establish this cardinality bound. questions.title: Replace a context-dependent bundle by one point table
questions.prompt: A verifier samples a bundle C of t point addresses. Prover A sees C and returns t symbols; prover B sees only a uniformly selected address C_J and returns f(C_J), with J uniform in [t]. For fixed deterministic provers, a consistency check fails with probability ε. Bound the change in any predicate on the whole bundle when A’s vector is replaced by (f(C₁),…,f(C_t)).
guide: Let N(C) be the number of coordinates at which A’s bundle answer differs from f. The check distribution gives E[N(C)]/t=ε, so Pr[N(C)>0]≤tε. Couple the original and replaced predicates using exactly the same sampled bundle; their outputs can differ only on this event.

No independence between coordinate errors is needed, and repeated addresses are allowed with the same fixed f value. The resulting acceptance change is at most min(1,tε). This is a quantitative consistency lemma for the stated bundle distribution. It neither proves f is multilinear nor transfers a bound to a different bundle distribution without another argument.

questions.title: Prove a local-to-global agreement lemma on an expander
questions.prompt: On an N-vertex d-regular connected graph of conductance Φ, two provers have binary answer functions f,g. With probability 1/2 test f(v)=g(v) at uniform v; otherwise test f(u)=g(v) on a uniform directed edge. If rejection is δ, bound both functions’ distance from one common constant. Identify why the same-vertex test matters.
guide: The same-vertex branch gives Pr[f≠g]≤2δ. The edge branch gives Pr[f(u)≠g(v)]≤2δ. By inserting f(v), and using the uniform endpoint marginal of a regular graph, obtain Pr_edge[f(u)≠f(v)]≤4δ.

Let S be the smaller label class of f. Conductance makes its directed edge-boundary probability at least 2Φ|S|/N, so f differs from its majority constant on at most 2δ/Φ of vertices. The distance of g from the same constant is at most 2δ/Φ+2δ. Without the same-vertex test, a bipartite graph admits opposite side-dependent f,g that agree across every tested edge but are not common constants.
questions.followup: How do you alter the proof for an irregular graph sampled from its stationary vertex distribution?

questions.title: Decode the perfect-consistency case completely

Perfect acceptance and full support imply equality at every incidence, so every coordinate restriction of B is affine. Induct on m, using the two endpoint restrictions in the last coordinate, to obtain a polynomial of individual degree at most one.

A line question uses O(m log q+log m) bits, its answer two field elements, and B’s point question m log q bits with one field-element answer. This proves the exact case directly. For q=2 every function already has a multilinear representation, and for imperfect acceptance a robust proximity theorem is still needed; perfect-case interpolation does not supply its quantitative constants.

questions.title: Agreement distance depends on the question distribution
questions.prompt: Let the address domain have size N and consistency questions follow μ. Show that μ-weighted disagreement at most ε need not imply small uniform Hamming distance. If μ(x)≥λ/N, then μ(S)≥λ|S|/N, so uniform disagreement is at most ε/λ. Assign the minimum allowed mass λ/N to a disagreement set and distribute remaining mass elsewhere to attain equality whenever the parameters permit it. Apply such a comparison before importing a proximity theorem whose distance measure differs from the protocol’s sampled incidence measure.

questions.title: Four contexts that no pair of local tables can satisfy
questions.prompt: The verifier draws independent uniform bits x,y, sends x to prover A and y to prover B, and accepts bits a,b iff a⊕b=xy. Compute the classical value by analyzing deterministic local tables, show why shared initial randomness cannot improve it, and compare with an optimizer permitted to see both questions.
guide: The four required equations are a₀⊕b₀=0, a₀⊕b₁=0, a₁⊕b₀=0 and a₁⊕b₁=1. XORing them gives 0=1, so at least one fails. Constant-zero answers satisfy three, yielding the exact classical value 3/4.

Shared initial randomness is a distribution over deterministic table pairs, whose average cannot exceed their maximum. By contrast, an illegal joint-question optimizer may set a=0 and b=xy and win every context. The discrepancy is enforced by repeated use of the same local table entries across incompatible global contexts, not by any computational limitation on the provers.

questions.title: A succinct circuit is a substantive prover restriction
questions.prompt: A proposed replacement for an exponential proof oracle asks the prover to send a size-s Boolean circuit C:{0,1}^q→{0,1}^a before any queries. Count circuits and all possible answer tables, and prove that polynomial-size circuit messages cannot represent every table. Explain the consequence for an oracle characterization and for conditional small-prover-circuit consequences.
guide: With a fixed finite gate basis, size-s circuits and output wiring have descriptions of O((s+a)log(s+q+a)) bits, up to an explicit gate-order encoding. There are 2^(a·2^q) arbitrary answer tables. For s,a polynomial in q, the number of circuit descriptions is vastly smaller, so some tables have no such circuit.

Sending and evaluating a circuit can enforce one globally consistent function efficiently, but only within the represented family. It cannot silently replace unrestricted exponentially long oracle proofs in a completeness theorem. Conversely, if a language’s complete prover strategies do admit polynomial circuits, those circuits can become a short Merlin witness; that is a conditional consequence requiring a separate premise about the honest strategy.

questions.title: Uniform marginals do not imply a classical local strategy
questions.prompt: For the XOR game a⊕b=xy, define a conditional answer distribution by choosing a uniformly and setting b=a⊕xy. Verify that neither prover’s answer marginal depends on the other question. Prove that this distribution is not a mixture of classical local answer tables, and explain which assumption a marginal-only soundness audit overlooks.
guide: For each x,y, both a and b are uniform, so A’s marginal is independent of y and B’s marginal independent of x. Nevertheless the required XOR relation holds with probability one. These are nonsignaling conditional distributions, defined here only as a mathematical relaxation of the classical strategy set.

Every deterministic local-table pair satisfies at most three of the four XOR constraints. Convex combinations therefore have success at most 3/4 and cannot realize this distribution. A soundness proof must use one common joint distribution over entire local response functions, rather than checking the separate answer marginals alone. This example makes no claim about what entangled strategies can realize.

questions.title: Measure how question leakage weakens separation
questions.prompt: In an explicit communication variant, A receives uniform X∈{0,1}^N and may send ℓ bits to B, which receives an independent uniform index I∈[N] and must output X_I. Prove that average error ε≤1/2 requires ℓ≥N(1−H₂(ε)), even with shared initial randomness. Contrast zero leakage with sending the entire question.
guide: Let R be shared randomness and M the ℓ-bit message. For each coordinate i let ε_i be B’s decoding error. Binary prediction gives H(X_i|M,R)≤H₂(ε_i); summing and applying concavity gives H(X|M,R)≤N H₂(ε). Since X is independent of R and uniform, I(X;M|R)≥N(1−H₂(ε)), while I(X;M|R)≤H(M|R)≤ℓ.

With no message, B has no information about any independent fair coordinate and succeeds with probability one half. Sending all N bits permits perfect success. This is a bounded, falsifiable modification of the noncommunication premise: answer-table counting alone does not quantify what a leaked question allows, whereas the information inequality supplies an explicit tradeoff.
questions.followup: What changes if worst-case error is required for every index rather than average error over I?
questions.deliverable: A complete entropy lower bound and a leakage-versus-error parameter plot or table.

questions.title: Compute the exact distance of the multilinear code
questions.prompt: Let C contain evaluations on F_q^m of all polynomials with individual degree at most one, q≥2. Prove its dimension and exact minimum Hamming distance. Derive a unique-decoding radius and compare q=2 with q≥2m. State all lengths in field symbols and bits.
guide: There are 2^m monomials and their evaluations are independent, so the dimension is 2^m and block length q^m. Induct on m: on every point where a nonzero leading coefficient is nonzero, the last-coordinate restriction has at most one root. This yields at least (q−1)^m nonzero evaluations. The product ∏(x_i−a_i) attains the bound.

Relative distance is (1−1/q)^m, and fewer than half that fraction of errors has at most one nearest codeword. At q=2 the code is every function on the Boolean cube, with relative distance 2^(−m) and no redundancy. For q≥2m, Bernoulli’s inequality gives relative distance at least 1/2. Multiply symbol counts by ceil(log₂ q) when reporting storage.
questions.followup: Why does a constant relative distance still not provide a polynomial-time decoder by itself?
questions.deliverable: Dimension and distance proofs with a parameter table.

questions.title: Analyze a line subtest without assuming the global theorem
questions.prompt: For q≥3, test f:F_q^m→F_q by choosing a uniform axis direction and line, then three distinct points on that line. Reject if their values are not affine. If β_i is the fraction of direction-i lines at distance at least ε from every affine function, lower-bound rejection in terms of the β_i. State exactly which global conclusion remains unproved.
guide: The first two distinct points determine one affine h. On an ε-far line, h disagrees with f at at least εq points, none of which are those first two. A uniformly selected third distinct point therefore detects disagreement with probability at least εq/(q−2). Averaging over directions and lines gives rejection at least [εq/(q−2)]·(∑_i β_i/m).

A rejection bound δ thus controls the average fraction of far lines, and each β_i is at most mδ(q−2)/(εq). This is a valid quantitative subtest lemma. It does not yet construct one global multilinear function close to f; that step needs a compatible local-to-global theorem with its dimension and error dependence, rather than simply reusing the one-line interpolation argument.
questions.followup: How does sampling the third point with replacement change the clean lower bound?
questions.deliverable: A subtest soundness proof and a precise missing-global-lemma statement.

questions.title: Off-cube evaluation can require every Boolean corner
questions.prompt: Let q>2 and choose x∈(F_q minus {0,1})^m. An algorithm is given only query access to an arbitrary Boolean-corner table v:{0,1}^m→F_q and must exactly evaluate its multilinear extension at x. Prove a worst-case deterministic lower bound of 2^m corner queries, including adaptive algorithms, and compare with the length of a point query to a proof oracle.
guide: The extension value is ∑_b v(b)∏_i x_i^(b_i)(1−x_i)^(1−b_i). Every coefficient is nonzero by the choice of x. Run a deterministic algorithm against the all-zero corner table. If any corner remains unqueried, change only that corner’s value; all answers seen by the adaptive algorithm remain unchanged, but the required evaluation changes by a nonzero amount.

Hence the worst-case exact computation needs every corner, even though the polynomial has individual degree one. A proof oracle storing the extension can answer the same evaluation with an m·ceil(log₂ q)-bit address and one field symbol. This exposes the computational role of an exponentially large encoded object; low degree and short addresses do not make direct corner expansion efficient.
questions.followup: What extra algebraic circuit representation of v could invalidate the black-box lower-bound premise?
questions.deliverable: An adaptive adversary proof and a query-length versus evaluation-cost comparison.

questions.title: Self-correct along a quadratic curve
questions.prompt: Suppose f differs from an unknown multilinear g:F_q^m→F_q on at most an α fraction of points. At target x choose independent uniform R,S∈F_q^m and query f(x+tR+t²S) at L distinct nonzero t, with q>L>2m. Derive the restriction degree, pairwise independence, a decoding radius and a Chebyshev failure bound.
guide: The truthful curve restriction has degree at most 2m. For distinct nonzero t,u, the coefficient matrix with rows (t,t²),(u,u²) has determinant tu(u−t)≠0. Thus the two queried points are independent uniform vectors. Error indicators are pairwise independent, even though the entire L-tuple need not be independent.

Let Z count corrupted evaluations, and t₀=floor((L−2m−1)/2). Unique univariate decoding succeeds when Z≤t₀. Since E[Z]≤Lα and Var(Z)≤Lα, failure is at most Lα/(t₀+1−Lα)² when the denominator is positive. Interpolate the recovered polynomial at zero to obtain g(x), without querying the possibly corrupted target itself.
questions.followup: Compare this with the affine-curve method, whose restriction degree is m but whose query errors need not be pairwise independent.
questions.deliverable: A curve-based corrector and all parameter inequalities needed for a nontrivial success guarantee.

questions.title: A nearby word can defeat axis-only correction at one target
questions.prompt: Let q≥3, m≥2, and define f(x)=g(x)+1 on the hyperplane x₁=0 and f=g elsewhere, where g is multilinear. At a target x★ on that hyperplane, a proposed corrector chooses a uniform coordinate direction, samples two distinct non-target points on that axis line and extrapolates affinely. Compute its exact success probability despite the global error rate 1/q.
guide: For every direction other than coordinate one, the whole line through x★ remains inside the corrupted hyperplane. On that line f equals the affine restriction of g plus one, so two sampled points reconstruct f(x★), which is wrong. In direction one, all non-target points have first coordinate nonzero and are correct, so extrapolation gives g(x★).

The success probability is exactly 1/m, while relative Hamming error is only 1/q. This is not a contradiction to proximity: errors may be highly concentrated around a chosen target. A corrector using random full-dimensional affine or quadratic curves obtains uniform marginals at each nonzero curve parameter and can prove a bound that holds for every fixed target.
questions.followup: Does repeating this axis-only corrector and taking a majority fix the example when m>2?
questions.deliverable: A geometric error analysis and a justified replacement sampling rule.

questions.title: Keep integer-grid encodings within a bit budget
questions.prompt: Let g be the multilinear polynomial interpolating integer Boolean-corner values of magnitude at most K. On I^m with I={0,…,N−1}, N≥2, bound the magnitude and bit length of every evaluation, and bound the bit size of coefficients. Explain why polynomial answer length does not imply that the full encoded table is polynomial size.
guide: Use g(x)=∑_b v_b∏_{i:b_i=1}x_i∏_{i:b_i=0}(1−x_i). Every summand is integral and has magnitude at most KN^m, so |g(x)|≤2^mKN^m. Signed evaluations therefore use O(log(K+1)+m log N+m) bits. Expanding the factors shows each coefficient is a signed sum of at most 2^m corner values, bounded by 2^mK.

A single point address has O(m log N) bits and its answer has the stated polynomial bit length when the parameters do. The full grid still contains N^m points, and the Boolean-corner representation already has 2^m values. Do not confuse a local answer bound with an efficient direct evaluator or a polynomial-size global certificate. This integer-grid accounting is separate from finite-field cardinality arguments.
questions.followup: What breaks if corner values are unrestricted rationals with unbounded denominator length?
questions.deliverable: Magnitude, coefficient and table-size bounds in one explicit parameter table.

questions.title: Prevent cancellation when checking many residuals
questions.prompt: A fixed multilinear residual A:F_q^m→F_q should vanish on the Boolean cube. Show why checking only ∑_b A(b)=0 is unsound. Construct a random-weight polynomial H(r)=∑_b A(b)∏_i r_i^(b_i), prove its identity-test bound, and express H(r) as a Boolean sum suitable for degree-two-per-coordinate sum-check.
guide: For m=1, residual values 1 and −1 cancel in odd characteristic despite both being nonzero. In H, each Boolean residual is the coefficient of a distinct monomial in r, so H is nonzero iff at least one residual is nonzero. Its total degree is at most m, giving Pr_r[H(r)=0]≤m/q for uniform independent field coordinates.

Write H(r)=∑_{b∈{0,1}^m} A(b)∏_i[(1−b_i)+r_i b_i]. The summand polynomial has individual degree at most two, so an ordinary sum-check adds at most 2m/q error when its final A evaluation is trusted. The combined algebraic error is at most 3m/q. The residual must be one fixed decoded function before r is chosen; adapting the whole residual after seeing r invalidates this coefficient argument.
questions.followup: How do self-correction failures for the final A evaluation enter the budget?
questions.deliverable: A cancellation example and a complete weighted-residual verification reduction.

questions.title: Compose structural testing, correction and computation checks
questions.prompt: Assume a structural test establishes, except with probability β, one fixed multilinear g at distance at most α from f. An algebraic verifier makes t adaptive evaluations and has ideal soundness γ. Use affine-line correction with m+1 distinct nonzero samples per target to derive an end-to-end error budget. Choose explicit α,β,γ for target η and state the field-size requirements.
guide: For any fixed target x and uniform direction R, each nonzero x+sR is uniform. The truthful restriction has degree at most m, and a union bound over m+1 queried points makes one correction fail with probability at most (m+1)α. This target-wise guarantee survives adaptive target selection when fresh directions are used.

Condition on the structural guarantee and couple all corrected answers with g. Total false acceptance is at most β+t(m+1)α+γ. One sufficient allocation is β≤η/3, γ≤η/3 and α≤η/[3t(m+1)], with q≥m+2 to provide distinct nonzero interpolation parameters and whatever larger q the algebraic checks require. State the assumed structural theorem explicitly; this composition does not prove its proximity conclusion.
questions.followup: How could robust decoding improve the required α compared with insisting that all m+1 samples are correct?
questions.deliverable: A dependency diagram, conditional composition proof and concrete η-budget.

questions.title: Extend every resource bound to individual degree d
questions.prompt: Replace multilinearity by individual degree at most d<q on F_q^m. Prove the evaluation code’s dimension and exact distance, derive affine-line degree and a basic target-wise correction bound, and choose q as a function of m,d for constant relative distance. Compare all table and local-message sizes with d=1.
guide: The monomial basis has (d+1)^m terms, the block length is q^m and the minimum distance is (q−d)^m, by the same tensor induction and a product of d distinct linear factors in each coordinate. Relative distance is (1−d/q)^m; q≥2md makes it at least one half by Bernoulli’s inequality.

An arbitrary affine-line restriction has total degree at most md, not d. If q≥md+2, interpolating from md+1 distinct nonzero points gives a failure bound (md+1)α against a fixed α-corrupted word, using uniform marginals. For both constant distance and this corrector take q≥max(2md,md+2). Local axis polynomials require d+1 coefficients, while point addresses remain m log q bits. Report the exponential dependence of the global coefficient count on m and the polynomial dependence of local messages on d.
questions.followup: For the quadratic-curve corrector, replace every occurrence of m by which degree parameter?
questions.deliverable: Generalized distance and correction proofs plus a d=1 versus d>1 resource comparison.

questions.title: Count strategies for a genuinely multiround verifier
questions.prompt: A classical verifier uses R random bits, k provers, r rounds, q-bit questions and a-bit answers, all polynomially bounded in n. Derive a padded local-history bound H, an explicit total strategy-table size and a nondeterministic exponential-time verification algorithm. Account for table lookup without assuming a unit-cost exponentially large random-access memory.
guide: A prover’s action can depend on all its own received questions and earlier answers, not merely its latest q-bit question. A safe encoding has H=O(r(q+a+log r)) bits, including stage information. One padded table per stage and prover therefore needs at most kra·2^H bits, still singly exponential for polynomial parameters.

Guess the entire collection before enumerating verifier tapes. For every one of the 2^R tapes simulate the interaction with those same local tables and count accepting tapes. Even scanning a full table for each lookup multiplies exponential factors into another 2^poly(n) bound. Counters use O(R) bits; table storage may be exponential, which NEXP permits and the single-prover PSPACE argument does not.
questions.followup: When can the previously sent answers be reconstructed from shorter local-history encodings?
questions.deliverable: A multiround table encoding and a machine-model-independent NEXP time bound.

questions.title: Local tableau constraints have an exponentially small naive gap
questions.prompt: For a nondeterministic T-time Turing computation with T=2^p(n), build an accepting tableau with O(T²) cells and constant-arity local constraints. Give address and answer lengths. Show why sampling a uniform constraint cannot by itself give constant soundness, and identify the precise gap the algebraic encoding must repair.
guide: Pad the machine to T steps and T tape positions, with an accepting state that persists. Each cell stores a symbol from a fixed alphabet augmented with head/state markers. Initial, transition and final conditions are expressible by O(T²) constant-size local constraints; time and position addresses use O(log T)=O(p(n)) bits.

Local tableau constraints alone need not have a constant violation gap. For example, take a machine that remains rejecting and alter only its final head/state cell to accepting; this satisfies the final acceptance check but breaks only O(1) local transition checks. Among Θ(T²) constraints, uniform inspection detects this with probability O(T^(−2)). Polynomially many checks still give exponentially small detection in n. BFL needs global algebraic consistency/proximity and computation checks, beyond short addresses and local constraints.
questions.followup: Does repeating the naive check n^100 times repair the gap when T=2^n?
questions.deliverable: A tableau specification, query-size count and a quantified failure of naive local sampling.

questions.title: Balance exponential table length against field redundancy
questions.prompt: An exponential computation has N=2^p(n) witness bits. Encode them as Boolean-corner values of a polynomial in m=ceil(log₂ N) variables and extend to F_q^m. Choose q polynomial in m with q≥2m. Bound the global table length, local address length, coefficient count and relative code distance, and show all storage remains singly exponential in n.
guide: The corner representation has 2^m field symbols, while the extended table has q^m symbols and point addresses of m·ceil(log₂ q) bits. For q=m^O(1), q^m=2^O(m log m). With m polynomial in n this is still 2^poly(n), even though it can exceed the original witness length by a superpolynomial factor.

The multilinear code’s relative distance is (1−1/q)^m≥1−m/q≥1/2 for q≥2m. A constant field instead gives exponentially deteriorating distance as m grows. The resource tradeoff is therefore deliberate: enlarge the encoded object while preserving polynomial local questions and answers. Count field-symbol bits separately; a short local address does not make the whole table polynomial.
questions.followup: What changes if a p(n)-bit answer rather than one field symbol is stored at each original address?

questions.title: Short question spaces yield shorter Merlin witnesses
questions.prompt: Restrict to a one-round constant-prover protocol with q(n)≤c log₂ n question bits per prover and polynomial answer length. Prove the resulting language lies in MA. If the verifier also uses O(log n) random bits, prove containment in NP. Explain why the same argument does not follow merely from short individual questions in many rounds.
guide: Each one-round local table has at most n^c entries and polynomial total size. Merlin sends all tables before Arthur samples verifier randomness; Arthur then simulates the original verifier by table lookup. Completeness uses honest tables, and soundness holds because every received table collection is a legal deterministic prover strategy.

If only O(log n) verifier random bits are used, the NP verifier can enumerate all polynomially many tapes and compare the exact acceptance fraction with the threshold. For many rounds, actions depend on local histories, whose total length may be polynomial even when each individual question is logarithmic. The number of distinct histories can then be exponential, invalidating the short-witness step.
questions.followup: How does the conclusion change when the number of provers is polynomial but their aggregate tables still fit in polynomial size?
questions.deliverable: MA and NP simulations with their exact encoding hypotheses.

questions.title: Derive the conditional circuit-to-MA consequence
questions.prompt: Suppose every YES instance x of a classical multiprover protocol has a complete local strategy implemented by a polynomial-total-size collection of circuits taking padded local histories as input. Prove L∈MA. State the circuit premise with quantifiers and explain why arbitrary dishonest circuits remain covered by soundness. Relate this lemma to the paper’s prover-complexity circuit consequence.
guide: Require one fixed polynomial bound p such that for every x∈L there exists a collection C_x of total size at most p(|x|) attaining the protocol’s completeness probability. Merlin sends C_x first. Arthur validates its syntax and simulates the verifier using these circuits on each prover’s own local history, with independent private verifier randomness as prescribed.

For x∉L, every circuit collection defines a legal classical local strategy, so the original soundness theorem applies. The circuit collection may depend on x because it is an MA witness; no efficient uniform strategy-construction algorithm is required. BFL’s stronger consequences obtain this premise from hypotheses about circuit complexity of the languages/functions implementing honest prover responses, not from table consistency alone.

questions.deliverable: A quantified lemma, a complete MA verifier and a statement of the additional circuit assumption.

questions.title: Allow exponentially many indexed provers in the upper-bound audit
questions.prompt: Consider a classical variant with provers indexed by b(n)-bit identifiers. The verifier contacts only polynomially many per run; each prover’s padded local history has at most H(n) bits and answer length a(n), with b,H,a polynomial. A global collection of response tables therefore has at most a·2^(b+H) bits, up to polynomial stage factors. Guess it once and enumerate all polynomial-length verifier random tapes, always looking up answers by identity and that prover’s own local history.

Even a naive scan per lookup stays within singly exponential time. The verifier must explicitly use only polynomial-length identifiers and polynomially bounded local histories; unrestricted identifier length or hidden unbounded interaction would change the count. questions.title: Construct an accepting exponential witness with padded NP queries
questions.prompt: A nondeterministic machine runs in T=2^p(n) time. Show how a deterministic EXP^NP machine can find a lexicographically first accepting nondeterministic choice string when one exists. Specify the padded NP query, its length, number of queries and why an unpadded original-size NP query would be a different claim.
guide: Use a query containing x, a unary T clock and a candidate prefix u, asking whether some extension of u describes an accepting T-step computation. An NP machine guesses the remaining O(T) choice bits and simulates the computation in time polynomial in the padded query length. First test existence; then append 0 whenever the corresponding completion query is YES, otherwise append 1.

There are O(T) prefix queries, each of length O(T+|x|), and constructing them plus processing their answers takes exponential time in n. Thus EXP^NP suffices for this deterministic witness selection. The NP oracle receives exponentially long padded instances; claiming polynomial-length original-input NP queries would require a different and substantially stronger reduction.
questions.followup: Does finding one accepting witness nondeterministically imply that the lexicographically first one is computable in deterministic EXP?

questions.title: Audit an attempted deterministic strategy-table simulation
questions.prompt: For total guessed-table length M=2^poly(n), compare nondeterministically guessing one table collection with deterministically enumerating all collections. Bound both running times including verifier-tape checks. Then state the precise complexity consequence of a polynomial-space simulation for every classical MIP verifier, using MIP=NEXP and IP=PSPACE without asserting an unproved separation.
guide: One nondeterministic branch writes M bits and checks all 2^R verifier tapes in exponential time. Exhaustively enumerating all 2^M table collections generally yields a doubly exponential deterministic algorithm, because M itself is exponential. The exact acceptance counter can be small even though the candidate-strategy search space is enormous.

A polynomial-space simulation for every such verifier would give NEXP⊆PSPACE. Since PSPACE⊆EXP⊆NEXP, this would imply NEXP=PSPACE. This is a conditional consequence, not a known contradiction. Any proposed local maximization shortcut must therefore justify global consistency of repeated local histories rather than silently discarding the exponential strategy constraints.
questions.followup: Which step uses nondeterminism only once, and why can it not be replaced by tape-by-tape optimizing guesses?
