questions.title: Test the product claim on a finite parallel repetition
questions.prompt: Repeat the classical XOR game a⊕b=xy twice in parallel, accepting only if both coordinates win. Encode each two-bit question and answer as an integer 0,…,3. Exhaustively enumerate all local functions A,B:{0,1,2,3}→{0,1,2,3}, verify the maximum success fraction, and compare with sequential repetition and the naive product (3/4)².
guide: There are 4^4=256 local functions per prover and 65,536 pairs. For each pair count the 16 question pairs satisfying (A(x) XOR B(y))=(x AND y), bitwise. Exhaustive enumeration gives maximum 10/16; for example A=[1,0,0,0] and B=[0,1,2,1] attain it in input order 0,1,2,3. This exceeds 9/16.

In sequential repetition, answers for the first game must precede the second questions. Conditional on every fixed prior joint history, the fresh game still has value at most 3/4, so accepting both has value at most 9/16, attained by independent optimal strategies. The parallel computation is a bounded reproducible counterexample to exact product multiplication, not a statement of a general parallel-repetition theorem.
questions.followup: What independence or information constraint in the sequential proof is unavailable when both question coordinates arrive together?

questions.title: Show the GI view is independent of the chosen isomorphism
questions.prompt: For isomorphic graphs G₀,G₁, analyze one graph-isomorphism proof round against a verifier whose challenge is any efficient function of its random tape, auxiliary input and the first graph H. Prove that two different witness isomorphisms induce the same entire verifier-view distribution. Count the isomorphisms giving each fixed H and response.
guide: Condition on the verifier’s random tape and on H. The initial relabeling of G₀ is uniform among Iso(G₀,H), a coset of Aut(G₀). For either legal challenge b, composing with any fixed witness maps this set bijectively to Iso(G_b,H). Therefore the response is uniform over the same set regardless of which witness isomorphism was used.

The distribution of H is uniform over the common labeled orbit, and the verifier’s challenge is fixed once its tape, auxiliary input and H are fixed. These conditional response laws imply equality of the full view, including the tape and any deterministic final output. This proves witness independence for this protocol; general witness indistinguishability and zero knowledge remain distinct notions.
questions.followup: Which part of the argument uses the fact that all isomorphism sets between fixed graphs have equal size?
questions.deliverable: A coset-counting proof for the entire view, including malicious challenge dependence.

questions.title: Separate geometric simulator tails from a mere mean bound
questions.prompt: For k sequential GI rounds, cap each exact rewind simulator at T attempts and derive total statistical error and strict runtime. Contrast this with an arbitrary simulator known only to have expected time p(n): state Markov’s cutoff bound and give a finite-mean runtime distribution for which no fixed polynomial cutoff makes its tail negligible.
guide: A GI trial succeeds with probability exactly one half even after fixing the verifier’s tape and prior state. Failure of all T attempts has probability 2^(−T), so coupling all k rounds gives statistical error at most k2^(−T). Taking T≥λ+ceil(log₂ k) makes the error at most 2^(−λ), with O(kT) verifier invocations.

For only E[time]≤p(n), cutoff p(n)/ε gives tail at most ε; negligible ε need not permit polynomial cutoff. A distribution placing mass proportional to 1/(j²2^j) at time 2^j has finite mean, but its tail at n^c is still at least an inverse polynomial divided by a logarithmic factor for every fixed c. The GI conversion relies on its stronger geometric tail, not just expected polynomial time.

questions.title: Witness indistinguishability can be vacuous
questions.prompt: Assume a polynomial-time one-way permutation family f_n. On common input x=f_n(w), consider the protocol where the prover sends w and the verifier checks f_n(w)=x. Prove witness indistinguishability and show that computational zero knowledge would contradict one-wayness. State the role of an efficient validity distinguisher and expected simulator runtime.
guide: Each x has exactly one witness, so comparing two witnesses for the same statement is vacuous: the protocol is witness indistinguishable. It nevertheless reveals that unique preimage in full. Membership in the permutation’s range is trivial, so language complexity alone does not prevent a particular proof protocol from leaking a hard-to-compute witness.

Given x, test a purported simulated view by checking whether its response w′ satisfies f_n(w′)=x. The real view always passes, so computational indistinguishability forces the simulator to produce valid preimages with overwhelming probability on random permutation outputs. This gives an inverter; if simulation is only expected polynomial time, truncate at a suitable polynomial multiple of its mean to retain a nonnegligible success probability.

questions.title: Handle aborting GI verifiers without rejection-sampling bias
questions.prompt: A malicious GI verifier may abort after seeing H instead of sending a legal challenge. A simulator immediately outputs every aborting attempt but outputs a non-aborting attempt only when its guessed bit matches. Show that this can bias the view. Design an exact simulator whose probability of retaining an attempt is one half for every H, including aborts.
guide: If the real abort probability is p, the proposed retain rule keeps aborts with probability one and valid challenges with probability one half. Its output abort probability becomes p/[p+(1−p)/2], which differs from p except at the extremes. Being able to fabricate an abort transcript does not justify retaining it at a different rate.

For a valid challenge retain only on a matching guessed bit, as usual. For an abort, retain only on an independent fair dummy coin and otherwise retry from the same verifier snapshot. Since the first-message distribution is independent of the guessed source on YES inputs, every H has retention probability one half. Conditional output therefore has exactly the real H and abort distribution, and expected trials remain two.

questions.title: Put the simulator outside the instance quantifier
questions.prompt: Write an auxiliary-input computational zero-knowledge definition for an efficient prover given a witness, including verifier, simulator, distinguisher, YES-instance, witness and auxiliary-input quantifiers. Explain why a formulation allowing a separate simulator S_(x,w) for each statement and witness becomes vacuous for such protocols.
guide: For each permitted efficient verifier V* there must be one permitted simulator S_V* whose output on x and auxiliary input z is indistinguishable from the entire real view for all polynomially bounded YES-instance/witness/auxiliary-input sequences in the chosen definition. Distinguishers receive the public data required by that definition, and the indistinguishability error is negligible in the security/input parameter.

If S can instead be selected separately after x,w are fixed, its code may hardcode w and run the real efficient prover with V*. Every such protocol then has a pointwise simulator, including one that transmits the witness verbatim. Uniformity and quantifier order prevent this loophole. State separately whether nonuniform distinguishers or simulators are allowed rather than changing conventions mid-proof.

questions.title: Compare simulation notions under postprocessing
questions.prompt: Prove closure of perfect, statistical and computational simulation under the appropriate final-view postprocessing. Then, assuming a secure stretch-doubling pseudorandom generator G, compare U_n with G(U_(n/2)) in statistical distance and efficient distinguishability. Use the example to explain why computational simulation should not be described as near equality of probability masses.
guide: Identical distributions remain identical under every deterministic map. Total variation cannot increase under a randomized channel, by coupling or by pulling events back to the original space. Computational indistinguishability survives efficient postprocessing because a distinguisher for the processed views can be composed with that postprocessing.

The generator’s image has size at most 2^(n/2), so uniform U_n lands there with probability at most 2^(−n/2), whereas G(U_(n/2)) always does. Statistical distance is therefore at least 1−2^(−n/2), despite computational indistinguishability under the explicit generator assumption. An inefficient image-membership test separates the distributions; this does not supply an efficient verifier with such a test.

questions.title: Resampling the verifier tape can bias a simulated view
questions.prompt: A generic rejection simulator has a uniform verifier tape bit r, but its per-attempt success probabilities are p(0)=1 and p(1)=1/2. Compare selecting r once and rewinding with that fixed tape against resampling r after every failure. Compute the output tape distribution and expected attempt counts in both procedures.
guide: Fixing r first preserves its intended uniform marginal: the expected attempts are (1/2)·1+(1/2)·2=3/2. Repeatedly resampling r gives overall success probability 3/4 per trial and expected attempts 4/3, but the retained tape is zero with probability (1/2)/(3/4)=2/3.

The faster procedure therefore changes the full view even when its accepted transcripts are locally valid. Standard rewinding fixes the sampled verifier tape and its pre-round state. For the GI simulator the exact one-half success probability is tape-independent, so this particular bias disappears; a generic simulation argument must establish that property rather than borrowing it without proof.

questions.title: Compose simulators across adversarial verifier states
questions.prompt: Consider k(n) sequential protocol invocations with a verifier retaining arbitrary polynomial-length state. Assume each invocation has an auxiliary-input black-box simulator with a uniform expected-time bound and error ε_i against every efficient continuation. Construct a sequential composition proof, bound total distinguishing advantage and expected time, and identify why honest-verifier simulation is an insufficient premise.
guide: Treat the complete current verifier snapshot, prior public transcript and retained auxiliary data as the auxiliary state for each invocation. Replace invocations one at a time in a hybrid argument, allowing the later efficient continuation to inspect everything produced so far. Under the stated uniform guarantee, the distinguishing losses add to at most ∑ε_i.

A uniform expected-time bound p(n) over all admissible snapshots gives total expected work O(kp(n)) by conditional expectation. The black-box simulator may rewind only within the current invocation while preserving the snapshot before it. questions.title: Extract an isomorphism from two accepted subset responses

questions.title: An unrelated challenge can answer at most one subset
questions.prompt: Fix the verifier’s tape and first certification message, and assume H is isomorphic to neither G₀ nor G₁. questions.title: Compute soundness for a biased hidden source
questions.prompt: Modify the basic GNI verifier so that its hidden source bit equals one with known probability p instead of 1/2, and use an exactly uniform relabeling. Derive optimal soundness on isomorphic graphs, an honest-verifier simulator on nonisomorphic graphs and k-round sequential soundness. Extend the bound to adaptive biases p(h)∈[α,1−α].
guide: When the inputs are isomorphic, both source choices induce the same challenge-graph distribution. The graph supplies no information about the source, but its prior is biased, so the optimal response is the more likely bit and succeeds with probability max(p,1−p). On nonisomorphic inputs the honest unbounded prover identifies the source perfectly.

An honest-verifier simulator draws the source bit and relabeling itself and writes the corresponding prover answer, so it needs no graph-isomorphism decision algorithm. With fresh choices in k rounds, soundness is max(p,1−p)^k. If every history-dependent bias stays inside [α,1−α], conditional success is at most 1−α and total soundness is at most (1−α)^k. This is an honest-verifier simulation statement for the basic protocol.

questions.title: Prove expected time for the pairing simulator’s fallback
questions.prompt: On nonisomorphic input graphs, freeze the verifier’s random tape and complete pre-challenge state, including prior-round state, after H and the test pairs are fixed. Assume every restored invocation and certificate check costs at most a polynomial P(n,k). Let M count answerable subsets among 2^k and D(n) bound exhaustive classification of H including its interleaved invocation overhead. Analyze the simulator, returning bit 0 if H matches neither input. Separate M=0,1 and M≥2.
guide: Every retry restores the same complete snapshot and tape, so M refers to one deterministic subset-response function and each attempt costs at most P(n,k). For M=0 emit the same partial abort view as the real prover. For M≥2, extraction is entered with probability p=M/2^k, and a fresh distinct answerable subset appears with probability (M−1)/2^k≥p/2. Conditional expected retries are at most 2/p, giving unconditional work O(P(n,k)).

For M=1 the entry probability is 2^(−k), and exhaustive classification contributes at most 2^(−k)D(n). Output the unique source bit if H matches one input; if it matches neither, output bit 0, exactly as prescribed in GMW’s prover and fallback. Permutation enumeration gives D(n)=2^O(n log n), so k≥ceil(log₂ D)+λ bounds this contribution by 2^(−λ). Interleaving search with retries preserves exact output behavior, including the rare unrelated-H case.

questions.title: The pairing openings must preserve the hidden source
questions.prompt: On isomorphic inputs, prove that the honest verifier’s full GMW pairing-certification transcript reveals no information about its hidden GNI source bit, even when the prover chooses its subset after seeing H and all test pairs. Analyze separately indices opened to both inputs and indices linked to H, including their permutation distributions.

At an input-opening index the disclosed order bit and input-to-pair permutations do not depend on the hidden source. At an H-link index, the disclosed member index is the hidden source XOR an unrevealed independent order bit, hence is itself independent of the source.

Given the graph endpoints, the linking permutation is uniform among isomorphisms between them: compose independent uniform isomorphism cosets and use their equal sizes. This law remains independent of the source jointly across indices. A subset chosen from the initial message cannot expose an order bit and its H-link at the same index. Thus the final source guess still succeeds with probability at most one half on isomorphic inputs.

questions.title: Track imperfect permutation sampling through GNI
questions.prompt: Suppose each relabeling permutation is sampled from a distribution within total variation ε of uniform. For the basic GNI test with a fair source bit, bound optimal one-round soundness on isomorphic graphs and k-round sequential soundness under fresh sampling. guide: Pushing a distribution through relabeling cannot increase total variation. Each source’s challenge law is within ε of the common ideal orbit law, so their mutual distance is at most 2ε. With equal priors, optimal source prediction is (1+TV)/2, giving success at most 1/2+ε. Fresh conditional sampling yields at most (1/2+ε)^k for all-round acceptance.

Fisher–Yates needs at most n bounded-integer choices. Draw each by fair-bit rejection sampling; every trial succeeds with probability at least one half. Capping each choice at L trials and using a specified fallback permutation changes the permutation law by at most n2^(−L) under coupling. questions.title: Audit the direct-certificate shortcut

questions.prompt: On the three-vertex path u−v−w, compare proper witnesses (1,2,1) and (1,2,3). A modified verifier opens both edges from the same freshly permuted committed coloring. Give an efficient distinguisher between the two views and explain why independently repeating single-edge rounds does not reveal this particular relation.
guide: The two openings expose colors at all three path vertices under the same permutation. Test whether the labels at u and w are equal. The test returns true with probability one for the first witness and false with probability one for the second; a global color permutation preserves equality relations.

Thus properness of each queried edge does not make their joint view witness-independent. In separate single-edge rounds with fresh permutations and commitments, the two endpoint-label pairs use independent color names, so cross-round equality of labels does not encode equality in one fixed witness. A simulator that fabricates each edge locally cannot be reused for two openings from one commitment vector without addressing their joint partition of colors.
questions.followup: What information would opening all three vertices of a triangle reveal about a proper 3-coloring?

questions.title: Optimize the honest edge challenge distribution
questions.prompt: For a non-3-colorable graph, define γ(p)=min_c ∑_e p_e·1[c is monochromatic on e], minimizing over all vertex 3-labelings. Formulate the LP maximizing γ and its dual. Solve the example K₄ with one pendant edge, comparing uniform sampling on all seven edges with an optimal distribution.
guide: Use variables p_e≥0, ∑p_e=1 and γ≤∑p_e bad_e(c) for every labeling c. The dual chooses a distribution over labelings to minimize the maximum edge’s expected monochromatic indicator. With binding commitments, γ is exactly the worst-case rejection probability of the resulting honest edge test.

For K₄ plus a pendant edge, uniform sampling gives γ=1/7: every labeling has a bad K₄ edge, and one can make exactly one edge bad while coloring the pendant properly. Put weight 1/6 on each K₄ edge and zero on the pendant to get γ=1/6. For the matching upper bound, distribute uniformly over six labelings whose unique bad K₄ edge ranges over those six choices, always extending properly to the pendant.
questions.followup: Why can an optimal distribution have minimum edge probability zero while retaining positive soundness gap?

questions.title: Reset access is an additional verifier power
questions.prompt: Add an interface allowing a verifier to reset the honest prover to the state just after one commitment vector was sent, preserving the prover’s random tape. Show how polynomially many resets recover a coloring on every nonisolated vertex. Explain precisely why this attack changes the standard interaction model and does not follow merely from a simulator’s ability to rewind a verifier.
guide: Ask a different edge after each reset to the same post-commitment snapshot. All openings use the same color permutation and per-vertex commitment randomness, so their labels can be combined. Querying every edge reveals the committed proper coloring on all nonisolated vertices; isolated vertices may receive arbitrary colors afterward.

In the ordinary protocol the real verifier cannot force the prover to reuse that state after a completed round; fresh rounds use fresh commitments and permutations. An offline simulator can rewind the verifier because it runs the verifier’s code and state, a power not granted symmetrically to the real verifier over the honest prover. This is an audit of an explicitly stronger reset interface, not a refutation of the standard sequential GMW proof.

questions.title: Open a whole triangle while preserving local witness independence
questions.prompt: For every edge e=(u,v) of G, add a new vertex w_e adjacent to u,v, retaining the original edge. Commit to a proper coloring of the resulting graph, and challenge a uniform designated triangle (u,v,w_e). Prove equivalence to 3-colorability of G, soundness, local view independence and a malicious-verifier simulation using a guessed triangle. Quantify graph and communication overhead.
guide: A proper coloring of G extends uniquely at each w_e to the missing third color, and every proper coloring of the enlarged graph restricts to one of G. There are N+m vertices and 3m edges, with m designated challenge triangles. Any fixed labeling of a non-3-colorable instance violates at least one designated triangle, so binding-good soundness is at most 1−1/m.

Every properly colored triangle has all three colors, and a uniform global permutation gives the same uniform distribution on its six ordered distinct triples for every witness. Guess the challenged triangle, commit to one such triple and dummy colors elsewhere, then apply the hiding-based rejection simulation with m possible challenges. Commitments grow from N to N+m and openings from two to three vertices; the same one-challenge conditioning issue still needs its proof.

questions.title: Separate graph size, repetition count and primitive security
questions.prompt: For N vertices and m edges, target proof soundness and simulation distinguishing advantage at most 2^(−λ). Assume primitive binding and hiding errors are at most 2^(−λ′) against the required enlarged reduction budget, and that the established simulation reduction loses at most CkmN for k rounds. Choose k,λ′ and give total communication in terms of commitment and opening lengths. State what is assumed rather than derived from one-wayness.
guide: Take k=ceil(m(λ+1)ln 2), making (1−1/m)^k≤2^(−λ−1). Require kN·2^(−λ′)≤2^(−λ−1) for accumulated binding failures and CkmN·2^(−λ′)≤2^(−λ) for simulation loss. For example λ′≥λ+ceil(log₂(2CkmN)) suffices when C≥1, with harmless small-parameter rounding.

If a commitment uses L_c(λ′) total bits and an opening uses L_o(λ′), communication is O(k[N L_c(λ′)+log m+2L_o(λ′)]), plus any explicitly charged setup. The hiding guarantee must cover the reduction’s increased circuit/time budget and any rejection-sampling cutoff. Negligible security from a qualitative one-wayness assumption does not automatically provide the concrete exponential bound 2^(−λ′); that is an additional primitive-security hypothesis of this calculation.

questions.title: A lattice of bounded monotone paths

questions.title: From partition functions to extremal scores and multiplicities
questions.prompt: For finite families F,G⊆2^[n] and a real score s(A)=Σ_i c_i1_{i∈A}, apply the activity inequality at z_i=e^(t c_i). questions.title: An exact audit of extremizers on a small cube
questions.prompt: Design a reproducible exhaustive study of nonempty F,G⊆2^[3]. Compute D=|F∨G||F∧G|−|F||G|, classify zero-gap pairs by family sizes, and test the conjecture that equality forces both families to be sublattices. Supply a certified counterexample or a complete finite verification, not a general theorem inferred from a sample.

questions.title: Construct the distributive-lattice embedding
questions.prompt: For a finite distributive lattice L, let J be its join-irreducible elements and put φ(x)={j∈J:j≤x}. Prove that φ is injective and preserves meet and join, then transfer a four-function inequality by extending functions by zero outside φ(L). Identify where distributivity is essential.
guide: Every nonzero element is a join of join-irreducibles, by induction down the finite order. This makes φ injective and gives φ(x∧y)=φ(x)∩φ(y).

In a distributive lattice a join-irreducible j is join-prime: j≤x∨y implies j=(j∧x)∨(j∧y), hence j≤x or j≤y. This proves union preservation. The zero extensions satisfy the Boolean pointwise condition because the embedded image is a sublattice.

questions.title: Verify association in a binary interaction model

questions.title: Conditioning on an increasing event can destroy association
questions.prompt: Let X_1,X_2 be independent fair bits and condition on X_1∨X_2=1. Compute the resulting covariance and exhibit the failed log-supermodularity inequality. Contrast this operation with conditioning on specified coordinate values.
guide: The conditional law is uniform on 01,10,11. Both conditional marginals are 2/3 and the joint-one probability is 1/3, so the covariance is −1/9.

The two positive states 01 and 10 have meet 00 of zero conditional mass. Their product is positive while the meet–join product vanishes. A coordinate slice, by contrast, is closed under meet and join and inherits the original lattice inequality.

questions.title: Differentiate expectations under an external field
questions.prompt: Let μ be a nonzero log-supermodular weight on a finite Boolean lattice and μ_t(x) proportional to μ(x)e^(tH(x)), where H(x)=Σ_i a_i x_i and a_i≥0. For every increasing real f prove dE_t f/dt=Cov_t(f,H)≥0, and derive nonnegative field-response entries ∂E x_i/∂h_j.

Both f and H are increasing, so FKG makes that derivative nonnegative. Taking f=x_i and varying only the jth field gives the response matrix entry Cov(x_i,x_j); its diagonal is Var(x_i), and the entire covariance matrix is positive semidefinite for a separate elementary reason.

questions.title: Association need not imply log-supermodularity
questions.prompt: Take independent fair U,V and define X=(U,V,U∨V). Prove that every pair of increasing functions of X is positively correlated, but the law of X is not log-supermodular on the three-cube. State which implication between association and the lattice condition this separates.
guide: The map (u,v)↦(u,v,u∨v) is coordinatewise increasing. Increasing functions of X therefore pull back to increasing functions of the independent pair (U,V), where Harris applies.

The support is {000,011,101,111}, each with mass 1/4. The meet of 011 and 101 is 001, absent from the support, while their join is 111. The lattice product inequality consequently fails although association holds.

questions.title: The exact two-bit criterion
questions.prompt: Let a strictly positive law on {0,1}² have unnormalized masses a,b,c,d at 00,10,01,11. Prove that ad≥bc is equivalent to positive association for every pair of increasing real functions. Compute Cov(X_1,X_2) exactly and explain why checking just this covariance suffices only in dimension two.

questions.title: When is Harris an equality?
questions.prompt: For increasing events A,B under a product law with all 0<p_i<1, call i essential to A if changing only bit i changes membership somewhere. Prove Cov(1_A,1_B)=0 exactly when A and B have disjoint essential-coordinate sets. Include constant events.
guide: If a coordinate i is essential to an increasing event, the averaged discrete derivative I_i(A)=P(A|X_i=1)−P(A|X_i=0) is strictly positive because every remaining configuration has positive mass.

Condition on X_i. Harris on each slice gives Cov(1_A,1_B)≥p_i(1−p_i)I_i(A)I_i(B), positive when i is shared. Conversely a Boolean function depends only on its essential coordinates, so disjoint essential sets give independence.

questions.title: A quantitative lower bound for a random hitting set
questions.prompt: Choose each element of [n] independently with probability p_i. For prescribed nonempty sets S_1,…,S_m, prove a product lower bound for hitting all of them. For S_1={1,2}, S_2={2,3} and common p, calculate the exact probability and its gap from the product bound.

For the overlapping pair, condition on bit 2: the exact probability is p+(1−p)p². Subtract [1−(1−p)²]² to obtain p(1−p)³. The shared essential coordinate explains the strict positive gap for 0<p<1.

questions.title: Differentiate a monotone event probability

questions.title: A martingale decomposition of monotone covariance

questions.title: Uniform extensions versus uniform choices of minima

questions.title: A correct uniform stationary law without a mixing claim
questions.prompt: On linear extensions of a finite poset, consider the lazy chain that with probability 1/2 stays put and otherwise selects a uniform adjacent position and swaps its elements only if they are incomparable. guide: Every allowed adjacent swap has the same transition probability in both directions, so the uniform distribution satisfies detailed balance. The added holding probability ensures aperiodicity.

To connect any extension to a target extension, move the target's first element leftward. Every element it crosses must be incomparable with it, since a forced predecessor would also precede it in the target. Fix that first element and repeat on the remaining poset. questions.title: Expose a permutation with a transposition coupling

questions.prompt: In a deterministic graph let X be its number of k-cliques, k≥3, and suppose each edge belongs to at most D of them. guide: Every selected clique conflicts with at most C(k,2)D candidate cliques, by assigning a shared edge and then a clique containing it. A maximal packing's conflict neighborhoods cover all k-cliques, proving the bound.

For random graphs the displayed inequality is pointwise in the realized D. It yields E Y≥E[X/(C(k,2)D)] when D>0, not the ratio E X/[C(k,2)E D]. Any use of average incidence needs an additional deterministic truncation or probability argument.
questions.followup: Calculate X,D and the actual packing size for K_{k+1}.

questions.title: Use a chromatic quantile to anchor a deletion variable
questions.prompt: Let u be the least integer with P(χ(G(n,p))≤u)>η, where 0<η<1/2. Define Y as the minimum vertices whose deletion leaves a u-colorable graph. Prove E Y≤√(2n ln(1/η)) and P(Y>2√(2n ln(1/η)))≤η. Include the vertex-exposure coupling.
guide: Two graphs differing only in one vertex's incident edges have deletion numbers differing by at most one: add that vertex to a deletion set on either side. Coupling all other edge variables identically yields n bounded Doob increments.
Since P(Y=0)>η, the lower Azuma tail forces the mean to be at most λ√n with λ=√(2ln(1/η)). The upper tail then bounds Y by 2λ√n except with probability η. The minimality of u also gives P(χ<u)≤η.

questions.title: Recover the correct dense no-triangle exponential scale
questions.prompt: Assume n=3r and 0<p<1 is fixed. Construct r² edge-disjoint triangles in K_n using three equal parts and modular addition. Use their surviving copies to lower-bound the expected maximum triangle packing in G(n,p), then prove P(G is triangle-free)≤exp(−c_p n²). Compare with the empty-graph lower bound.
guide: Index each part by Z_r and use triangles (a_i,b_j,c_{i+j}). Every cross-part edge appears in exactly one of these triangles. Each triangle survives with probability p³, so the expected optimum packing is at least r²p³.

Maximum packing is one-edge Lipschitz. Azuma over C(n,2) edges gives P(Y=0)≤exp(−(r²p³)²/[2C(n,2)]), which is exp(−Ω_p(n²)). The event of no edges has probability (1−p)^{C(n,2)}, proving a matching exponential order for fixed p.

questions.title: Generalize the sparse critical-subgraph calculation
questions.prompt: Let r≥3, β∈(0,1), p=n^−α and c>0 fixed. Prove that every set of at most cn^β vertices is r-colorable with high probability whenever α>β+2(1−β)/r. Use a minimal non-r-colorable subgraph and display the exponent that controls the union bound.
guide: A vertex-minimal non-r-colorable graph has minimum degree at least r: otherwise remove a low-degree vertex and extend an r-coloring. A t-vertex witness therefore has at least rt/2 edges.

The probability of some witness is bounded by Σ_t C(n,t)C(C(t,2),⌈rt/2⌉)p^{⌈rt/2⌉}. Up to fixed constants its tth term is at most [C n^{1−αr/2}t^{r/2−1}]^t. At t≤cn^β the base tends to zero under the stated inequality; fixed small t and rounding are harmless.

questions.title: A family of constant-width chromatic windows
questions.prompt: Assume the small-subgraph coloring lemma with β=1/2 and the finite-η deletion estimate. For fixed r≥3 and α>1/2+1/r, prove that for every fixed η>0 there exists an integer u(n,η) with P(u≤χ(G(n,n^−α))≤u+r)≥1−3η for all sufficiently large n.
guide: The deletion estimate leaves at most c_η√n vertices outside a u-colorable graph except with probability η. The generalized sparse lemma says every such leftover vertex set is r-colorable except with another probability tending to zero.

Use disjoint palettes for the retained and deleted subgraphs, giving χ≤u+r. The quantile definition gives P(χ<u)≤η. Keep n's threshold dependent on η and r; this fixed-error statement alone is not yet a single center sequence with error o(1).

questions.title: Repair the quantifiers in an asymptotically certain window
questions.prompt: Suppose that for every fixed η>0 and all large enough n there is u(n,η) such that P(u≤χ_n≤u+r)≥1−3η. Construct one deterministic sequence v_n for which P(v_n≤χ_n≤v_n+r)→1. Show how the construction accommodates structural lemmas valid only for each fixed c_η.
guide: Choose η_j↓0 and increasing thresholds N_j so that the fixed-η_j probability bound and the needed structural lemma both hold for all n≥N_j. Choose the thresholds strictly increasing even when earlier estimates already hold.

Set j(n)=max{j:N_j≤n} and v_n=u(n,η_{j(n)}). Then j(n)→∞ and the error is at most 3η_{j(n)}. This diagonal construction allows c_η to grow slowly with n without asserting a uniform structural estimate that has not been proved.

questions.title: Compare two concentration mechanisms for the same packing
questions.prompt: For maximum edge-disjoint k-clique packing Y in G(n,1/2), assume E Y≥a n²/k^4 and a median m≥b n²/k^4, with positive fixed a,b. Compare the no-clique exponent from edge-exposure Azuma with the certifiable-variable bound using a certificate of C(k,2)Y present edges. State which mean–median comparison is still required if only the expectation hypothesis is known.
guide: Azuma gives a lower-tail exponent of order (E Y)²/n², namely n²/k^8. A b-clique witness uses C(k,2)b edge coordinates, and packing has edge replacement effect one.

The Talagrand certificate inequality with high threshold m and lower value zero gives P(Y=0)≤2exp(−m/[4C(k,2)]), hence exponent Ω(n²/k^6). The median lower bound is an additional input unless it is derived from concentration; substituting a mean without conversion is invalid.

questions.title: Concentrating an independence number does not determine χ
questions.prompt: For even n=2m, construct two graphs on n vertices with the same independence number m but chromatic numbers 2 and m+1. Use them to explain exactly what a concentration interval for α(G) implies through χ(G)≥n/α(G), and why it supplies no comparable upper bound.
guide: K_{m,m} has independence number m and chromatic number two. The disjoint union of K_{m+1} with m−1 isolated vertices also has independence number 1+(m−1)=m, but chromatic number m+1.

If α lies between a−t and a+t, the deterministic inequality yields only χ≥n/(a+t). A coloring partitions vertices into independent sets, but the existence of one large independent set does not guarantee a sequence of equally large sets in the remaining graph.

questions.title: Sharpen the window in the very sparse range
questions.prompt: For p=n^−α with fixed α>1, determine χ(G(n,p)) with high probability when 1<α<2 and when α>2. At α=2 compute the limiting probabilities of χ=1 and χ=2. Prove the absence of cycles by a first-moment calculation.
guide: The expected number of cycles is at most Σ_{k≥3}(np)^k/(2k)=o(1) because np→0. Thus the graph is a forest with high probability and needs at most two colors.

For 1<α<2 the expected edge count tends to infinity and P(no edges)=(1−p)^{C(n,2)}→0, so χ=2 with high probability. For α>2 no edge occurs with high probability, so χ=1. At α=2 the empty probability tends to e^{−1/2}, with all remaining mass on χ=2.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §7.3

questions.title: Grouping coordinates can make the denominator larger
questions.prompt: Let N=bk independent fair bits and L=Σ_i X_i. Compare singleton exposure with a gradation that reveals b blocks of k bits each. Compute replacement effects, squared-effect sums and actual variance. Explain why the number of exposure stages alone cannot rank two gradations.
guide: A singleton replacement changes L by at most one, so its worst-effect squared sum is N. Replacing an entire k-bit block changes L by at most k, giving b k²=Nk for the block bound.

The true variance is N/4 in both representations. If the block's independent internal structure is retained, its MGF still reflects k Bernoulli terms and recovers the sharper denominator. A theorem using only one worst block effect discards that information.
questions.followup: Give a statistic, such as chromatic number under vertex exposure, where a large block has an unusually small total effect.

questions.title: Expected query variance is not a pathwise budget
questions.prompt: Determine OR of N independent Bernoulli(p) bits by reading until the first one or until all bits are exhausted. Compute the expected number of queries and the maximum total query variance along a path. Compare the two as Np→∞ and explain which budget the adaptive theorem permits.
guide: The probability that query j is reached is (1−p)^{j−1}, so E Q=[1−(1−p)^N]/p. Each queried bit has global effect one and variance p(1−p).

Thus expected accumulated query variance is (1−p)[1−(1−p)^N], while the all-zero path has variance Np(1−p). The source theorem requires a bound for every path; replacing that by the expectation would omit a possible long branch.
questions.followup: Can one add a separate exceptional-path probability and then use a stopped argument?

questions.title: Prove the local MGF lemma quantitatively
questions.prompt: For 0≤p≤1 show that p e^{(1−p)a}+(1−p)e^{−pa}≤exp(p(1−p)a²) whenever |a|≤1. Use this to identify the ε=δ=1 specialization of the adaptive variance theorem and its allowable deviation range.
guide: The constant and linear Taylor terms are one and zero, and the quadratic coefficient is p(1−p)/2. For k≥3 the absolute coefficient is at most p(1−p)/k!, since p^{k−1}+(1−p)^{k−1}≤1.
For |a|≤1, Σ_{k≥3}|a|^k/k!≤(e−5/2)a²<a²/2. Hence the expression is at most 1+p(1−p)a²≤exp(p(1−p)a²). With λ=α/(2σ), the condition λC<1 is αC<2σ and the resulting two-sided exponent is −α²/4.
questions.followup: How does reducing the allowed |a| improve the coefficient toward one half?
questions.deliverable: A Taylor proof with a numerical remainder bound and the translated theorem parameters.

questions.title: A decision tree can be forced to inspect every bit
questions.prompt: For parity Y=X_1⊕…⊕X_N under independent fair bits, prove that every deterministic exact decision tree queries all N distinct coordinates on every path. Compute its path variance budget using effects one and compare it with Var(Y). Explain why the adaptive theorem need not be sharp.
guide: If a leaf leaves one bit unread, two full assignments consistent with its answers and differing only at that bit have opposite parity. Therefore no such leaf determines Y exactly.

Every path has N query contributions of 1/4, so σ²=N/4, whereas Y itself is a fair bit with variance 1/4. The query-variance proxy is an upper bound built from worst coordinate effects, not an identity for the output's variance.
questions.followup: Which argument fails if the algorithm may output a parity guess with a small error probability?

questions.title: An addressing function with a short exact query strategy
questions.prompt: Use ℓ fair selector bits to choose one of N=2^ℓ independent Bernoulli(p) data bits, and let Y be the selected bit. Show every coordinate has global effect at most one. Construct an exact query tree with maximum variance budget ℓ/4+p(1−p), and compare it with querying all coordinates.
guide: Read the selector first, then read exactly the selected data bit. The selector choices remain fair independent bits and the final data query has success probability p regardless of the address.

The path budget is ℓ/4+p(1−p), compared with ℓ/4+Np(1−p) for reading all data. Repeating the construction on m independent blocks and summing outputs gives a nontrivial family with effect one and total budget m times the short-tree budget.

questions.title: A path-budget MGF proof without a fixed query count
questions.prompt: Assume the local two-point MGF inequality with coefficient (1+ε)/2 for |a|≤δ. For an exact finite adaptive query tree with maximum effect C and every root-to-leaf variance sum at most v, prove E exp(λ(Y−E Y))≤exp((1+ε)λ²v/2) for |λ|C≤δ. Allow different tree depths.
guide: At a node querying bit i, write the two child means as μ+(1−p_i)b and μ−p_i b. Coupling the remaining independent variables identically proves |b|≤c_i.

Both child subtrees have remaining path budget at most v−p_i(1−p_i)c_i². Apply induction to their centered MGFs and then the local two-point lemma to their mean shifts. Leaves have zero residual fluctuation, so unequal depths cause no difficulty.

questions.title: Convert an exceptional query budget into an exceptional probability
questions.prompt: Suppose an adaptive reveal martingale has increments bounded by C, predictable conditional variances V_N, and P(V_N>v)≤η. Using the conditional Bernstein MGF lemma as an explicit assumed input, prove a tail bound of the form η+2exp(−t²/[2(v+C²+Ct/3)]). Define a stopping rule and account for its variance overshoot.
guide: Stop just after the first step whose accumulated predictable variance exceeds v, or at termination. Each single conditional variance is at most C², so the stopped process has pathwise variance budget at most v+C².

On the event V_N≤v the stopped and original processes coincide. Apply the two-sided Bernstein martingale bound to the stopped process and add the probability η of disagreement. This is a valid replacement for an expected-budget shortcut because the exceptional event is charged explicitly.
questions.followup: Can stopping immediately before an announced variance increment remove the C² overshoot?

questions.title: A small coordinate effect need not bound a dependent reveal
questions.prompt: Let X_1=…=X_N=B for a fair bit B and define f(x)=N^−1Σ_i x_i on the full cube. Each single-coordinate replacement effect is 1/N. Compute the Doob martingale under the dependent law and show why the first increment violates the product-space coupling conclusion.
guide: The unconditional expectation is 1/2. Revealing X_1 reveals B and therefore f(X)=B completely, so the first martingale increment has absolute value 1/2 and all later increments vanish.

The deterministic coordinate sensitivity is indeed 1/N on the ambient cube. But completions conditional on X_1=0 and X_1=1 differ in every remaining coordinate, so an identical-completion coupling is unavailable. Independence is the missing hypothesis.

questions.title: Check the admissible variance-sensitive deviation scale
questions.prompt: Let Y∼Bin(N,p_N), with p_N=N^−β and fixed 0<β<1. Apply the ε=δ=1 adaptive theorem with all bits queried to deviations t=√(Np_N)log N. Verify its side condition, compute the exponent scale, and compare with absolute-increment Azuma at the same t.
guide: Here C=1 and σ²=Np_N(1−p_N). The normalized deviation is α=t/σ≈log N. The side condition α<2σ holds because N^{(1−β)/2} dominates log N.

The adaptive bound is at most 2exp(−Θ(log²N)). Absolute-increment Azuma gives exponent t²/(2N)=Θ(p_N log²N), which tends to zero and is uninformative after capping the probability at one. The improvement comes with a verified deviation range.

questions.title: Weighted occupancy with nonuniform probabilities
questions.prompt: Throw m independent balls into n bins with probabilities q_j. Let Z=Σ_j w_j1_{bin j empty}, with 0≤w_j≤W. Derive E Z, prove a replacement effect at most W rather than 2W, and establish nonpositive covariance between distinct empty-bin indicators.
guide: The mean is Σ_j w_j(1−q_j)^m. Moving one ball can empty its old bin and fill its new bin; these contributions have opposite signs, so their net absolute change is at most max(w_old,w_new)≤W.

For distinct bins i,j, joint emptiness has probability (1−q_i−q_j)^m≤[(1−q_i)(1−q_j)]^m. Hence Var Z≤Σ_j w_j²a_j(1−a_j), where a_j=(1−q_j)^m. This variance calculation and the bounded-difference tail are separate statements.

questions.title: A Hilbert-space center obtained from a second moment
questions.prompt: Let v_i lie in a real Hilbert space and ε_i be independent fair signs. Prove E||Σ_i ε_i v_i||²=Σ_i||v_i||² and derive an upper tail above √(Σ_i||v_i||²). Explain when Jensen's bound for the mean is attained, using orthogonal and collinear examples.
guide: All cross inner products vanish after expectation because E ε_i ε_j=0 for i≠j. Jensen gives E||Σ ε_i v_i||≤√Σ||v_i||².

Replacing one sign changes the norm by at most 2||v_i||, and fair-sign centering halves the martingale effect to ||v_i||. Azuma gives an upper tail exp(−t²/[2Σ||v_i||²]) above the stated deterministic center. Orthogonal vectors make the norm constant and Jensen an equality; repeated collinear vectors generally do not.

questions.title: Weighted neighborhood expansion under a biased cube law
questions.prompt: Let independent biased bits carry product law μ, let a=μ(A)>0, and use weighted Hamming distance d_c with weights c_i>0 and V=Σc_i². Prove μ{d_c(X,A)>√(V ln(1/a)/2)+√(V ln(1/b)/2)}≤b for 0<b<1, using the range form of bounded differences.
guide: The distance D to A changes by at most c_i when bit i changes. Thus P(D−E D≤−t) and P(D−E D≥t) are each at most exp(−2t²/V), regardless of the coordinate biases.
Since P(D=0)=a, the lower-tail inequality implies E D≤√(V ln(1/a)/2). Apply the upper tail at √(V ln(1/b)/2). No uniform-counting interpretation is needed for the biased measure.

questions.title: Collisions are much less Lipschitz than empty bins
questions.prompt: For m independent uniform throws into n bins, let C=Σ_j C(N_j,2) count colliding pairs. Compute E C and the exact worst replacement effect m−1. Derive the resulting bounded-difference tail and explain why its fluctuation scale is poor when m=n.
guide: Each pair of balls collides with probability 1/n, so E C=C(m,2)/n. Moving a ball from a bin of size a to another of size b changes C by b−(a−1), whose absolute value is at most m−1.

The range-form denominator is m(m−1)², producing a scale m^{3/2}. When m=n, the mean is only Θ(n), and pair-indicator covariance calculations give variance Θ(n), so this worst-effect concentration is very coarse.

questions.title: Separate a variance-dependent center from a range-dependent tail

A sign replacement changes Z by at most 2||v_i||. The range-form inequality gives P(Z≥E Z+t)≤exp(−t²/[2Σ||v_i||²]). Replacing that denominator by Σ4p_i(1−p_i)||v_i||² needs a variance-sensitive theorem and its jump/deviation hypotheses.

questions.title: Poissonize empty bins and pay for conditioning back
questions.prompt: Replace m uniform balls in n bins by independent Poisson(m/n) bin counts and let Z be the number empty. Derive a Chernoff bound using independent empty-bin indicators. Transfer it to exactly m balls by conditioning on the total count, explicitly paying the factor 1/P(Poisson(m)=m). Compare the two natural centers.
guide: In the Poissonized model Z∼Bin(n,e^{−m/n}); standard MGF optimization gives its binomial tail. Conditional on the total m, the bin counts have the multinomial occupancy law, as follows by cancelling the factorial terms in their joint probability.

For any event E, P(E|total=m)≤P(E)/P(total=m). Stirling's estimate, assumed or proved, makes the conditioning factor Θ(√m). The Poissonized center ne^{−m/n} differs from n(1−1/n)^m; bound this deterministic shift before asserting a tail about the exact fixed-m mean.

questions.title: A bounded-effect surrogate for collision count
questions.prompt: For m=n uniform throws, define φ_L(0)=0 and φ_L(k)−φ_L(k−1)=min(k−1,L), and C_L=Σ_jφ_L(N_j). Prove replacement effect at most L, identify when C_L=C, and derive a tail for C around E C with an explicit occupancy-failure and expectation-shift term.
guide: Moving a ball changes C_L by the difference of two increments in [0,L], so the effect is at most L. Since φ_L(k)=C(k,2) for k≤L+1, equality holds whenever every bin has load at most L+1.

A union bound gives P(max N_j≥L+2)≤n[e/(L+2)]^{L+2}. Also 0≤E(C−C_L)≤C(n,2)P(max N_j≥L+2). Apply bounded differences to C_L with denominator nL² and add the bad-load probability and this deterministic center shift. Choose L to make both errors explicit.

questions.title: Isolated vertices: exact covariance and an edge effect
questions.prompt: In G(n,p) let I count isolated vertices. Compute E I and Cov(1_{u isolated},1_{v isolated}) for u≠v. Prove edge replacement effect at most two and give a bounded-difference tail. Explain the covariance sign by comparing this model with empty bins from independent throws.
guide: A vertex is isolated with probability a=(1−p)^{n−1}. Two vertices are both isolated when all 2n−3 incident edges are absent, so their covariance is (1−p)^{2n−3}−(1−p)^{2n−2}=p(1−p)^{2n−3}≥0.

Changing one edge affects isolation only at its two endpoints, so the full replacement effect is at most two. Range-form bounded differences gives P(|I−E I|≥t)≤2exp(−t²/[2C(n,2)]). The positive covariance comes from the shared required-absent edge; occupancy emptiness had a different dependence mechanism.
questions.followup: Use the covariance formula to write Var I exactly and compare sparse p=c/n with the tail proxy.
questions.deliverable: Exact first two moments and a correctly scaled edge-exposure bound.

questions.title: A Hilbert-space center cannot be used in every norm
questions.prompt: Take v_i=e_i in R^n and independent fair signs. Compute ||Σ_i ε_i e_i|| in ℓ_1, ℓ_2 and ℓ_∞. Use the examples to refute a universal bound E||Σ ε_i v_i||≤√Σ||v_i||² in arbitrary normed spaces, while retaining valid sign-Lipschitz concentration.
guide: Each e_i has norm one in all three spaces. The random sum has norms n, √n and one respectively, and these values are deterministic.

Thus the proposed square-root center fails in ℓ_1 by a factor √n. The reverse triangle inequality still bounds sign replacement by 2||v_i|| in every normed space, so concentration about the actual mean remains valid even when a Hilbert second-moment identity is unavailable.

questions.title: Compute convex distance to a threshold family
questions.prompt: Let A={y∈{0,1}^n:Σ_i y_i≥k} and let x have r<k ones. Prove d_T(x,A)²=(k−r)²/(n−r). Give an explicit convex combination attaining the minimum and a matching lower bound; handle r≥k separately.
guide: Any y∈A must turn at least k−r of x's zero coordinates into ones, regardless of any additional flips. Every convex mismatch vector therefore has total mass at least k−r on the n−r zero coordinates, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives squared norm at least (k−r)²/(n−r).

Average uniformly over y obtained by adding exactly k−r of those zero coordinates and changing no existing ones. The resulting mismatch vector is (k−r)/(n−r) on the zeros and zero elsewhere, attaining the lower bound. For r≥k, x∈A and distance is zero.
questions.followup: Compare this formula with ordinary Hamming distance k−r.

questions.title: Convex distance tensorizes on product target sets
questions.prompt: For nonempty A⊆Ω_1×…×Ω_r and B⊆Ω_{r+1}×…×Ω_n, prove d_T((x,z),A×B)²=d_T(x,A)²+d_T(z,B)². Justify the convex-hull identity involved; do not assume independent random coordinates are needed for this geometric identity.
guide: The mismatch set for A×B is U_A(x)×U_B(z). Its convex hull equals conv U_A(x)×conv U_B(z): one inclusion is immediate, and the other follows by multiplying convex-combination coefficients.

The squared Euclidean norm of a concatenated vector is the sum of squared norms, and the two factors can be minimized independently. Independence enters Talagrand's probability theorem, not this deterministic product-distance calculation.

questions.title: Find the sharp elementary comparisons with Hamming distance
questions.prompt: For nonempty A⊆{0,1}^n and h=d_H(x,A), prove h/√n≤d_T(x,A)≤√h. Give examples attaining each bound and explain why neither d_T=d_H nor d_T=√d_H is generally correct.
guide: Every mismatch vector has ℓ_1 norm at least h, so every convex combination does too. Cauchy–Schwarz gives its ℓ_2 norm at least h/√n. A nearest actual mismatch vector has exactly h ones and norm √h, proving the upper bound.

For the lower bound take x=0 and A consisting of all h-element subsets; their symmetric average has all coordinates h/n. For the upper bound take A a singleton at Hamming distance h, so no convexification reduces the norm.

questions.title: A dependent law violates the exponential-integral inequality
questions.prompt: Let X equal 0^n or 1^n with probability 1/2 each, and take A={0^n}. Compute μ(A)E exp(d_T(X,A)²/4) and determine the smallest integer n for which it exceeds one. Explain what remains true geometrically despite this failure.
guide: There is only one target, so d_T(0^n,A)=0 and d_T(1^n,A)=√n. The product in question is [1+e^{n/4}]/4.

It exceeds one when n>4ln3, first at n=5. The mismatch convex hull and all deterministic distance comparisons remain valid, but the measure is not a product measure and the stated probabilistic inequality fails.

questions.title: Separate two weighted-sum events by convex distance
questions.prompt: For independent bits and weights w_i≥0, let S=Σ_iw_iX_i and A={S≤a}. Prove d_T(x,A)≥(S(x)−a)/||w||_2 when S(x)>a. Deduce P(S≤a)P(S≥a+t||w||_2)≤e^{−t²/4}, assuming Talagrand's inequality.
guide: For every y∈A, S(x)−a≤S(x)−S(y)≤Σ_i w_i1_{x_i≠y_i}. The same lower bound holds after convexifying mismatch vectors. Cauchy–Schwarz then gives the distance estimate.

The high-sum event lies outside the convex-distance t-neighborhood of A. The Talagrand tail bound is at most e^{−t²/4}/P(A), giving the product inequality when P(A)>0; the zero-probability case is trivial.

questions.title: Compute convex distance with primal and dual certificates
questions.prompt: For explicitly listed A⊆{0,1}^n, design a reproducible algorithm returning upper and lower certificates for d_T(x,A), with gap at most 10^−6 on test instances. Use a threshold family as an analytic baseline. State how rational convex coefficients and a normalized dual vector certify the two bounds.
guide: Minimize ||Uθ||² over θ≥0, Σθ=1, where columns of U are mismatch vectors. Any feasible θ gives an upper bound. Any vector α with ||α||_2≤1 gives a lower bound min_{y∈A}α·u(x,y), by convex separation or the dual distance formula.

Numerical solver output alone is not a certificate: round θ, renormalize it and evaluate its norm with error control; scale a rational α conservatively to ensure norm at most one. Failure means the certified gap exceeds tolerance or the threshold-family baseline is missed, not merely that two floating outputs disagree.

questions.title: Find the sharp exponent for product subcube targets
questions.prompt: Let A fix an arbitrary set of binary coordinates to zero, under an independent product law with arbitrary biases. Determine the largest universal c for which μ(A)E exp(c d_T(X,A)²)≤1 holds for every such subcube and every dimension. Compare it with Talagrand's general exponent 1/4.
guide: For a fixed-to-zero coordinate with success probability p, squared convex distance contributes X_i and target mass contributes 1−p. Independence factors the expression into ∏_i(1−p_i)(1−p_i+p_i e^c).

At c=ln2 each factor is 1−p_i²≤1. Conversely the one-coordinate factor is 1+p(e^c−2)+O(p²) as p↓0, so any c>ln2 fails. Thus ln2 is sharp for this target class; this does not establish that exponent for arbitrary target sets.

questions.title: A union can be closer than every individual target
questions.prompt: Let x=000 and A_1={100}, A_2={010}, A_3={001}. Compute d_T(x,A_i) and d_T(x,A_1∪A_2∪A_3). Generalize to n singleton targets e_i and explain the difference from ordinary distance to a union.
guide: Each singleton target has its one mismatch vector e_i, of norm one. The union target has the simplex conv{e_1,e_2,e_3}; its minimum norm is attained at (1/3,1/3,1/3), giving 1/√3.

In n dimensions every point of this simplex has coordinate sum one, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives minimum norm 1/√n, attained at the uniform vector. Ordinary Hamming distance to the union is still one: convexification mixes different nearest witnesses.

questions.title: Convex distance to a parity class
questions.prompt: Let A be the even-parity class of {0,1}^n under the uniform product measure. Compute d_T(x,A) for x in and outside A. Evaluate E exp(d_T(X,A)²/4), and explain why a parity obstruction can have tiny convex distance even though it cannot be repaired without a coordinate change.
guide: For odd x, flipping any one bit reaches A, so all standard unit mismatch vectors belong to the mismatch set. Their average gives distance at most 1/√n.

Every mismatch to an even-parity point has an odd positive number of ones, hence ℓ_1 norm at least one; convexification and Cauchy–Schwarz give the reverse bound. Half the cube has distance zero and half has squared distance 1/n, so the exponential moment is [1+e^{1/(4n)}]/2.

questions.title: Certify a long increasing subsequence
questions.prompt: Let Z_1,…,Z_n be independent real random variables, with ties allowed, and let L be the longest strictly increasing subsequence length. Prove one-coordinate replacement effect one and b-coordinate certifiability of L≥b. Deduce P(L≤b−s)P(L≥b)≤exp(−s²/(4b)) for integer b≥1.
guide: Deleting the changed coordinate from an optimal increasing subsequence loses at most one element. Comparing in both directions proves the replacement effect, regardless of ties or whether the optimizer changes completely.

A specified increasing subsequence of b indices and their actual values remains increasing when all other coordinates change. It is a b-coordinate certificate. Substitute f(b)=b and t=s/√b in the certificate theorem; do not assume a formula for E L.

questions.title: Certify a maximum disjoint-pattern packing
questions.prompt: Let H be a fixed graph with h≥1 edges and no isolated vertices. In a graph with independent edge indicators, let Y be the largest number of edge-disjoint H-copies. Prove replacement effect one and a certificate of at most hb coordinates for Y≥b, then derive its median-centered lower tail.
guide: Removing one edge destroys at most one copy in an optimal edge-disjoint packing, even though it may destroy many nonpacked copies. This proves effect one for the optimum packing statistic.

A packing of b copies uses exactly hb present edges and certifies Y≥b. For an integer median m≥1, P(Y≥m)≥1/2 and the theorem gives P(Y≤m−s)≤2exp(−s²/(4hm)). The theorem applies to this packing, not to the raw number of H-copies.

questions.title: A weighted matching needs both an effect and a witness bound
questions.prompt: In a fixed graph, each edge is independently available and has deterministic weight in [a,W], where 0<a≤W. Let X be the maximum available matching weight. Prove replacement effect W and for every b>0 a certificate for X≥b using at most min(⌊|V|/2⌋,⌈b/a⌉) present edges. Write the resulting two-event tail with its W factor.
guide: Delete a changed edge from an optimal matching to lose at most W. To certify a value at least b, take edges from a witness matching until their total first reaches b; the number selected is at most ⌈b/a⌉ and never exceeds the matching size bound.
For sensitivity W, scale X by W or use the scaled certificate inequality directly. With f(b)=min(⌊|V|/2⌋,⌈b/a⌉), the bound is P(X≤b−s)P(X≥b)≤exp(−s²/[4W²f(b)]), for a nonzero certificate bound.

questions.title: Convert a median tail without silently changing centers
questions.prompt: Let X be a nonnegative integer statistic with effect one and certificate bound f(b)≤rb for integers b≥1, r≥1. Starting from the two-event certificate inequality, derive upper and lower tails about an integer median m≥1 and prove |E X−m|≤C(√(rm)+r) for an absolute constant C.
guide: For the lower tail use high threshold m: P(X≤m−s)≤2e^{−s²/(4rm)}. For the upper tail put b=m+s and low threshold m, giving P(X≥m+s)≤2e^{−s²/[4r(m+s)]}, with integer rounding handled explicitly.

Integrate or sum the tails. For s≤m bound m+s≤2m to get a Gaussian integral of order √(rm); for s>m use m+s≤2s to get an exponential tail of scale r. Enlarging constants handles lattice endpoints. This extra argument is what permits replacing a median by the mean.

questions.title: An independent set certifies absent edges
questions.prompt: For G(n,p), let α be the largest independent-set size. Prove edge replacement effect one, determine a valid certificate size for α≥b, and derive the certificate tail scale. Explain why listing only the b selected vertices is not a b-coordinate certificate in the independent-edge product space.
guide: Changing one edge can destroy at most one vertex from an independent set, so the optimum changes by at most one. An independent set on b vertices is certified by the absence of all C(b,2) internal edge coordinates.

Thus f(b)=C(b,2) is valid, yielding P(α≤b−s)P(α≥b)≤exp(−s²/[4C(b,2)]) for b≥2. The typical deviation scale supplied by this certificate is order b, not √b. Coordinates are random edges; vertex labels alone reveal none of their required nonedges.

questions.title: A budgeted coverage optimum is certifiable
questions.prompt: Fix integers k,L,b≥1 and subsets S_1,…,S_m of a universe, each of size at most L, and independently activate them. Let X be the maximum number of elements covered by at most k active sets. Prove effect L and a certificate using at most min(k,b) coordinates for X≥b, then compare the bound with disjoint equal-size sets as a benchmark.
guide: Deactivating one chosen set removes at most L covered elements. From any cover witnessing at least b elements, discard redundant sets or add useful sets until b elements are reached; at most b sets are needed because each useful addition contributes at least one new element, and never more than k are used.

The two-event bound is exp(−s²/[4L²min(k,b)]) for a deficit s below b. For m disjoint L-element sets, X=L min(B,k), where B is the number active. This benchmark permits exact binomial tails and exposes when the generic certificate bound loses constants or saturation information.

questions.title: Independent thinning yields a stronger conditional benchmark
questions.prompt: A deterministic host graph contains an edge-disjoint packing of b copies of a fixed h-edge graph H. Retain each host edge independently with probability p. Prove that the surviving optimum packing stochastically dominates Bin(b,p^h), derive a Chernoff lower tail, and compare it with the generic hb-coordinate certificate scale.
guide: Each of the b fixed copies survives exactly when its h edges survive. Their edge sets are disjoint, so these survival indicators are independent Bernoulli(p^h). All surviving fixed copies form an available packing.

Hence P(Y≤(1−δ)bp^h)≤exp(−δ²bp^h/2) for 0<δ<1. This bound is centered at a certified lower benchmark bp^h, rather than the unknown median of the optimum. It cannot be transferred to overlapping witness copies by claiming their survival indicators are independent.

questions.title: Short witnesses do not imply small replacement effects
questions.prompt: For n=2r+1 independent bits, let R be the longest consecutive run of ones. Show that R≥b has a b-coordinate certificate but that R does not have replacement effect one. Give two strings differing in a single bit with a change of r+1, and state a valid global effect bound.
guide: Fixing b consecutive one coordinates certifies a run of length at least b. But the string 1^r 0 1^r has longest run r, while changing its middle bit gives a run of length 2r+1, a change r+1.

A changed zero can merge the runs on its two sides. The improvement is at most min(left,right)+1≤⌈n/2⌉; the same bound follows for deletion by symmetry. Certifiability alone therefore does not justify the effect-one form of the theorem.

questions.title: Use occupied-bin witnesses when balls greatly outnumber bins
questions.prompt: Throw m independent balls into n bins with arbitrary destination probabilities and let D count occupied bins. Prove effect one and b-coordinate certifiability of D≥b. Derive a median lower-tail bound at scale √n, and compare it with the √m scale from exposing every ball by Azuma.
guide: One moved ball can empty its old bin and fill a new bin, with opposite contributions, so the number of occupied bins changes by at most one. One representative ball from each of b distinct bins certifies D≥b.

An integer median q satisfies q≤n, and the certificate theorem gives P(D≤q−s)≤2e^{−s²/(4q)}≤2e^{−s²/(4n)}. When m≫n this can improve the full ball-exposure scale √m. It remains a median-centered statement until a conversion argument is supplied.

questions.title: Compute the full C4 derivative profile
questions.prompt: Let X count unordered four-cycles in G(n,p), n≥4. Compute E X and expected derivatives for one edge, two adjacent edges, two disjoint edges, a three-edge path, and a full four-cycle. Identify incompatible partial edge sets and obtain E' up to absolute constants.
guide: There are 3C(n,4) four-cycles. A fixed edge lies in (n−2)(n−3) cycles; two adjacent edges lie in n−3 cycles; two disjoint edges occur as opposite edges in two cycles. Multiply by p to the number of missing cycle edges.

Thus the listed expectations are 3C(n,4)p^4, (n−2)(n−3)p³, (n−3)p², 2p², p and one. Three edges must form a path, and four must form a cycle. For large n, E'=Θ(max(n²p³,1)), retaining the highest derivative even when p is tiny.

questions.title: A count dominated by degree fluctuations
questions.prompt: Let Y=Σ_v C(d(v),3), counting three-edge stars in G(n,p). Derive the mean and all nonzero derivative-expectation types through order three. Compare E' with the triangle-count profile, and explain the role of the common center.
guide: The mean is nC(n−1,3)p³. For a fixed edge either endpoint can be the center, giving E_1=2C(n−2,2)p². Two adjacent fixed edges have a forced common center and n−3 choices for the remaining leaf, giving (n−3)p.

Two disjoint edges cannot lie in one three-star. A third derivative is one exactly when the fixed three edges form a star. Thus E'=Θ(max(n²p²,np,1)). This profile records the large influence of high-degree centers rather than treating star indicators as independent.

questions.title: A diverging mean can coexist with almost certain zero
questions.prompt: Let Z∼Bernoulli(ε), X_i∼Bernoulli(p) independently, and Y=ZΣ_{i=1}^N X_i. Compute its mean and derivative expectations. Choose ε→0 and N so that E Y→∞ but P(Y=0)→1, and explain how E' diagnoses the failure of relative concentration.
guide: Here μ=εNp, the Z derivative has expectation Np, each X_i derivative has expectation ε, and each mixed derivative ∂_Z∂_{X_i}Y equals one. Therefore E'=max(Np,ε,1).

Take fixed p=1/2, ε=N^−1/2. Then μ=√N/2 diverges but Y=0 with probability at least 1−N^−1/2. The derivative in the rare gate is much larger than the mean, so the Kim–Vu scale does not falsely promise concentration from μ alone.

questions.title: Keep graph vertices distinct from polynomial variables
questions.prompt: Assume the Kim–Vu bound P(|Y−μ|>a_k√(EE')λ^k)≤d_ke^−λ N^{k−1}, where N is the number of independent variables. For triangle count in G(n,p), choose λ so the probability is at most n^−D for fixed D>0. State a sufficient derivative-ratio condition for relative error o(1).
guide: The independent variables are potential edges, so N=C(n,2), not n. Since k=3, the polynomial prefactor is N²=O(n^4). Taking λ=(D+5)ln n plus a fixed constant absorbing d_3 makes the tail at most n^−D for large n.

When μ≥E', the relative threshold is a_3λ³√(E'/μ). Thus μ/E'≫log^6 n is sufficient for relative concentration at this failure level. All constants depend on fixed degree and D; the Kim–Vu inequality itself is assumed as the deep input.

questions.title: The Boolean polynomial must be multilinearized
questions.prompt: For independent Bernoulli(p) variables X_i, consider Y=(Σ_i X_i)². Express the same Boolean function as a multilinear nonnegative polynomial, compute μ,E_1,E_2, and compare with formally differentiating the unmultilinearized square. Explain which derivative profile belongs in Kim–Vu.
guide: On the Boolean cube X_i²=X_i, so Y=Σ_i X_i+2Σ_{i<j}X_iX_j. Hence μ=Np+N(N−1)p², E_1=1+2(N−1)p and E_2=2.

Differentiating the original algebraic square yields 2Σ X_i and expectation 2Np, a different expression because ordinary differentiation does not preserve equality restricted to {0,1}^N. Kim–Vu's hyperedge/partial-derivative definition uses the squarefree representation of the random statistic.

questions.title: Make rooted triangle concentration simultaneous
questions.prompt: For each vertex x of G(n,n^−α), let Y_x count triangles containing x, with fixed 0<α<2/3. Compute μ and E' for Y_x and use the stated Kim–Vu theorem to prove max_x|Y_x/μ−1|→0 in probability. Choose λ explicitly and include the union bound over roots.
guide: The mean is C(n−1,2)p³. A derivative in an edge incident to x has expectation (n−2)p²; a derivative in an edge not incident to x has expectation p². Nonempty higher derivatives include the value one, giving E'=Θ(max(np²,1)).

The ratio μ/E' has polynomial order min(np,n²p³), which diverges polynomially throughout α<2/3. Set λ=C log n with C>6. The relative threshold O(log³n√(E'/μ)) tends to zero, while n·O(n^4e^−λ) tends to zero. No independence between different roots is required.
questions.followup: Why does the calculation stop giving relative concentration at α=2/3?
questions.deliverable: A rooted derivative audit and a simultaneous concentration proof with all factors counted.

questions.topic: Kim–Vu: derivative expectations matter

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §7.8

questions.title: A general derivative criterion for a fixed graph
questions.prompt: Let H be a fixed simple graph with v vertices, e≥1 edges and no isolated vertices. For its unlabeled-copy count in G(n,p), show up to H-dependent constants that μ/E' is the minimum of n^{v(F)}p^{e(F)} over nonempty edge-subgraphs F⊆H, where v(F) counts incident vertices. Deduce a sufficient Kim–Vu relative-concentration criterion and identify its density threshold for p=n^−α.
guide: Fixing a derivative edge set isomorphic to F leaves O_H(n^{v−v(F)}) completions and e−e(F) independent edges. Conversely every compatible fixed F has Θ_H of that many completions for n sufficiently large; multiple embeddings contribute only H-dependent constants.

Since μ=Θ_H(n^v p^e), divide by the largest nonempty derivative expectation to obtain the minimum ratio. Requiring every such n^{v(F)}p^{e(F)}≫log^{2e}n suffices with λ=C log n. For a fixed power p=n^−α this holds when α<min_F v(F)/e(F); this is a sufficient theorem-derived threshold, not a claim of necessity for every concentration notion.
questions.followup: Evaluate the criterion for triangles, four-cycles and a graph with a dense core plus a pendant edge.
questions.deliverable: A general derivative comparison and three explicit density calculations.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §7.8

questions.title: A simple polynomial whose highest derivative cannot be omitted
questions.prompt: Let Y count length-two paths from a fixed root x with distinct remaining vertices in G(n,p), counting each unordered edge set once. Compute μ and the first- and second-derivative expectation types. Determine when μ/E' diverges for p=n^−α, and compare the result with rooted triangle counts.
guide: A path may have x as an endpoint or as its center if 'from a root' is ambiguous; fix the endpoint convention explicitly. With endpoint x, choose its neighbor u and then v≠x,u, giving μ=(n−1)(n−2)p².

For an edge xu, there are n−2 completions and derivative expectation (n−2)p. For an edge uv not incident to x, either endpoint can be the middle vertex, giving 2p. A compatible two-edge path derivative is one. Thus E'=Θ(max(np,1)) and μ/E' diverges polynomially for α<1.
questions.followup: Repeat the calculation when x is required to be the center, and identify the constant-factor changes.

questions.title: Nonnegative values are not the coefficient hypothesis
questions.prompt: Consider Y=X_1+X_2−2X_1X_2 on two independent Bernoulli bits. Verify Y≥0 pointwise, compute its multilinear coefficients and derivative expectations, and explain why the stated nonnegative-coefficient Kim–Vu theorem does not apply. Show that adding a constant cannot repair the offending coefficient.
guide: The values are zero at 00 and 11 and one at 01 and 10, so Y is a nonnegative indicator. Its unique multilinear coefficient of X_1X_2 is −2.

The expected first derivatives are 1−2p and the second derivative is −2. The theorem's E_i are built from nonnegative monomial weights, a structure absent here. A constant shift changes only the empty monomial and leaves the negative degree-two coefficient untouched.
questions.followup: Can a different representation using additional independent coordinates be asserted without constructing it?
questions.deliverable: A four-state table and a precise hypothesis failure, without claiming the statistic is unconcentrated.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §7.8

questions.title: Prove the BSC rate converse with an error indicator
questions.prompt: A uniform message M from a codebook of size 2^{nR} is sent through BSC(p), and a decoder has average error P_e. Prove nR≤n[1−H_2(p)]+1+P_e nR. Derive the asymptotic converse for P_e→0, proving the needed conditional-entropy estimate rather than invoking capacity as a black box.
guide: With output Y, H(Y)≤n and H(Y|M)=nH_2(p), so I(M;Y)≤n[1−H_2(p)]. Let E indicate decoding error; conditioning on E gives H(M|Y)≤H(E)+P_e log_2|C|≤1+P_e nR.
Use H(M)=I(M;Y)+H(M|Y). If P_e→0 and rates remain finite, the inequality forces limsup R≤1−H_2(p). This complements random-coding achievability and specifies the average-message error convention.
questions.followup: How does the estimate improve if, on error, only |C|−1 alternatives are possible?
questions.deliverable: A self-contained information-theoretic converse and the limiting quantifiers.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §15.1

questions.title: Achievability from a random parity-check matrix
questions.prompt: Choose an m×n binary matrix H with independent fair entries and use code ker H. For BSC(p), decode by selecting a noise vector of weight at most t with the observed syndrome, rejecting ambiguities. Prove an ensemble error bound P(weight noise>t)+Vol(n,t)2^−m and a rate lower bound 1−m/n.
guide: For any distinct noise vectors z,z', their difference is nonzero, and a random row has dot product zero with it with probability 1/2. Thus P_H(Hz=Hz')=2^−m. Union-bound over competing low-weight noise vectors for each actual typical z.

The kernel dimension is n−rank H≥n−m even if H is rank deficient. Choose t=(p+δ)n and m/n>H_2(p+δ). The averaged noise-decoding error tends to zero, so some matrix works; linear translation symmetry makes this decoder's error the same for every transmitted codeword.
questions.followup: Why does a rank-deficient matrix not invalidate either the collision probability or the rate lower bound?
questions.deliverable: A linear-code construction, a syndrome-collision bound and a complete rate calculation.

questions.title: Turn average-message reliability into maximum-message reliability
questions.prompt: Suppose a length-n code has M messages and average decoding error at most ε_n. Show there is a subcode of at least M/2 messages with maximum error at most 2ε_n. Define the subcode decoder carefully and calculate the rate loss. Explain why this does not convert random-noise reliability into worst-case error correction.
guide: At least half the messages have individual error at most 2ε_n by Markov's inequality. Retain those messages. Use the old decoder when it outputs a retained message, and otherwise output any fixed retained message or declare failure.

For a retained transmitted message, every formerly correct output remains correct; reassigning discarded outputs cannot increase error. The subcode rate decreases by at most 1/n. The bound still averages over channel noise for each message and imposes no minimum-distance guarantee.
questions.followup: How does retaining a 1−θ fraction trade rate loss against the maximum-error multiplier?
questions.deliverable: A decoder construction and a rate/error tradeoff valid for every n.

questions.title: A finite numerical random-coding guarantee
questions.prompt: For BSC(p) with 0<p<1/2 and rate R<1−H_2(p), derive the bound 2e^{−2δ²n}+2^{−n[1−R−H_2(p+δ)]} for an appropriate typical-ball decoder, with 0<δ<1/2−p. For p=0.1,R=0.4 choose δ explicitly and give an n sufficient for error at most 10^−3.
guide: Hoeffding bounds atypical noise weight by at most 2e^{−2δ²n}; a one-sided version can improve the factor. The Hamming-ball inequality Vol(n,(p+δ)n)≤2^{nH_2(p+δ)} controls confusion with other random codewords.

Choose, for example, δ=0.02 and evaluate g=1−0.4−H_2(0.12)>0. It is sufficient to take n at least max{ln(4000)/(2δ²),log_2(2000)/g}, with integer radius rounding absorbed by choosing t=⌊(p+δ)n⌋ and keeping the entropy upper bound.
questions.followup: How would you optimize δ numerically, and which term dominates for the displayed conservative choice?
questions.deliverable: A finite error bound, a computed entropy gap and a reproducible blocklength calculation.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §15.1

questions.title: Repeat the argument for an erasure channel
questions.prompt: Each transmitted bit is independently erased with probability e∈(0,1), and the receiver knows the erased positions. Use a random k×n generator matrix to show reliable transmission at every rate k/n<1−e. Bound the probability that the unerased columns fail to determine the message without assuming full matrix rank.
guide: Condition on m unerased coordinates. For any fixed nonzero message difference, its image in those m random columns is all zero with probability 2^−m. A union bound over fewer than 2^k differences bounds rank failure by 2^{k−m}.

With high probability m≥(1−e−δ)n. If k≤(1−e−2δ)n, the conditional failure probability is at most 2^{−δn}; add the binomial atypical-erasure probability. This argument itself also ensures injective encoding for a good matrix, because a message difference invisible everywhere is invisible on every unerased set.
questions.followup: Why is the entropy penalty H_2(p) for bit flips replaced here by the erasure fraction e?
questions.deliverable: A complete random-linear-code proof with separate noise and rank-failure events.

questions.title: Investigate a decoder with the wrong noise radius
questions.prompt: For BSC(p), consider random codebooks and a decoder accepting a unique codeword within radius qn, with fixed q∈(0,1/2). Derive a rigorous guarantee when q>p and R<1−H_2(q). Show why q
guide: For q>p, use the same typical-noise plus confusion decomposition, now with q controlling both the noise tail and ball volume. A positive exponent requires the stated rate inequality; failure of this sufficient inequality is not itself a theorem that every such decoder fails.

For q<p, the law of large numbers makes P(weight noise≤qn) tend to zero, so the prescribed candidate-list decoder cannot output the transmitted word except on that rare event. For n≤16 enumerate all noise vectors with exact BSC weights and compare observed errors to the proven bound for seeded random codebooks.
