questions.title: A covering version of the random-code calculation
questions.prompt: For D∈(0,1/2), choose M uniform independent centers in {0,1}^n. Prove that the expected fraction of strings farther than Dn from every center is at most exp(−M Vol(n,⌊Dn⌋)/2^n). Using a standard Stirling estimate as an explicit input, show rates above 1−H_2(D) permit vanishing uncovered fraction. Compare the quantifiers with channel coding.
guide: For each fixed source string, a uniform center covers it with probability V/2^n. Independence of centers makes its uncovered probability (1−V/2^n)^M≤e^{−MV/2^n}; average over all source strings.

Stirling gives V≥2^{nH_2(D)−O(log n)}. With M=2^{nR} and R>1−H_2(D), the expected uncovered fraction tends to zero, hence some center set works. This is an average source-covering guarantee; it neither requires disjoint balls nor corrects adversarial channel errors.
questions.followup: What extra logarithmic factor in M would ensure every source string is covered by a union bound?

questions.title: Two concrete code transformations have different guarantees
questions.prompt: Let C⊆{0,1}^n have size M and minimum distance d. Delete t fixed coordinates to puncture the code, assuming t<d; prove size is preserved and distance is at least d−t. Separately, fix a common value on t coordinates and shorten: prove a subcode of size at least M/2^t and distance at least d remains after deletion.
guide: If two codewords become identical after puncturing, they differed in at most t<d positions, impossible. Each pair loses at most t differing coordinates, proving the distance lower bound.

For shortening, partition by the 2^t possible patterns and keep a largest fiber. All retained words agree on the deleted coordinates, so deleting them loses no pairwise distance. Track the new length n−t and the distinct cardinality losses before forming rate bounds.
questions.followup: Why do these minimum-distance facts alone not determine BSC decoding error at a given rate?

questions.title: The fair input maximizes one-use BSC information
questions.prompt: Let X∼Bernoulli(q), N∼Bernoulli(p) independently and Y=X⊕N, with p∈(0,1/2). Compute I(X;Y), prove its maximum over q is 1−H_2(p), and identify the maximizing q. Explain how this calculation differs from constructing a long reliable code.
guide: The output-one probability is p+(1−2p)q. Therefore H(Y)=H_2(p+(1−2p)q), while H(Y|X)=H_2(p), giving the exact mutual-information expression.

Binary entropy is uniquely maximized at one half, and p+(1−2p)q=1/2 exactly when q=1/2. This proves the single-use optimizer; a coding theorem still requires a block construction, a decoder and a vanishing-error argument.

questions.title: An explicit state below the sphere bound that still loses
questions.prompt: In the adaptive Liar Game with five items, five yes/no questions and at most one lie, show that the initial normalized sphere weight is 30/32<1 but every first question allows Carole a successor state of weight greater than one. Examine all split sizes using complement symmetry.
guide: A first question containing s items produces successor lie-budget counts (5−s,s) or (s,5−s), ordered as zero-budget then one-budget. With four questions left, their unnormalized weights are 25−4s and 5+4s, divided by 16.

By complement symmetry take s≤2. Then the larger successor weight is (25−4s)/16≥17/16>1. The existing weight defense now wins for Carole. This is a concrete integrality obstruction, not a failure of the necessary sphere calculation.
questions.followup: Which additional spare capacity would be needed to balance both first successors below one?

questions.title: Write an exact finite-state solver
questions.prompt: For a state x=(x_0,…,x_k) with q questions left, derive an exact recursive winning criterion for Paul by considering integers 0≤a_i≤x_i in a question. Give the two successor vectors and the terminal condition. Specify memoization and complement symmetry sufficient to compute all states with total at most eight and k≤2.
guide: Set x_{k+1}=a_{k+1}=0. One branch has y_i=a_i+(x_{i+1}−a_{i+1}); the other has z_i=(x_i−a_i)+a_{i+1}. Paul wins iff some a makes both successors winning with q−1 questions.

At q=0 the state wins iff Σ_i x_i≤1. Memoize by the count tuple and q; exchanging a with x−a swaps branches, so only one representative is needed. The recursion is exact because item labels within a common remaining-budget class are strategically interchangeable.
questions.followup: How should the solver output a human-checkable adversary certificate for a losing state?

questions.title: A perfect sphere-bound example from a parity-check code
questions.prompt: Let q=2^r−1 and let H be the r×q binary matrix containing every nonzero column of F_2^r exactly once. Use ker H as fixed answer strings to identify 2^{q−r} items despite one arbitrary lie. Prove unique syndrome decoding and equality in the sphere count.
guide: No nonzero codeword has weight one or two, since no column is zero and no two columns coincide. A one-bit error has syndrome equal to its unique column, so the error position is recoverable; syndrome zero means no error.

The r rows have full rank because the standard basis columns occur. Thus the code has 2^{q−r} words, and each radius-one ball has q+1=2^r strings. Their disjoint balls exhaust all 2^q possible response strings, meeting the count exactly for this special nonadaptive construction.
questions.followup: Why does this special equality construction not prove the converse of the sphere bound for arbitrary q?

questions.title: Question-size constraints change even the no-lie capacity
questions.prompt: With no lies, allow q adaptive membership questions but require every queried subset of the original candidate set to have at most s elements, where s≥1. Let N_s(q) be the maximum identifiable number. Prove N_s(0)=1 and N_s(q)=N_s(q−1)+min(s,N_s(q−1)), and solve its exponential-then-linear behavior.
guide: At the root, the Yes branch contains at most s candidates and both branches must contain at most N_s(q−1) identifiable candidates. Their sum is at most the displayed recurrence.

Conversely split candidates into a Yes group of size min(s,N_s(q−1)) and a No group of size N_s(q−1), then use optimal subtrees; questions can be restricted to the current branch without increasing their size. Capacity doubles until it first reaches or exceeds s, then grows by s per extra question.

questions.title: Allow a final list of L candidates
questions.prompt: Modify the adaptive Liar Game so Paul succeeds when at most L candidates survive, with L≥1. Prove that normalized chip weight greater than L lets Carole win. Deduce a necessary sphere bound for n initially equal-budget items and discuss the equality case without asserting a converse.
guide: The same average-of-successor-weights identity lets Carole retain a weight above L at every step. With zero questions remaining the weight is exactly the number of surviving chips, so at least L+1 survive.

For n items and k lies, the necessary condition is nΣ_{j≤k}C(q,j)≤L2^q. The proof changes the terminal threshold but not the integer feasibility of root partitions; equality or slack below the threshold still requires an actual questioning strategy.

questions.title: Generalize the adversary weight to an alphabet of answers
questions.prompt: Suppose every question partitions candidates into ℓ≥2 answer classes and at most k answers may be changed to any of the other ℓ−1 symbols. Derive the normalized weight B_ℓ(q,k)=ℓ^−qΣ_{j≤k}C(q,j)(ℓ−1)^j, prove its average-successor identity, and obtain the adaptive impossibility bound.
guide: If Carole picks a uniformly random reported symbol, a given candidate receives a lie with conditional probability (ℓ−1)/ℓ at every round, even when future questions adapt. Its survival probability is exactly the displayed binomial-tail expression.

Averaging over the ℓ successors preserves total weight. Thus weight greater than one yields a deterministic weight-maximizing adversary and the necessary condition nΣ_{j≤k}C(q,j)(ℓ−1)^j≤ℓ^q. This extends the obstruction; it does not construct balancing questions below it.

questions.title: Measure the gap between counting and exact play
questions.prompt: Use the exact chip-state recursion to enumerate k=1 states of at most eight chips and q≤7. Compare minimax winning status with normalized weight≤1. questions.title: A chip has a binomial movement law even in an adaptive game
questions.prompt: Fix any adaptive Paul strategy and let Carole answer each question with a fresh fair bit. For one specified chip, prove its movement indicators are independent fair bits up to q rounds, despite the adaptively chosen partitions. Explain why movements of different chips need not be independent, and give identical and complementary examples.
guide: Condition on the entire history before a round. Whether the chip is selected is already fixed, and one of the two fresh answers moves it; its conditional movement probability is exactly one half. Iterating these conditional probabilities gives the product law for that chip's movement sequence.

Two chips always placed on the same side have identical movement indicators; two always placed on opposite sides have complementary indicators. Linearity of expectation over survival indicators remains valid, but a binomial law for the total number of survivors generally does not follow.

questions.title: Add marked erasures to fixed-answer identification
questions.prompt: For a nonadaptive binary answer code, allow up to k≥0 adversarial bit flips and 0≤s≤q marked erasures. Prove that minimum distance at least 2k+s+1 guarantees unique identification. Derive the necessary sphere bound MΣ_{j≤k}C(q−s,j)≤2^{q−s} for any fixed erased coordinate set, and explain the roles of t<d puncturing.
guide: If two codewords both fit a received word after s erased coordinates and k errors each, they differ in at most 2k+s coordinates, contradicting the distance bound. Conversely a distance at most 2k+s allows erasing up to s disagreements and splitting the remaining disagreements between two error patterns.

Fix an erased coordinate set. Any successful code has distinct punctured words and disjoint radius-k balls in the remaining q−s coordinates. Counting these balls gives the necessary inequality. This concerns fixed answer strings; adaptive question trees require their own state analysis.

questions.title: Build the dyadic split by carrying bundles
questions.prompt: Given finitely many chips at positive integer levels with total weight W=Σ_i x_i2^−i≥1, construct an original-chip subset of weight exactly 1/2. Give a binary-carry algorithm that records bundles and use the subset to specify a safe first Tenure move.
guide: Repeatedly merge two level-i bundles into one bundle of weight 2^{−(i−1)}, retaining the list of original chips in each bundle. If no level-one bundle could be formed, at most one bundle at every positive level would remain, with total weight strictly below one.

A level-one bundle supplies weight exactly 1/2; its complement has weight at least 1/2. Promoting either chosen part doubles its weight, so both successors have weight at least one. Bundles are only a bookkeeping device; the actual move splits original chips, not artificial merged pieces.

questions.title: Only chips that can arrive by the deadline count
questions.prompt: Suppose the Tenure Game must be won within h moves. Show that its exact winning criterion is Σ_{1≤i≤h}x_i2^−i≥1, regardless of chips at deeper levels. Prove both directions and treat h=0 and an initially tenured chip separately.
guide: Chips initially deeper than h cannot reach level zero by the deadline. The smaller-successor weight defense applied only to levels at most h keeps their weight below one if the truncated initial weight is below one.

If the truncated weight is at least one, ignore deeper chips and use the ordinary dyadic winning strategy on levels at most h. Every surviving useful chip moves up at each round, so the strategy ends within h moves. An initial level-zero chip is an immediate win; otherwise h=0 cannot suffice.

questions.title: Promotions by a fixed number of levels
questions.prompt: Modify the binary Tenure Game so every retained chip moves from level i to max(0,i−d), with fixed integer d≥1, while the other side is deleted. Prove the exact threshold Σ_i x_i2^{−⌈i/d⌉}≥1. Translate an optimal strategy from the ordinary game.

The modified game is therefore identical, at the effective-level level, to the ordinary binary Tenure Game. Aggregate counts with equal effective level and apply the dyadic threshold and splitting construction. The original level i itself is not the correct exponent when d>1.

questions.title: An ℓ-way Tenure Game and an ℓ-adic split
questions.prompt: Let Paul partition chips into ℓ≥2 groups, after which Carole retains one group, promotes it by one level and deletes all others. Prove the exact criterion Σ_i x_iℓ^−i≥1. Establish the ℓ-adic partition lemma needed for the winning direction, rather than using only an averaging argument.
guide: The average of the ℓ successor weights is the current weight, so below one Carole can preserve a weight below one. For the converse, merge ℓ same-level chips into one bundle at the next level.

If fewer than ℓ bundles remain at every positive level, their total weight is less than Σ_{i≥1}(ℓ−1)ℓ^−i=1. Thus weight at least one supplies enough level-one bundles to extract ℓ disjoint parts of weight 1/ℓ; assign leftover chips arbitrarily. Every successor has weight at least one.
questions.followup: How do you recover a partition of the original chips from merged bundles?
questions.deliverable: A full threshold proof including a constructive ℓ-adic lemma.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §15.3

questions.title: A weight-one state need not split without dyadic structure
questions.prompt: Consider a variant with indivisible chips of arbitrary positive weights: retain one of two parts, double its chip weights and delete the other part; reaching individual weight at least one wins. Show that three chips of weight 1/3 have total one but lose against a minimizing Carole. Identify the failed subset-sum step.
guide: Every partition splits the three chips as 0 versus 3 or 1 versus 2. Carole chooses the smaller-weight side. In the nontrivial split only one chip survives, with new weight 2/3; in the trivial split no chip survives.

From total weight below one, choosing the smaller successor preserves total weight below one and prevents an individual chip of weight one. The missing property is a subset of total weight exactly 1/2, which dyadic chips guarantee and these thirds do not.
questions.followup: Does total weight strictly above one repair the statement for arbitrary indivisible weights?
questions.deliverable: A complete losing strategy and a pinpointed failure of the dyadic argument.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §15.3

questions.title: The dyadic weight is an exact random-answer success probability
questions.prompt: Let Carole independently choose either retained side with probability 1/2 each round. Prove that Paul's maximum probability of eventually obtaining tenure is min(1,W), where W=Σ_i x_i2^−i. For W≤1 construct a prefix-free binary tree whose leaves have the given chip depths, proving the required coding lemma by dyadic interval packing.
guide: Each chip at level i survives its first i choices with probability 2^−i under any Paul strategy, so the probability of any success is at most W. For W≤1, pack disjoint dyadic intervals of lengths 2^−i in [0,1); their binary addresses form a prefix-free collection.

At each node assign chips to its two descendant subtrees. A fair answer path reaches each chip leaf with exactly its dyadic probability, and the leaf events are disjoint, giving success probability W. If W≥1, the deterministic threshold strategy succeeds for every answer path and hence with probability one.
questions.followup: Why is an arbitrary collection of binary strings of the right lengths insufficient without prefix-freeness?
questions.deliverable: A sharp probabilistic theorem, an elementary coding construction and the matching upper bound.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §15.3

questions.title: Expected duration at exact weight one
questions.prompt: Assume W=1 and fair independent Carole choices. Prove that any strategy which wins on every branch has expected stopping time Σ_i i x_i2^−i, and construct one using a prefix tree. Work out the state x_1=1,x_2=1,x_3=2. Justify extending play after a first win when computing individual chip probabilities.
guide: In a full fictitious continuation, each chip's eventual tenure indicator has expectation 2^−i, so the expected number tenured is one. A surely winning strategy has at least one tenured chip on every answer path; consequently there is exactly one almost surely, ruling out overlapping success events.

The unique successful chip's tenure time is its starting level i, and its success probability is 2^−i. Therefore E T=Σ_i i x_i2^−i. The example has value 1/2+1/2+3/4=7/4, attained by leaf words 0,10,110,111. The continuation is only analytical and does not delay the actual stopping time.
questions.followup: Which step breaks when W>1 and success events may overlap?
questions.deliverable: A duration identity, a legal strategy tree and a worked heterogeneous example.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §15.3

questions.title: A sharp robustness threshold before play
questions.prompt: Before the ordinary Tenure Game begins, Carole may delete up to r chips, where r is a fixed nonnegative integer. Determine a necessary and sufficient winning condition for Paul in terms of W and the r largest individual dyadic weights. Specialize to n chips all at level k.
guide: After the deletion phase the ordinary threshold applies. Carole minimizes remaining total weight by deleting the r heaviest chips, or all chips if fewer than r are present.

Paul can win against every allowed deletion exactly when W minus the sum of those largest weights is at least one. For one level k this becomes n−r≥2^k, with the convention that a negative remaining count means no chips. This is a worst-case robustness statement, not an average deletion estimate.
questions.followup: How would a level-dependent deletion cost turn the preliminary adversary step into a knapsack problem?
questions.deliverable: A sharp criterion and its homogeneous specialization.

questions.title: Restricting legal splits destroys the threshold converse
questions.prompt: Modify the game so Paul must select all or none of the chips at each occupied level. Show that for n≥2 chips all at one positive level, Carole can win immediately even when their total dyadic weight is arbitrarily large. Explain why the usual carry lemma does not produce a legal move in this variant.
guide: With only one occupied level, every legal selected set is either the entire chip set or empty. Carole retains the empty side and deletes all chips, so Paul loses in one move.

By choosing n as large as desired the initial total n2^−k can exceed one by any factor. The ordinary theorem requires the ability to separate individual equal-level chips; carrying bundles proves existence of an arbitrary chip subset, not a union of whole levels.
questions.followup: What minimal relaxation of the move restriction makes the homogeneous level-k threshold attainable again?
questions.deliverable: A legal-move counterexample and a precise statement of the lost splitting freedom.

questions.title: Construct a deterministic chooser directly
questions.prompt: In T rounds in dimension d, Pusher gives v_t∈{−1,1}^d before Chooser selects ε_t. Use Φ_t=Σ_j cosh(λS_{t,j}) to construct a deterministic chooser with ||S_T||_∞≤√(2T ln(2d)). Prove the potential update against an adaptive Pusher.
guide: For a fixed current vector, the average potential of the two sign choices is cosh(λ)Φ_{t−1}, because each coordinate increment has magnitude one. Choose the sign with no larger than this average.
Then Φ_T≤d(coshλ)^T≤d e^{Tλ²/2}. Since cosh(λs)≥e^{λ|s|}/2, the norm is at most ln(2d)/λ+Tλ/2. Optimize λ=√(2ln(2d)/T). The rule is deterministic and uses only the current state and offered vector.
questions.followup: How does the same potential handle entries in [−1,1]?
questions.deliverable: An explicit online sign rule and its optimized discrepancy guarantee.

questions.title: A geometric greedy rule gives a different bound
questions.prompt: Let Pusher offer arbitrary vectors v_t∈R^d with ||v_t||_2≤L_t. Choose ε_t to make ⟨S_{t−1},ε_tv_t⟩≤0. Prove ||S_T||_2²≤Σ_tL_t² and compare the induced infinity bound with exponential-potential balancing for sign vectors.
guide: Expand ||S_{t−1}+ε_tv_t||_2². The cross term is nonpositive by the choice of sign, so the squared norm increases by at most ||v_t||². Sum this inequality over all rounds.

For sign vectors L_t²=d, the guarantee is √(Td), whereas a coordinate exponential potential gives √(2Tln(2d)). The Euclidean rule remains useful for small vector norms or when Euclidean rather than coordinate error is the objective.
questions.followup: Can the chooser use this argument in an arbitrary norm without an inner product?

questions.title: Control every prefix without a union bound over times
questions.prompt: Suppose fresh fair Chooser signs multiply adaptive predictable vectors with |v_{t,j}|≤a_t, where Σ_t a_t²≤V deterministically. Prove P(max_{t≤T,j≤d}|S_{t,j}|≥u)≤2d exp(−u²/(2V)) using the maximal martingale inequality. Contrast it with a union over all dT coordinate-time pairs.
guide: For each coordinate, S_{t,j} is a martingale with conditional sign-MGF at most exp(λ²a_t²/2). Apply the maximal exponential-supermartingale argument separately to its positive and negative excursions.

Union-bound only over coordinates and signs, giving 2d rather than 2dT. Setting u=√(2Vln(2d/η)) controls every prefix with failure at most η. Predictability of v_t is essential: it must be selected before the current fresh sign is seen.
questions.followup: How does the result change if Pusher sees ε_t before offering v_t?

questions.title: A nonadaptive construction saturating the linear scale
questions.prompt: Take d=2^T coordinates indexed by σ∈{−1,1}^T. At round t let the offered vector have coordinate v_{t,σ}=σ_t. Prove that every Chooser sign sequence produces final infinity norm T. Compare this with the logarithmic-dimension upper bound and state what the example does not prove for d=T.
guide: For a realized Chooser sequence ε, use the coordinate indexed by σ=ε. Its final sum is Σ_t ε_tσ_t=T, while no coordinate can have absolute sum larger than T.

The offered vectors were fixed before play, so this lower bound needs no adaptivity. Since ln d=Tln2, the generic √(Tln d) scale is already order T here. The construction does not establish the √(Tln T) lower bound in the d=T regime.
questions.followup: How many coordinates suffice if only a specified subset of sign sequences needs to be defeated?

questions.title: A fixed bias creates linear drift
questions.prompt: Let Chooser independently choose ε_t=1 with probability q≠1/2, and let Pusher always offer the scalar vector one. Show that |S_T| has linear order T with high probability. Give an explicit deviation inequality and explain why a fair-sign martingale proof cannot be reused.
guide: E S_T=(2q−1)T. Hoeffding for the sum of signs gives P(|S_T−(2q−1)T|≥u)≤2exp(−u²/(2T)). This is concentration around the nonzero drift, obtained from independent increments with range length two.
Take u=|2q−1|T/2 to obtain |S_T|≥|2q−1|T/2 except with probability at most 2exp(−(2q−1)²T/8). The increments have nonzero conditional mean, so centering or a different choosing strategy is necessary.
questions.followup: What if the bias q_t tends to one half but Σ_t(2q_t−1) remains large?
questions.deliverable: A quantitative drift counterexample and the failed martingale hypothesis.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §§15.4–15.5

questions.title: Round predictable fractional choices online
questions.prompt: At each round an adaptive adversary offers x_t∈[0,1] and v_t∈[−1,1]^d before a bit B_t is chosen. For E_T=Σ_t(B_t−x_t)v_t, prove a randomized infinity bound √((T/2)ln(2d/η)) with failure η. Then construct a deterministic sign-choice potential achieving the corresponding positive-success threshold.
guide: Choose B_t conditionally Bernoulli(x_t). Each coordinate increment has mean zero and range length at most one, so its conditional MGF is at most e^{λ²/8}. Summing and union-bounding gives 2d e^{−2u²/T}.

Use a sum of positive and negative exponentials of coordinate errors. The x_t-weighted average of its two child potentials grows by at most e^{λ²/8}, so choose a child no larger than that average. Optimizing yields a deterministic final bound √((T/2)ln(2d)), valid against adaptive offered pairs.
questions.followup: Why does independent rounding with probability one half fail to preserve the same error center for arbitrary x_t?
questions.deliverable: A predictable-rounding theorem and an explicit deterministic potential rule.

questions.title: Compute exact small vector-game values
questions.prompt: For sign-vector games with d≤4 and T≤6, design an exact minimax solver and compare optimal Chooser play with the cosh-potential rule. State the recurrence, symmetry reductions and a reproducible tie-breaking convention. Require an explicit adversarial sequence whenever the greedy rule is suboptimal.
guide: With t rounds left and sum s, the value satisfies V_t(s)=max_{v∈{−1,1}^d}min_{ε∈{−1,1}}V_{t−1}(s+εv), with V_0(s)=||s||_∞. Memoize integer states.

Coordinate permutations and sign flips preserve the game, while v and −v give the same two choices. Verify d=1 and the all-sign-pattern lower bound as baselines. A greedy-versus-optimal gap must be witnessed by a complete branch strategy or checked recurrence values, not only a simulated random opponent.
questions.followup: How does the state space change for vectors with entries in {−1,0,1}?
questions.deliverable: A minimax specification, baseline results and certified greedy counterexamples if any.

questions.title: A square sign matrix forces square-root discrepancy
questions.prompt: For T=d=2^r construct the Sylvester sign matrix H recursively and prove H^TH=T I. Show that every sign vector ε has ||Hε||_∞≥√T. Explain why this is an offline lower bound and why it is weaker than the assigned online game's matching logarithmic lower bound.
guide: Start with H_1=(1) and form H_{2m}=[[H_m,H_m],[H_m,−H_m]]. Block multiplication proves orthogonal columns by induction.

For every ε∈{−1,1}^T, ||Hε||_2²=ε^T(TI)ε=T². With T coordinates, the maximum absolute coordinate is at least √T. Presenting H's columns in any order gives the same obstruction even to a chooser who sees the full matrix.
questions.followup: What property of an adaptive lower-bound strategy must go beyond this orthogonality argument?
questions.deliverable: A recursive matrix construction and a norm-based universal sign lower bound.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §§15.4–15.5

questions.title: Solve the sign-vector game in dimensions one and two
questions.prompt: For T-round games with vectors in {−1,1}^d, determine the exact value for d=1 and d=2. Prove that in dimension two the value is one for odd T and two for positive even T, with value zero at T=0. Supply both chooser invariants and a final-round adversary argument.
guide: In one dimension, choose signs to keep the running sum zero at even times and of magnitude one at odd times. In dimension two use U=(S_1+S_2)/2 and V=(S_1−S_2)/2: each offered direction changes exactly one of U,V by ±1, so keep each at zero or magnitude one.

At odd times exactly one of U,V is odd, giving infinity norm one; at even times the bound is two. For the even-time lower bound, immediately before the last move both original coordinates are odd. If their magnitudes are both one, Pusher offers the other diagonal direction so neither sign reaches zero; if a magnitude is larger, any final move leaves a magnitude at least two.
questions.followup: Why does this exact small-dimensional behavior differ greatly from a random-sign walk bound?
questions.deliverable: Exact values, deterministic invariants and matching adversary lower bounds.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §§15.4–15.5

questions.title: The exact intersection criterion for one-sided error balls
questions.prompt: For a fixed binary answer string x, let D_k(x)={z:z≥x coordinatewise, |z|−|x|≤k}. Prove D_k(x) and D_k(y) intersect exactly when both |supp(x)\supp(y)|≤k and |supp(y)\supp(x)|≤k. Give a two-bit example distinguishable with one one-sided lie but not one arbitrary lie.
guide: Any common received string must contain supp(x)∪supp(y). Thus it needs at least |supp(y)\supp(x)| additions from x and the reverse number from y. These necessary conditions are sufficient by taking their union as the received support.

For x=00,y=11,k=1, the directed balls are {00,01,10} and {11}, disjoint. Their ordinary Hamming distance is only two, so radius-one undirected balls overlap. This criterion is for nonadaptive fixed answer strings.
questions.followup: On a constant-weight layer, simplify the criterion to a Johnson-distance condition.
questions.deliverable: A necessary-and-sufficient intersection proof and an explicit coding separation.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §15.6

questions.title: Counting one-sided errors on a fixed weight layer
questions.prompt: Let every nonadaptive truthful answer string have weight w and allow at most k No→Yes changes, with 0≤k≤q−w. Prove that disjoint error sets require M C(q−w,k)≤C(q,w+k). Explain why this counts only the outer layer and is a necessary bound rather than a construction.
guide: Each weight-w codeword has exactly C(q−w,k) received strings in the weight-(w+k) layer obtained by adding k ones. Unique decoding requires these top-layer shadows to be disjoint across codewords.
There are C(q,w+k) strings in that layer, proving the count. Lower layers must also be disjoint, but this argument alone does not coordinate them or produce a family attaining the top-layer bound.
questions.followup: Compare this bound for w≈q/2,k=1 with the adaptive order 2^{q+1}/q.
questions.deliverable: A finite layer-count bound and an explicit comparison of its asymptotic strength.

questions.title: Count adaptive response strings by their first deviation
questions.prompt: Fix a deterministic adaptive question tree and one hidden item. Let its completely truthful path contain z No answers. Prove that with at most one No→Yes lie there are exactly z+1 possible reported answer strings, even though the questions after a lie may differ from those on the truthful path.
guide: There is one completely truthful response string. If a lie is used, the path agrees with the truthful path until its first deviation, which must occur at one of the z truthful No positions.

After that deviation the remaining answers are forced truthful along the new branch because no lie budget remains. Different first-deviation positions give distinct strings. This argument explains why the k=1 count survives adaptivity without replacing the entire tree by fixed codewords.
questions.followup: Construct a two-question adaptive example where using the truthful path's No count fails for k=2.
questions.deliverable: A bijection between possible first-lie positions and corrupted response strings.

questions.title: Improve the explicit error term in the k=1 upper bound
questions.prompt: Assume the standard k=1 counting inequality n≤2^q exp(−u²/(2q))+2^{q+1}/(q−u), for 0<u<q. Choose u=√(6q ln q) for sufficiently large q and derive A_1(q)≤(2^{q+1}/q)[1+O(√(ln q/q))]. Track both terms instead of only asserting an asymptotic equivalent.
guide: The first term becomes 2^q q^−3, which is smaller than 2^{q+1}/q by a relative factor 1/(2q²). The second term equals (2^{q+1}/q)/(1−u/q).
Since u/q=√(6ln q/q)→0, expand or bound 1/(1−x)≤1+2x for x≤1/2. This yields the displayed quantitative upper error. The premise is an established k=1 counting bound, not a uniform-in-k estimate.
questions.followup: How would a different constant in u affect the balance of the exponentially small and denominator terms?
questions.deliverable: An explicit parameter choice and a controlled relative-error calculation.

questions.title: An exact recursion respecting the direction of lies
questions.prompt: Let x_0 candidates have no lie remaining and x_1 have one No→Yes lie remaining. A membership question includes a_0 and a_1 of those candidates. Derive both observed-answer successor states and an exact minimax recursion. Explain why a No answer eliminates every candidate inside the question.
guide: For an observed No, truthful Yes cannot be changed, so only outside candidates survive: (x_0−a_0,x_1−a_1). For an observed Yes, inside candidates retain their budgets, while outside one-budget candidates consume their lie: (a_0+x_1−a_1,a_1).

Paul wins with q questions iff some allowed integer pair (a_0,a_1) has both successor states winning with q−1 questions. At q=0 the total candidate count must be at most one. Unlike the ordinary liar game, complementing a question does not simply swap these two successors without also reversing lie direction.
questions.followup: Extend the successor formulas to k remaining-budget classes.
questions.deliverable: A directional chip-state recurrence and its terminal condition.

questions.title: Expose the first point where a fixed-string argument fails
questions.prompt: Construct a depth-two adaptive question tree and one hidden item whose truthful answers are No,Yes, but whose possible reports with at most two No→Yes lies number three rather than Σ_{j≤2}C(1,j)=2. Enumerate the paths and formulate a correct state-based counting method for general k.
guide: Ask a first question excluding the item. After a reported No, ask a question containing it; after a reported Yes, ask a question excluding it. The truthful path is NY.

The possible reported strings are NY with no lie, YN with one lie, and YY with two lies. The second lie opportunity exists only after the first lie changes the branch. For general k count reachable tree states with a remaining budget and actual item membership, rather than directed Hamming balls around one fixed truthful string.

questions.title: Compare exact adaptive and nonadaptive half-liar capacities
questions.prompt: For q≤5 and one one-sided lie, design exact computations of adaptive capacity using the chip recursion and nonadaptive capacity using disjoint directed balls. Specify baseline cases, a maximum-independent-set formulation, and a checkable certificate for any claimed gap between capacities.
guide: Make a graph on all 2^q truthful strings, joining pairs whose directed radius-one balls intersect. A maximum independent set gives a nonadaptive code, with incompatibility decided by the two directed support differences.

Compute adaptive states by memoized minimax over (x_0,x_1,q). A nonadaptive lower certificate is a listed code; an adaptive lower certificate is a question tree. Upper certificates require a proved search exhaustion or branch-and-bound proof. Compare finite values with, but do not infer them from, the fixed-k asymptotic formula.

questions.title: A simple explicit code for any fixed lie budget
questions.prompt: For m independent binary identification bits, repeat each truthful membership answer k+1 times and allow at most k total No→Yes lies. Give a decoder identifying 2^m items in q=m(k+1) questions. Explain why the same block decoder can fail for two-direction lies.
guide: A truthful Yes block is all ones, since Yes cannot be changed. A truthful No block contains at least one zero because converting all k+1 positions would exceed the entire lie budget. Decode a block as Yes exactly when all its reports are Yes.

Thus all m original bits are recovered and the rate is 1/(k+1). This is a constructive baseline, much less efficient than the fixed-k asymptotic capacity but valid at every blocklength of this form. An arbitrary Yes→No flip would corrupt the all-ones test.
questions.followup: What minimum block length is required by this decoder when the total lie budget is k?

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §15.6

questions.title: Reversing the permitted lie direction preserves capacity
questions.prompt: Prove that a game permitting only No→Yes lies has the same adaptive capacity as a game permitting only Yes→No lies, by transforming queries and answers. Show with q=2,k=1 that either one-sided game can distinguish two items while the ordinary two-direction liar game cannot.
guide: Complement every queried subset and invert every reported bit. A truthful membership bit and a permitted upward corruption then become a truthful complement bit and a permitted downward corruption, preserving the number of lies and the question-tree structure.

For two items ask the same separating question twice; in the upward model only 00 can change and never to 11 with one lie, so the two items remain distinguishable. In the ordinary game a nonseparating first question gives no advantage. A separating answer leaves one candidate with one lie remaining and one with none, a one-question state of weight 3/2>1, which Carole wins.
questions.followup: Give the explicit two-step adaptive impossibility argument rather than relying only on a fixed-code distance claim.
questions.deliverable: A direction-reversal bijection and exact two-question examples.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §15.6

questions.title: The entropy deficit is a relative entropy
questions.prompt: For a joint law P of finite X_1,…,X_n, prove Σ_iH(X_i)−H(X_1,…,X_n)=D_2(P||∏_iP_i). Derive nonnegativity from the log-sum inequality and characterize equality, including zero-probability states.
guide: Expand the base-two log likelihood ratio under P. The joint term contributes −H(P); each marginal log term contributes +H(P_i). Whenever P(x)>0, each corresponding marginal mass is positive, so the product denominator is nonzero.

The log-sum inequality gives nonnegative relative entropy with equality exactly when P equals the product law on its whole support. Normalization then extends the equality to all states, giving mutual independence rather than merely pairwise independence.
questions.followup: Compute the deficit for a uniform parity class and explain why all pairwise projections can miss it.
questions.deliverable: An exact deficit identity and an equality proof that treats zero masses carefully.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §15.7 · basic inequalities

questions.title: Bound a binomial coefficient within a polynomial factor
questions.prompt: For 0<r<n and p=r/n, prove (n+1)^−1 2^{nH_2(p)}≤C(n,r)≤2^{nH_2(p)}. Derive the upper bound by entropy of a uniform r-subset, and the lower bound by locating a mode of Bin(n,p).
guide: A uniform r-subset has entropy log_2 C(n,r) and each coordinate has Bernoulli(p) entropy. Subadditivity gives the upper bound.

guide: One edge deletion is necessary and sufficient per K4 component, so the distance is n/4 edits, normalized as 1/(4n). A sampled induced subgraph is non-3-colorable exactly when it contains all four vertices of at least one component.

A union bound gives rejection at most (n/4) C(s,4)/C(n,4)=O(s^4/n³) for fixed s. The obstruction count is linear, while fixed dense-model farness requires quadratic edit distance; ε here shrinks with n.
questions.followup: What changes if each K4 vertex is replaced by a growing equal-size independent class?
questions.deliverable: An exact edit distance and a normalized sampling estimate.

questions.title: Triangle samples alone cannot test 3-colorability
questions.prompt: Construct the 11-vertex Mycielski graph of C5: retain cycle vertices v_i, add u_i adjacent to the two cycle neighbors of v_i, and add w adjacent to all u_i. Prove it is triangle-free and has chromatic number four. Explain why a tester checking only triangles targets the wrong obstruction family.
guide: The original C5 has no triangle, the u_i are mutually nonadjacent, w has no original-vertex neighbors, and a triangle involving one u_i would require its two cycle neighbors to be adjacent, which they are not. A 3-coloring of C5 extends to a 4-coloring by copying colors to u_i and using a new color at w.

If a 3-coloring of the full graph existed, let w have color three, so no u_i does. Replace each original vertex of color three by the color of its copy u_i. Adjacency of copies to neighbors preserves properness and yields a 2-coloring of C5, impossible.
questions.followup: Why does a single non-3-colorable finite example not by itself establish dense-model farness for large inputs?
questions.deliverable: An explicit adjacency description, two graph proofs and the testing implication.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §§17.1–17.2

questions.title: A maximal packing gives only a quadratic witness count
questions.prompt: Let τ(G) be the minimum edge deletions making G triangle-free and ν(G) the maximum number of edge-disjoint triangles. Prove ν≤τ≤3ν. Deduce ν≥εn²/3 for an ε-far graph and explain why this does not yet prove the removal lemma's δn³ triangle count.
guide: Every deletion set must meet every triangle of an edge-disjoint packing, requiring at least one distinct edge per packed triangle. Conversely remove all three edges of a maximal packing: any remaining triangle would be edge-disjoint from it and contradict maximality.

Thus ε-farness forces Ω(εn²) edge-disjoint triangles, but the removal conclusion is cubic in n for fixed ε. The extra abundance is precisely the structural content supplied by regularity or another proof of triangle removal.
questions.followup: Give a graph where τ=ν and discuss how close τ can be to 3ν.
questions.deliverable: Two deterministic inequalities and a clear accounting of the missing factor of n.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §17.3

questions.title: Prove a quantitative counting lemma for a regular triple
questions.prompt: Let A,B,C each have m vertices and all three cross-pairs be η-regular with densities at least d, where 0<η<min(d/2,1/4). Prove there are at least (1−2η)(d−η)^3m³ triangles with one vertex in each part. State the regularity thresholds used on each neighborhood.
guide: All but fewer than ηm vertices of A have at least (d−η)m neighbors in B, and the same holds for C; otherwise those exceptional vertices and the full opposite class violate regularity. At least (1−2η)m vertices are typical for both.

For each typical a, both neighborhoods have size at least (d−η)m≥ηm. Regularity of (B,C) therefore gives at least (d−η)|N_B(a)||N_C(a)| edges between them. Sum over typical a; each triangle is counted exactly once at its A vertex.
questions.followup: Which parts fail if one dense pair is not regular?
questions.deliverable: A full counting proof with every subset-size requirement checked.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §17.3

questions.title: Check the deletion budget and the resulting δ
questions.prompt: For 0<ε<1, assume an ε/4-regular equitable partition with exceptional set V_0, k between ⌈4/ε⌉ and T, and common class size c. Delete exceptional, internal, irregular-pair and density-below-ε/2 edges. Bound the four costs by εn²/4, εn²/8, εn²/4 and εn²/4, then derive the valid removal parameter δ=ε³/(512T³).
guide: The sum of the displayed costs is 7εn²/8<εn², so an ε-far graph retains a triangle. It lies across three distinct nonexceptional classes, each pair regular and of density at least ε/2.

At least c/2 vertices in one class have at least εc/4 neighbors in each other class. Every such vertex lies in at least (ε/4)^3c² triangles, and c³≥n³/(4T³) for the standard partition bounds. Multiplying yields ε³n³/(512T³). The regularity partition theorem is the explicitly assumed deep input.
questions.followup: How must n<T be handled when the displayed δn³ is below one?
questions.deliverable: A complete cost ledger and a factor-checked abundance constant.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §17.3

questions.title: A sampled triangle count can have constant mean and vanishing detection
questions.prompt: Let G have a hub joined to every vertex of K_{m,m}, so n=2m+1. For a uniform s-subset with s=⌊n^{1/3}⌋, compute the expected sampled triangle count asymptotically and show its chance of containing any triangle tends to zero. Identify why an expectation-only argument fails.
guide: Every triangle consists of the hub and one vertex from each side, so T=m². The expected sampled count is m² C(s,3)/C(n,3), tending to 1/4.

Every sampled triangle requires including the hub, an event of probability s/n=O(n^−2/3). Conditional on that rare event, many triangles can appear. The graph can be made triangle-free by deleting only m hub edges, so it is not a fixed-ε far input; removal-based detection is unaffected.
questions.followup: What second-moment or structural information would turn an expected count into a detection probability?
questions.deliverable: An exact expectation formula and a rare-hub upper bound on rejection.

questions.title: Full-support query noise destroys exact one-sided certification
questions.prompt: Suppose each adjacency answer is independently flipped with fixed probability θ∈(0,1/2), including repeated queries. Prove that no tester using an almost-sure finite bounded number of queries can both reject some far input with positive probability and accept every triangle-free graph with probability one. Contrast this with two-sided high-confidence testing.
guide: Fix internal random coins on a positive-measure set yielding some finite rejecting transcript on the far graph. Under the empty graph every finite response pattern has positive probability because both answers have nonzero noise probability, even with adaptive queries.

Therefore that rejecting behavior also has positive probability on a triangle-free input, contradicting exact one-sided acceptance. Repetition can make false rejection very small, but cannot make it exactly zero with a bounded finite number of full-support noisy observations.
questions.followup: What changes with a one-sided oracle noise model that never reports a nonexistent edge?
questions.deliverable: A transcript-support impossibility proof and a precise distinction between zero and small error.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §17.3

questions.title: Use triangle removal to force a cyclic arithmetic progression
questions.prompt: Assume triangle removal. For fixed α>0 and sufficiently large odd N, prove every A⊆Z_N of size at least αN contains distinct a,b,c with a+b=2c. Build a tripartite graph on three copies of Z_N using differences a,b and doubled c, and count its edge-disjoint trivial triangles under the contrary assumption.
guide: Put edges x–y when y−x∈A, y–z when z−y∈A, and x–z when (z−x)/2∈A; division by two is valid for odd N. Triangles correspond to a,b,c∈A with a+b=2c.

If only trivial progressions exist, triangles are (x,x+a,x+2a), totaling |A|N, and are edge-disjoint because each of their edge types identifies x,a uniquely. Thus at least |A|N≥αN² deletions are needed, making the 3N-vertex graph α/9-far. Removal forces Ω_α(N³) triangles, contradicting the O(N²) count for large N.
questions.followup: Explain why a nontrivial solution in an odd cyclic group has three distinct elements.
questions.deliverable: A complete graph reduction with all scale factors and the assumed removal input named.

questions.title: Derive a superpolynomial barrier from a supplied progression-free set
questions.prompt: Assume the deep construction that for arbitrarily large m there is A⊆[m] with no nontrivial three-term progression and |A|≥m e^{−C√ln m}. Thin A to a prescribed comparable size, embed it in Z_{4m+1}, and use the tripartite construction to show that no uniform triangle-removal lower bound δ(ε)≥cε^b can hold for fixed c,b>0.
guide: With N=4m+1 and s=|A|, only trivial cyclic progressions occur because a+b and 2c lie below N. The graph has n=3N vertices, exactly sN edge-disjoint triangles, and normalized deletion distance ε_m=s/(9N), attained by deleting all edges of one type.

Its triangle density is s/(27N²)=ε_m/(3N). Choose the thinning so ε_m→0 with ε_m bounded below by a constant times e^{−C√ln m}. For every fixed b, [ε_m/(3N)]/ε_m^b→0, since ln N dominates √ln m. The progression-free construction is assumed; the reduction and parameter comparison are the student's proof.
questions.followup: What query lower bound follows specifically for a tester that samples independent vertex triples?
questions.deliverable: A supplied-construction reduction and a quantified failure of every polynomial δ lower bound.

questions.title: Balanced blow-ups preserve triangle edit distance exactly
questions.prompt: Let H be a fixed graph and replace every vertex by an independent class of m vertices, every base edge by a complete bipartite block. Prove T(H^{(m)})=m³T(H) and τ(H^{(m)})=m²τ(H). For the lower bound use uniformly chosen representatives from all classes.
guide: Each triangle uses three distinct classes and corresponds to a unique base triangle, with m³ choices. Deleting every block corresponding to an optimal base deletion set proves the distance upper bound.

After any triangle-destroying deletion set D in the blow-up, choose one uniform representative per class. The surviving representative graph is triangle-free, so at least τ(H) base edges are missing. Its expected number of missing edges is |D|/m², forcing |D|≥m²τ(H).
questions.followup: Does the same representative proof extend to induced forbidden-pattern edit distance, where additions may also be needed?
questions.deliverable: Exact count and distance scaling with a randomized lower-bound certificate.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §17.3

questions.title: What raw triangle count alone can certify
questions.prompt: Let G have T triangles and maximum degree Δ≥2. Prove T/(Δ−1)≤τ(G)≤T, where τ is triangle-deletion distance, and compare these bounds with triangle removal. Give examples showing that Θ(n²) triangles can coexist with only O(n) required deletions.
guide: Each deleted edge destroys at most its number of common neighbors, at most Δ−1. Charging every original triangle to one deleted edge proves the lower bound. For the upper bound choose one edge from each original triangle and delete their union.

The hub over K_{m,m} has m² triangles but deletion of m hub edges suffices, illustrating the O(n) distance possibility. Removal runs in the opposite useful direction: fixed quadratic distance forces cubic abundance, whereas a raw count below that scale may permit concentrated, easily destroyed triangles.
questions.followup: Check both inequalities on disjoint triangles and on complete graphs.
questions.deliverable: Two incidence bounds and a quantitatively contrasting family.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §17.3

questions.title: A hereditary property that is not edge-monotone
questions.prompt: Prove that a graph has no induced three-vertex path P3 exactly when each connected component is a clique. Show this property is hereditary but not closed under edge deletion, using a three-vertex example. Describe the full edge/nonedge certificate for an induced P3.
guide: If a component is not complete, choose two nonadjacent vertices with a shortest connecting path. Its first three vertices form an induced P3, since a shortcut would contradict shortestness. Conversely a disjoint union of cliques has no such induced path.

Vertex deletion preserves the clique-component description. Deleting one edge from K3 produces P3 and violates the property, proving failure of edge monotonicity. The witness requires two present edges and the absent endpoint edge, not merely a two-edge subgraph.
questions.followup: What forbidden induced graph describes complements of these graphs?
questions.deliverable: A structural characterization and a minimal edge-deletion counterexample.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §17.4

questions.title: Derive a tester from a quantitative induced-removal input
questions.prompt: Assume that every ε-far graph contains at least δn^h unordered induced copies of some forbidden H with h≤h_0, where h_0,δ depend only on ε. Design a one-sided tester with failure η by sampling independent blocks of h_0 distinct vertices. Explain how to handle the unknown H and h within each block.
guide: Query every pair in a block and reject if it contains any forbidden induced graph of size at most h_0. Its first h sampled vertices form a uniform h-subset, which is an H-copy with probability at least δn^h/C(n,h)≥δ, under the assumed normalization.

Use r=⌈ln(1/η)/δ⌉ independent blocks, giving miss probability at most e^{−rδ}. All valid graphs have no forbidden induced witness and are always accepted. If n<h_0, inspect the full graph. The abundance assertion is the assumed deep input, not something proved by the sampling calculation.
questions.followup: How would labeled-copy normalization change the displayed per-block success estimate?
questions.deliverable: A tester, query budget O(rh_0²), and a factor-checked rejection bound.

questions.title: Unbounded minimal obstructions need not be far
questions.prompt: For the hereditary property of chordality, prove that each cycle C_ℓ, ℓ≥4, is a minimal forbidden induced graph: it is not chordal but every proper induced subgraph is chordal. Compute its exact edit distance to chordality and explain compatibility with an ε-dependent bounded-witness theorem.
guide: A chordless cycle of length at least four is nonchordal by definition. Every proper induced subgraph of a cycle is a disjoint union of paths, hence a forest and chordal.

Deleting one cycle edge makes a path, so the edit distance is exactly one, normalized as 1/ℓ². Thus arbitrarily large minimal obstructions exist, but their normalized distances tend to zero. A witness bound for fixed ε-far inputs does not bound all minimal forbidden graphs.
questions.followup: Why would a theorem bounding all minimal forbidden sizes be much stronger than testability?
questions.deliverable: A minimal-obstruction proof and an exact normalized-distance calculation.

questions.title: A concrete semi-hereditary property beyond hereditary ones
questions.prompt: For n≥2 let P mean 'triangle-free and containing at least one edge'; define its one-vertex case to be accepted. Show P is not hereditary, but is semi-hereditary with hereditary envelope H=triangle-free. Give an explicit M(ε) and derive a tester from triangle-freeness testing with a suitable accuracy adjustment.
guide: A graph with one edge and at least two isolated vertices belongs to P, but its induced two-isolate subgraph does not. P is contained in H. The only n≥2 graphs in H but outside P are edgeless, and adding one edge repairs them.

Therefore for n>1/√ε no H-graph is ε-far from P, establishing the semi-hereditary condition. More quantitatively d_P(G)≤d_H(G)+1, so for n²≥2/ε, ε-farness from P implies ε/2-farness from H. Treat smaller n exactly and invoke the triangle-free tester at ε/2 for larger n.
questions.followup: Why must a naive tester that checks P on every induced sample fail one-sided correctness?
questions.deliverable: A nonhereditary example, an explicit envelope threshold and a valid testing reduction.

questions.topic: Induced removal, hereditary properties and oblivious testing

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §17.4

questions.title: Complementation preserves induced testing structure
questions.prompt: For any hereditary property P, define its complement property by G∈P^c iff the complement graph lies in P. Prove heredity, equality of dense edit distances under complement, and a query-preserving transfer of one-sided testers. Identify the forbidden induced family for complements of disjoint unions of cliques.
guide: Complementation commutes with taking induced vertex sets and converts each edge addition into a deletion and each deletion into an addition. It is a bijection preserving the number of edited unordered pairs.

Simulate each query to the complement by inverting the original adjacency bit, so query complexity and one-sided correctness are preserved. Complements of cluster graphs are complete multipartite graphs; the forbidden induced P3 becomes its complement, an edge together with an isolated vertex.
questions.followup: Why does the corresponding statement for non-induced forbidden copies require additional care?
questions.deliverable: A structural, metric and algorithmic transfer proof with an explicit forbidden graph.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §17.4

questions.title: A uniform subquadratic envelope gives an oblivious tester
questions.prompt: Let P⊆H, where H is hereditary and has an oblivious one-sided tester. Assume every n-vertex H-graph is within g(n)=o(n²) edits of P, and P is decidable on every finite graph. Prove P is semi-hereditary and construct an oblivious one-sided tester, explicitly handling the sample-size cutoff without rejecting valid P-graphs for nonhereditary sample failures.
guide: Triangle inequality gives d_P(G)≤d_H(G)+g(n). Choose M so g(n)≤εn²/2 for n≥M. Then ε-farness from P implies ε/2-farness from H, and an H-graph cannot be ε-far from P for sufficiently large n.

Choose a fixed sample size Q larger than M and the H-tester's required size. If fewer than Q vertices are returned, the whole graph is known and P can be decided exactly. If Q are returned, use only the H-test on a uniform required subsample. At n=Q this is still sound by Q>M; do not apply P directly to large induced samples.
questions.followup: Which step uses uniform subquadratic closeness over all H-graphs rather than closeness on average?
questions.deliverable: A general envelope theorem and a fully specified oblivious testing construction.

references.title: Alon–Spencer · The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition · §17.4

questions.title: Recover abundance from a bounded-witness corollary plus a finite removal theorem
questions.prompt: Assume P is hereditary and every γ-far graph has a forbidden induced witness of size at most W_P(γ). Also assume the induced-removal theorem only for finite forbidden families. Prove these two inputs imply a quantitative abundance statement sufficient to test P. Distinguish the roles of the two deep inputs.
guide: Fix ε and let F consist of every non-P graph with at most W_P(ε/2) vertices; this is a finite isomorphism family. If G could be edited within fewer than εn²/2 steps to an induced-F-free G', the witness contrapositive would make G' less than ε/2-far from P.

The two edit paths would then make G less than ε-far from P, a contradiction. Therefore an ε-far G is ε/2-far from induced-F-freeness. Apply finite-family induced removal to obtain many copies of one member of F, then the elementary sampling lemma. The existence of one witness alone was insufficient; finite removal supplies abundance.
questions.followup: How are strict versus weak edit-distance thresholds handled by replacing ε/2 with ε/3?
questions.deliverable: A reduction from bounded witnesses to abundance with all dependencies on ε explicit.

questions.title: Present-edge observations cannot certify a cluster-graph obstruction
questions.prompt: A deterministic query transcript records only the edges observed present and ignores all nonedge answers. Prove that such a transcript can never certify failure of the cluster-graph property. Contrast it with a fully observed induced P3 and explain the consequence for one-sided tester design.
guide: Every collection of observed present edges can be completed to the complete graph on the same vertices, which is a single clique and satisfies the property. Therefore positive-edge observations alone never force a violation in all compatible completions.

An induced P3 fixes two edges present and the endpoint pair absent, and every graph with that induced triple fails the property. A one-sided tester needs a transcript incompatible with every valid input; for a nonmonotone hereditary property this can require nonedge information.
questions.followup: What analogous distinction arises between ordinary C4 copies and induced C4 copies inside K4?

questions.title: A semi-hereditary property cannot simply be checked on every sample
questions.prompt: For P='triangle-free with at least one edge' on n≥2, take a valid graph consisting of one edge and n−2 isolates. For fixed sample size s≥2 compute the chance that the induced sample fails P. Explain why rejecting whenever the sample fails P violates one-sided correctness, despite P being one-sided testable.
guide: The sample has an edge only if it contains both endpoints of the unique edge, with probability s(s−1)/[n(n−1)]. Every other sample is edgeless and hence fails P.

Thus naive rejection occurs with probability 1−s(s−1)/[n(n−1)], tending to one on valid inputs. A correct envelope-based tester checks the hereditary condition on large samples and reserves exact P-membership for input sizes known to be fully observed below its fixed cutoff.
questions.followup: Why is the analogous rule safe for a genuinely hereditary property?
questions.deliverable: An exact rejection probability and a corrected sample decision rule.

openProblems.title: P versus NP: distinguish a barrier from a proof
openProblems.prompt: Open question: does P equal NP? For a bounded seminar task, compare exact SAT, gap approximation and verification. Prove the conditional consequence of a polynomial-time SAT algorithm using NP-completeness. Then identify why a reduction or an integrality-gap example alone cannot establish P≠NP.
guide: The unrestricted P versus NP problem remains unsolved in the cited Clay Mathematics Institute entry. No solution is expected here.

The bounded task uses Cook–Levin and transitivity: a polynomial SAT algorithm gives a polynomial algorithm for every language in NP. A reduction transfers a known difficulty claim; an integrality gap obstructs a particular relaxation. Neither alone rules out every polynomial algorithm.

openProblems.title: P versus BPP: local derandomization versus universal simulation
openProblems.prompt: Open question: does BPP=P? As a bounded research exercise, prove that an efficiently computable generator with O(log m) seed length fooling every relevant polynomial-size circuit on m random bits, padded so m is at least the input length, to error below 1/6 derandomizes a bounded-error decision procedure.
